lessons.title: What Digital Signal Processing Is and Where It Lives
lessons.content:
Imagine you are on a video call with your nani in Rajshahi. She is sitting next to a ceiling fan that hums, a rickshaw bell rings outside, and a pressure cooker whistles in the kitchen. Yet on your phone her voice comes through clear, the echo of your own voice does not bounce back at you, and the call uses only a small slice of mobile data. None of that happened by luck. Inside both phones, tiny programs were doing arithmetic on long lists of numbers, thousands of times every second. That arithmetic is called digital signal processing, or DSP, and this course is about how it works.

What a signal is, again: In Signals and Systems you met the idea that a signal is any quantity that changes with time or space and carries information. Your voice is air pressure changing with time. An ECG is a tiny voltage from the heart changing with time. A photo is brightness changing across space. A stock price chart, the temperature in Dhaka every hour, and the vibration of a bridge are signals too. A system is anything that takes a signal in and gives a changed signal out, like an amplifier, a filter or a whole phone.

What makes it digital: A digital signal is a signal that has been turned into a list of numbers. We look at the signal at regular moments, called samples, and write down a number for each moment, rounded to a fixed number of bits. So a second of phone-quality voice becomes 8,000 numbers. Once a signal is a list of numbers, a computer, a phone chip or a microcontroller can process it with ordinary arithmetic: add, multiply, store, repeat. That is the whole secret of DSP: signals become numbers, and processing becomes arithmetic.

A tiny example of processing: Suppose a temperature sensor gives these readings every minute: 30, 34, 29, 31, 36, 30. The values jump around because of noise. A simple DSP trick is the 3-point moving average: each output is the average of the current and the two previous inputs. The first full output is (30 + 34 + 29) / 3 = 31, the next is (34 + 29 + 31) / 3 = 31.33, then (29 + 31 + 36) / 3 = 32, then (31 + 36 + 30) / 3 = 32.33. The new list is smoother. You just built a digital low-pass filter with one line of arithmetic: y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2]) / 3.

The DSP chain: Most real DSP systems follow the same chain. A sensor (microphone, electrode, camera, antenna) turns the physical quantity into a voltage. An analog anti-aliasing filter removes frequencies that are too high to be sampled safely. An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples the voltage and turns each sample into a binary number. A processor runs the DSP algorithm on those numbers. A digital-to-analog converter (DAC) turns the processed numbers back into a voltage, and a reconstruction filter smooths the steps into a clean analog signal for a speaker or a motor. Some systems skip the last part: a heart-rate app only needs the number on the screen.

Why not stay analog: Before digital chips were cheap, filters and equalizers were built from resistors, capacitors, inductors and op-amps. They worked, but every component has a tolerance, say plus or minus 5 percent, so two analog filters built from the same diagram never behave exactly the same. They drift with heat and age. To change the filter you must change the hardware. A digital filter is just a list of coefficients in memory. Copy it to a million phones and every phone behaves identically. Want a different filter? Upload new numbers. Digital also lets us do things that are nearly impossible in analog, like perfectly linear-phase filters, adaptive filters that learn, and storing a signal for years without losing quality.

The costs of digital: DSP is not free. Sampling loses information unless we sample fast enough, which is the sampling theorem of lesson 3. Rounding each sample to a fixed number of bits adds a small error called quantization noise, which is lesson 4. The ADC, DAC and processor cost money and power, and every algorithm has a delay because the processor needs some samples before it can compute. For very high frequencies, like the first stage of a radio receiver at gigahertz, analog circuits still do part of the job. Good engineers know both sides.

Where DSP lives, sound: Every phone call is DSP from end to end. The microphone signal is sampled, noise is reduced, echo of the loudspeaker is cancelled, the voice is compressed by a speech codec so it fits in a small bit rate, and the other phone decodes it. Music streaming uses audio codecs such as MP3 and AAC, which throw away sounds the ear cannot hear well. A Bluetooth speaker may run an equalizer to boost bass. Noise-cancelling earphones listen to outside noise and play its opposite.

Where DSP lives, pictures and video: An image is a 2D signal and a video is a 3D one (two space dimensions plus time). Your phone camera runs DSP to remove noise, sharpen edges, balance colour and combine several shots in night mode. JPEG compression is built on a transform closely related to the DFT. Face filters, QR code scanners and video calls all start with image processing, which is DSP in two dimensions.

Where DSP lives, communication: Wi-Fi, 4G and 5G use a method called OFDM, where the transmitter builds its signal with an inverse FFT and the receiver takes it apart with an FFT. The FFT is the star of lessons 15 and 16. Equalizers in the receiver undo the distortion of the channel, and error correction runs on top. Without fast DSP chips, mobile internet in a crowded place like Gulistan at rush hour would be impossible.

Where DSP lives, health and science: A hospital ECG machine samples the heart signal a few hundred times per second, removes the 50 Hz hum picked up from the mains wiring (Bangladesh mains is 50 Hz), removes slow baseline drift caused by breathing, and finds each heartbeat to compute heart rate. Ultrasound and MRI build images through heavy DSP. Seismologists detect earthquakes from noisy ground vibration; radar and sonar measure distance from echoes.

What Signals and Systems already gave you: You have already met continuous-time signals, the idea of linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, convolution, Fourier series and the Fourier transform, the Laplace transform, and a first look at sampling, the DTFT and the z-transform. We will recap each of these briefly when we need it. This course goes deeper on the discrete side: how to compute things exactly on a computer, by hand for small cases and with fast algorithms for big ones, and how to design filters that meet a specification.

The notation we will use: Continuous signals are written with round brackets, like x(t), where t is time in seconds. Discrete signals are written with square brackets, like x[n], where n is an integer sample index: 0, 1, 2 and so on. If we sample x(t) every T seconds we get x[n] = x(nT). The sampling frequency is fs = 1/T samples per second. With fs = 8,000 Hz, T = 0.125 ms, and sample number 8,000 happens exactly at t = 1 second. You will see x[n] in every lesson, so get comfortable with it now.

Numbers are frequencies too: One of the most powerful ideas in DSP is that every signal can be seen in two ways: as values over time, and as a mix of sine waves of different frequencies. The time view tells you what happened when. The frequency view tells you which pitches or rhythms are present. A 50 Hz hum is a single spike in the frequency view, which is why it is easy to remove once you look there. The DFT and FFT are the tools that move us from the time view to the frequency view on a computer.

Course map, part 1, foundations: Lessons 2 to 4 cover how a real signal becomes numbers: the ADC/DAC chain, the sampling theorem and aliasing, and quantization with its famous 6.02N + 1.76 dB rule. Lessons 5 to 9 cover discrete-time signals, system properties, convolution by hand, difference equations and the difference between FIR and IIR systems.

Course map, part 2, transforms: Lessons 10 to 14 are about the z-transform, its inverse, poles and zeros, frequency response and the DTFT. Lessons 15 to 18 are about the DFT, the FFT, circular convolution and using the DFT to look at real spectra.

Course map, part 3, filters and practice: Lessons 19 to 22 are filter design: specifications and linear phase, FIR design with windows, IIR design with the bilinear transform, and filter structures. Lesson 23 is multirate DSP (changing the sampling rate), lesson 24 is DSP hardware and fixed-point arithmetic, lesson 25 is a tour of applications, and lesson 26 is a capstone where you design a notch filter that removes 50 Hz hum from an ECG.

Real life example 1, a bKash customer care call: When you call a helpline, your voice is sampled at 8,000 samples per second. A noise suppressor estimates the background noise (traffic, a fan) and reduces it. An echo canceller learns how much of the agent's voice leaks from your speaker back into your microphone and subtracts it. A codec squeezes the speech into a low bit rate. At the call centre, the same steps happen in reverse. If any one of those steps were missing, you would hear yourself echo, or the call would need far more bandwidth.

Real life example 2, a fitness band: A cheap fitness band shines a green LED into your wrist and measures how much light comes back. Blood flow changes that amount slightly with each heartbeat, so the signal is a weak pulse buried in noise from arm movement. The band samples the light, filters out movement noise using the accelerometer as a reference, finds the peaks, and computes beats per minute. If the time between two peaks is 0.8 seconds, the heart rate is 60 / 0.8 = 75 beats per minute. All of this runs on a small chip from a coin-sized battery, which is only possible because DSP algorithms can be made very efficient.

Common mistakes: Students often think digital means perfect. It does not: sampling and quantization both introduce errors, and the goal is to make those errors small enough not to matter. Another mistake is mixing up x(t) and x[n], or forgetting that n has no unit while t has seconds. A third is thinking DSP is only about audio. It is about any signal: heartbeats, images, radio waves, sensor readings and even stock prices.

What exams ask from this chapter: Draw and explain the block diagram of a DSP system (sensor, anti-aliasing filter, ADC, processor, DAC, reconstruction filter). List advantages and disadvantages of DSP over analog processing. Name applications in different fields. Explain the difference between continuous-time, discrete-time and digital signals. These are short questions, but they appear in almost every DSP exam, so learn the block diagram well.

Recap: DSP turns signals into numbers and processes them with arithmetic. The chain is sensor, anti-aliasing filter, ADC, processor, DAC and reconstruction filter. Digital processing is repeatable, flexible and cheap to copy, but it pays with sampling limits, quantization noise, cost and delay. DSP runs inside phone calls, music, cameras, Wi-Fi, ECG machines and radar. In the next lesson we zoom into the first link of the chain: how an analog signal actually becomes digital.
key_points: A digital signal is a list of numbers x[n] taken at regular sampling instants and rounded to a fixed number of bits.
DSP means processing those numbers with arithmetic, for example a moving average y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2]) / 3.
The DSP chain: sensor, anti-aliasing filter, ADC, processor, DAC, reconstruction filter.
Digital beats analog in repeatability, flexibility, storage and special abilities like linear phase and adaptive filters.
Digital costs: sampling limits, quantization noise, hardware cost and power, and processing delay.
DSP lives in phone calls, music codecs, cameras, Wi-Fi/4G (OFDM with FFT), ECG machines, radar and seismology.
Every signal has a time view and a frequency view; the DFT/FFT moves between them on a computer.
This course goes deeper on the discrete side of Signals and Systems: z-transform, DFT, FFT, filter design and practice.
lessons.tip: Keep one notebook page called 'The DSP chain' with the six blocks drawn big. Every time a lesson adds something (sampling rate, bits, filter type), write it under the block it belongs to.
lessons.task: Take any 8 numbers that jump around, for example the daily high temperature for a week plus one, or your phone battery percentage every hour. Compute a 3-point moving average by hand and plot both lists on graph paper. Notice how the smoothed curve lags slightly behind the original.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of digital signal processing?
options: Building filters from resistors and capacitors
Turning a signal into numbers and processing it with arithmetic
Sending signals only through optical fiber
quiz.explain: DSP samples and quantizes a signal into a list of numbers, then processes it with operations like add, multiply and store.

quiz.q: In a typical DSP system, what comes right before the ADC?
quiz.explain: An analog anti-aliasing filter removes frequencies too high to be sampled safely, and only then does the ADC take samples.

quiz.q: The 3-point moving average of 30, 34, 29 is:
Which is NOT a true advantage of digital over analog processing?
options: Every copy of the filter behaves identically
Filters can be changed by loading new coefficients
Digital processing has no error of any kind
Signals can be stored without quality loss
quiz.explain: Digital processing still has sampling and quantization errors; the aim is to keep them small, not zero.

quiz.q: If the time between two heartbeats is 0.8 s, the heart rate is:
quiz.explain: Beats per minute = 60 / 0.8 = 75.

lessons.title: Analog vs Digital and the ADC/DAC Chain
lessons.content:
Think of a glass of water poured slowly from a jug. The water level rises smoothly; at every instant it has some exact height, like 3.14159 cm. Now imagine you are only allowed to look at the glass once every second, and you must write the height on a ruler marked only in whole millimetres. Your notebook will say 31 mm, 34 mm, 37 mm. That notebook is a digital version of the pouring. You lost some detail twice: between your looks, and between the ruler marks. This lesson is about exactly those two steps and the hardware that does them.

Two questions about any signal: To classify a signal, ask two separate questions. First, is time continuous or discrete? A continuous-time signal has a value at every instant t. A discrete-time signal only has values at separate instants n = 0, 1, 2 and so on. Second, is the amplitude continuous or discrete? Continuous amplitude means any real value is allowed. Discrete amplitude means only certain levels are allowed, like the millimetre marks.

Four combinations: Continuous time and continuous amplitude is an analog signal: the voltage from a microphone. Discrete time and continuous amplitude is a sampled signal: the output of a sample-and-hold circuit, where each sample can still be any value. Continuous time and discrete amplitude is rare in theory but appears in a DAC output staircase or a digital logic waveform. Discrete time and discrete amplitude is a digital signal: a list of integers stored in memory. A computer can only hold the last kind, so the ADC must do both steps: sampling (discretize time) and quantization (discretize amplitude).

Why computers need digital: A computer stores everything as bits. A bit pattern has a fixed size, so it can only represent a finite set of values. A memory chip also has a finite size, so we can only store a finite number of samples per second. That is why we cannot store a perfect analog waveform: it would need infinitely many samples, each with infinitely many digits. Digital signals give up perfection in exchange for something we can store, copy and compute.

Step 1, the anti-aliasing filter: Before sampling, the analog signal passes through a low-pass filter that removes frequencies above half the sampling rate. If it did not, high frequencies would fold down and pretend to be low frequencies after sampling, a problem called aliasing. A phone that samples voice at 8 kHz first limits the voice band to about 3.4 kHz. We work through aliasing with numbers in the next lesson; for now just remember that this filter is analog and must come before the ADC, because once aliasing happens it cannot be undone digitally.

Step 2, sample-and-hold: Converting a voltage to a number takes time, from nanoseconds to microseconds. If the input changes during that time, the result can be wrong. A sample-and-hold circuit solves this. In sample mode, a switch connects the input to a small capacitor, which charges to follow the input. At the sampling instant the switch opens, and the capacitor holds that voltage steady while the converter works. Then the switch closes again for the next sample. Think of it as taking a photo so the converter can study a still picture instead of a moving scene.

Step 3, quantization and coding: The ADC compares the held voltage against a set of levels and outputs the binary code of the nearest (or next lower) level. An N-bit ADC has 2^N levels. If the input range is 0 to Vref, the step size is Vref / 2^N. For example, an Arduino Uno style 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has 1,024 levels and a step of 5 / 1024 = 4.88 mV. A reading of 512 means about 512 x 4.88 mV = 2.5 V. The quantization error and its noise get a full lesson of their own (lesson 4).

Flash ADC: The fastest type. It uses 2^N - 1 comparators, each comparing the input with one reference level from a resistor ladder, all at the same time. The comparator outputs look like a thermometer (all ones below the input, zeros above), and an encoder turns that into binary. A 3-bit flash ADC needs 7 comparators; an 8-bit one needs 255. That count doubles with every extra bit, so flash ADCs are fast but power-hungry and limited to modest resolution. They are used in oscilloscopes and radar.

Successive approximation (SAR) ADC: The everyday workhorse in microcontrollers. It works like guessing a number with yes/no questions, a binary search. Worked example: 3-bit SAR, Vref = 8 V, so each step is 1 V; input 5.3 V. First guess the middle code 100 (4 V). Is 5.3 at least 4? Yes, keep the 1. Next try 110 (6 V). Is 5.3 at least 6? No, so that bit becomes 0. Next try 101 (5 V). Is 5.3 at least 5? Yes, keep it. Result: 101, which is 5. An N-bit SAR needs N comparison steps, one per bit, using only one comparator.

Sigma-delta ADC: The type inside most audio chips. It samples very fast with a very coarse quantizer (often just one bit), uses feedback to push the quantization noise up to high frequencies, then a digital filter removes that noise and reduces the sample rate. The result is high resolution, like 24 bits, at audio rates. It is a beautiful example of trading speed for precision, and it uses the multirate ideas of lesson 23.

Choosing an ADC, a quick sizing: Suppose you want to record heart sounds with a stethoscope microphone, with useful content up to about 1 kHz, and you want to see details as small as 1 mV on a 0 to 3.3 V range. Speed first: you need to sample faster than twice the highest frequency, so at least 2 kHz, and in practice a bit more, say 4 kHz, to leave room for the anti-aliasing filter. Resolution next: 3.3 V / 1 mV = 3,300 levels are needed. 2^11 = 2,048 is not enough, 2^12 = 4,096 is enough, so a 12-bit ADC fits. A cheap 12-bit SAR ADC inside a microcontroller can easily do 4 kHz, so you do not need a flash or an expensive audio chip.

Resolution is not accuracy: A 16-bit ADC prints 16 bits, but that does not mean all 16 are meaningful. Noise from the sensor, the amplifier, the power supply and the reference voltage can make the last few bits jump randomly. Datasheets therefore also quote the effective number of bits (ENOB), which is usually lower than the nominal resolution. Another real-world effect is timing jitter: if the sampling instants wobble slightly, a fast-changing signal is measured at the wrong moment, which adds noise too. Good layout, a clean clock and a stable reference matter as much as the number on the box.

The processor in the middle: Once samples are numbers, any processor can work on them: a general CPU, a microcontroller, a dedicated DSP chip, an FPGA, or a GPU. What matters is that the processor finishes the work for one sample before the next sample arrives, which is called real-time processing. At 48,000 samples per second, the processor has about 20.8 microseconds per sample. Lesson 24 looks at the hardware tricks that make this possible.

The DAC: A digital-to-analog converter goes the other way: it takes a binary code and outputs a proportional voltage. One classic design is the R-2R resistor ladder, where each bit switches a branch that contributes a binary-weighted current. With a 3-bit DAC and 1 V steps, code 101 gives 5 V and code 011 gives 3 V. Simple, but the output only changes at sample instants.

Zero-order hold and the staircase: Most DACs hold each output value constant until the next sample arrives. This is called a zero-order hold, and the output looks like a staircase. A staircase has sharp corners, and sharp corners contain high-frequency content: copies of the signal spectrum around fs, 2fs and so on. The hold also slightly reduces high frequencies inside the band, an effect called sinc droop, which some systems correct digitally.

The reconstruction filter: The last block is an analog low-pass filter after the DAC. It removes the staircase corners, keeping only frequencies below fs/2, so the speaker receives a smooth waveform. Because of this filter it is sometimes also called the anti-imaging filter. Oversampling DACs make its job easier, again using multirate tricks.

Advantages of the digital route, summarized: Exact repeatability, programmability, easy storage and transmission without degradation, error correction, very complex algorithms (adaptive filters, FFTs, speech recognition), and cheap mass production since the same chip runs different software. Disadvantages: limited bandwidth set by the sampling rate, quantization noise, added delay, cost and power of converters, and design complexity.

Real life example 1, recording a song in a Dhaka home studio: A singer sings into a condenser microphone. An audio interface on the desk contains a preamplifier, an anti-aliasing filter, and a sigma-delta ADC running at 48 kHz with 24 bits. The laptop software applies reverb, compression and equalization, all as arithmetic. To listen, the interface's DAC and reconstruction filter turn the numbers back into a voltage for the headphones. Every block in this lesson is sitting on that desk.

Real life example 2, a digital weighing scale at a bazar shop: A load cell turns the weight of a kilo of potatoes into a tiny voltage, a few millivolts. An amplifier boosts it, a filter removes noise, and an ADC samples it a few times per second. The microcontroller averages a few readings (a moving average again), subtracts the empty-pan offset, multiplies by a calibration constant, and shows 1.000 kg on the display. No DAC is needed here: the output is just a number.

Common mistakes: Students often say the ADC only samples. It samples and quantizes, two different steps with two different errors. Another mistake is putting the anti-aliasing filter after the ADC; aliasing has already happened by then. A third is thinking more bits always means a better system; bits only help if the analog noise of the sensor and amplifier is smaller than the step size.

What exams ask: Classify signals by time and amplitude. Draw the block diagram from sensor to speaker and explain each block. Explain the purpose of sample-and-hold. Compare flash, SAR and sigma-delta ADCs in terms of speed, resolution and hardware. Calculate the step size of an N-bit ADC, the number of comparators in a flash ADC, or trace a SAR conversion bit by bit like the 5.3 V example.

Recap: Digital signals are discrete in both time and amplitude. The ADC chain is anti-aliasing filter, sample-and-hold, quantizer and coder. Flash ADCs are fastest (2^N - 1 comparators), SAR ADCs do a binary search in N steps, sigma-delta ADCs trade speed for high resolution. On the way out, a DAC makes a staircase and a reconstruction filter smooths it. Next lesson: how fast must we sample, and what goes wrong if we do not?
key_points: Classify signals by two questions: is time continuous or discrete, and is amplitude continuous or discrete.
A digital signal is discrete in both time (sampling) and amplitude (quantization).
The anti-aliasing filter is analog and must come before the ADC; aliasing cannot be undone later.
Sample-and-hold freezes the input so the converter sees a steady voltage.
An N-bit ADC has 2^N levels and step size Vref / 2^N (10-bit, 5 V gives 4.88 mV).
Flash ADC uses 2^N - 1 comparators; SAR does a binary search in N steps; sigma-delta trades speed for resolution.
A DAC with zero-order hold makes a staircase; the reconstruction (anti-imaging) filter smooths it.
Real-time means finishing each sample's work before the next one arrives (about 20.8 microseconds at 48 kHz).
lessons.tip: When you meet a new ADC in a datasheet, write three numbers next to it: bits, input range and maximum sample rate. From those you can work out step size and the highest frequency it can handle.
lessons.task: Trace a 4-bit SAR conversion by hand with Vref = 16 V (1 V steps) for inputs 11.6 V and 3.2 V. Write each guess, the yes/no answer and the bit kept. Then check: the final codes should be 1011 and 0011.

quiz.q: A signal that is discrete in time but can take any amplitude value is:
quiz.explain: Sampling makes time discrete; until quantization, each sample can still be any real value.

quiz.q: How many comparators does a 3-bit flash ADC need?
quiz.explain: A flash ADC needs 2^N - 1 comparators: 2^3 - 1 = 7.

quiz.q: What is the step size of a 10-bit ADC with a 0 to 5 V range?
Why is a sample-and-hold circuit used?
options: To keep the input steady while the ADC converts
To increase the number of bits
quiz.explain: Conversion takes time; holding the voltage constant prevents errors from the input changing mid-conversion.

quiz.q: Which filter smooths the staircase output of a DAC?
quiz.explain: The analog low-pass reconstruction filter after the DAC removes the high-frequency images caused by the staircase.

lessons.title: The Sampling Theorem and Aliasing, Worked
lessons.content:
Have you ever watched a cricket highlight where the bowler's car wheels in the background seem to spin backwards, or a ceiling fan in a video that looks almost frozen? Nothing is wrong with the wheel or the fan. The camera only takes a fixed number of pictures per second, and between pictures the wheel turns by an amount that fools your eyes. That illusion has a name, aliasing, and it is the single most important danger in turning analog signals into digital ones. This lesson shows exactly when it happens, how to compute the fake frequency, and how engineers avoid it.

Sampling in one line: We sample a continuous signal x(t) every T seconds to get x[n] = x(nT). The sampling frequency is fs = 1/T. A sine wave of frequency f hertz becomes x[n] = cos(2 pi f n / fs). Notice that f and fs only appear together as the ratio f/fs. That ratio is all the samples know about. Two different analog frequencies that give the same ratio, up to whole turns of the circle, produce exactly the same samples.

The key worked example: Sample a 7 kHz cosine at fs = 10 kHz. The samples are cos(2 pi x 0.7 n). Now sample a 3 kHz cosine at the same rate: cos(2 pi x 0.3 n). Because 0.7 = 1 - 0.3, and cosine does not care about whole turns or about sign, cos(2 pi x 0.7 n) = cos(2 pi n - 2 pi x 0.3 n) = cos(2 pi x 0.3 n) for every integer n. The two lists of samples are identical. After sampling, nobody, not even a perfect computer, can tell whether the original was 7 kHz or 3 kHz. The 7 kHz tone has taken on an alias: it now pretends to be 3 kHz.

The alias formula: For a real tone of frequency f sampled at fs, the apparent frequency is fa = |f - k fs|, where k is the whole number that brings the result into the range 0 to fs/2. Worked: f = 7 kHz, fs = 10 kHz, k = 1 gives |7 - 10| = 3 kHz. f = 12 kHz, k = 1 gives |12 - 10| = 2 kHz. f = 26 kHz, k = 3 gives |26 - 30| = 4 kHz. f = 4 kHz is already below 5 kHz, so k = 0 and it stays 4 kHz. Only tones below fs/2 come out unchanged.

Folding picture: Draw a frequency line from 0 to fs/2, then imagine the line folding back and forth like a paper fan at every multiple of fs/2. With fs = 10 kHz, the folds are at 5, 10, 15, 20 kHz and so on. A tone at 7 kHz is 2 kHz past the fold at 5, so it lands 2 kHz before it: 3 kHz. A tone at 12 kHz goes past 10 (which folds back to 0) by 2 kHz, so it appears at 2 kHz. This is why fs/2 is also called the folding frequency.

A worked mix: Suppose x(t) = cos(2 pi 1000 t) + cos(2 pi 6000 t) + cos(2 pi 9500 t) is sampled at fs = 8 kHz, so the Nyquist frequency is 4 kHz. The 1 kHz tone is below 4 kHz and stays at 1 kHz. The 6 kHz tone is past the fold: |6 - 8| = 2 kHz. The 9.5 kHz tone: |9.5 - 8| = 1.5 kHz. So the digital signal looks like tones at 1, 1.5 and 2 kHz, and two of those are lies. If you then played this through a speaker, you would hear a chord that was never in the original. If instead fs were 20 kHz, the Nyquist frequency would be 10 kHz and all three tones would survive unchanged. The minimum safe choice is any fs above 2 x 9.5 = 19 kHz.

The digital frequency view: In DSP we often write a sampled sinusoid as cos(w n), where w = 2 pi f / fs is the digital frequency in radians per sample. Then the useful range is w from 0 to pi, which matches 0 to fs/2. Any w outside that range is equivalent to one inside it, because adding 2 pi to w does not change cos(w n) for integer n. Lesson 5 builds on this idea.

The sampling theorem: A signal whose highest frequency is fmax can be perfectly recovered from its samples if fs > 2 fmax. This is the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem. The minimum rate 2 fmax is called the Nyquist rate. Half the sampling rate, fs/2, is called the Nyquist frequency: the highest frequency a given system can represent. Do not mix them up: the Nyquist rate is a property of the signal; the Nyquist frequency is a property of the sampler.

Why strictly greater: Try sampling sin(2 pi x 5000 t) at exactly fs = 10 kHz. The samples are sin(pi n), which is 0 for every n. You captured nothing at all. With a cosine instead you would get +1, -1, +1, -1, but a cosine with a phase shift gives a smaller amplitude, so at exactly twice the frequency the amplitude and phase are ambiguous. That is why the theorem needs fs strictly greater than 2 fmax, and why real systems leave a margin.

What sampling does to the spectrum: In Signals and Systems you saw that sampling multiplies x(t) by a train of impulses, and in the frequency domain this makes copies of the original spectrum centred at 0, fs, 2fs, 3fs and so on. If the original spectrum fits inside minus fmax to plus fmax and fs > 2 fmax, the copies do not overlap, and an ideal low-pass filter can cut out the original. If fs is too small, the copies overlap, and the overlapping parts add together. That overlap is aliasing in the frequency picture: the tail of one copy lands inside the band of another.

Perfect reconstruction in theory: If the copies do not overlap, an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff fs/2 recovers x(t) exactly. In the time domain this is the same as placing a sinc function at every sample and adding them up, which is called sinc interpolation. Real systems cannot build an ideal filter because it would need to see the whole future, but a good reconstruction filter after the DAC comes close, as you saw in lesson 2.

The anti-aliasing filter: Real signals are rarely band-limited by nature. A microphone also picks up ultrasound, and electronic circuits produce high-frequency noise. Any energy above fs/2 will alias into the band. So before the ADC we place an analog low-pass filter that strongly attenuates everything above fs/2. Because no real filter has a vertical edge, the filter needs room: a transition band between the top of the useful band and fs/2.

Telephone voice: Classic telephone systems sample at 8 kHz, so the Nyquist frequency is 4 kHz. The voice band is limited to about 300 to 3,400 Hz. The gap from 3.4 kHz to 4 kHz is the room the anti-aliasing filter needs to roll off. That is also why phone voices sound slightly thin: the higher parts of speech, which help us tell s from f, are cut. Wideband voice calls (often called HD voice) sample at 16 kHz to keep more of those sounds.

CD audio at 44.1 kHz: Human hearing goes up to about 20 kHz in young people. CD audio samples at 44.1 kHz, so the Nyquist frequency is 22.05 kHz. That leaves a guard band of 2.05 kHz above 20 kHz for the anti-aliasing filter. Professional video and many audio systems use 48 kHz, giving a 24 kHz Nyquist frequency and a slightly roomier filter. Higher rates like 96 kHz are used in studios, mostly to make filtering and processing easier.

Oversampling: Sampling much faster than needed, for example at 4 or 64 times the Nyquist rate, pushes the copies of the spectrum far apart. Then a cheap, gentle analog filter is enough, and a sharp digital filter followed by rate reduction does the precise work. Sigma-delta ADCs from lesson 2 are built on this idea, and lesson 23 shows how the rate is lowered safely afterwards.

The wagon wheel, in numbers: Paint one mark on a wheel and film it at 24 frames per second. If the wheel turns 24 times per second, the mark is in the same place in every frame: the wheel looks frozen. If it turns 25 times per second, the mark moves 1/24 of a turn forward each frame: it looks like it turns slowly forward at 1 turn per second. If it turns 23 times per second, the mark moves 23/24 of a turn forward, which looks the same as 1/24 of a turn backward: the wheel seems to roll slowly backwards at 1 turn per second. Same formula: |23 - 24| = 1.

Real life example 1, a mobile tower and FM radio: An engineer at a telecom company in Dhaka wants to digitize a signal band 2 MHz wide. Sampling at 5 MHz gives a Nyquist frequency of 2.5 MHz, comfortably above 2 MHz. If a strong interference at 3 MHz sneaks through because the anti-aliasing filter is weak, it lands at |3 - 5| = 2 MHz, right at the top of the useful band. The interference cannot be removed digitally, because after sampling it is indistinguishable from a real 2 MHz signal. The fix must be a better analog filter before the ADC.

Real life example 2, a smartwatch step counter: Walking produces arm swings around 1 to 3 times per second, so the useful content is a few hertz. Sampling the accelerometer at 50 Hz is plenty: the Nyquist frequency is 25 Hz. But if the watch is used on a bus on a rough road in Old Dhaka, engine vibration at, say, 45 Hz would alias to |45 - 50| = 5 Hz, close to walking frequencies, and might be counted as steps. The accelerometer chip's built-in low-pass filter is what prevents this.

Common mistakes: Thinking that sampling at exactly 2 fmax is enough. Confusing Nyquist rate (2 fmax, signal property) with Nyquist frequency (fs/2, system property). Thinking a digital filter after the ADC can remove aliasing; it cannot, because the alias is already sitting inside the band. Forgetting to fold more than once for very high frequencies: use the formula with the right k, not just f - fs.

What exams ask: State the sampling theorem and define Nyquist rate. Given a signal like x(t) = 3cos(2 pi 1000 t) + 2cos(2 pi 4000 t), find the Nyquist rate (here 8 kHz). Given fs and a tone, find the alias frequency. Explain the purpose of the anti-aliasing filter and why there is a guard band. Sketch the spectrum after sampling with and without overlap.

Recap: Samples only know the ratio f/fs, so frequencies differing by whole multiples of fs, or mirrored around them, become identical after sampling. The apparent frequency is |f - k fs| folded into 0 to fs/2. To avoid aliasing, fs must be strictly greater than 2 fmax, and an analog anti-aliasing filter must remove anything above fs/2 before the ADC. Telephone uses 8 kHz, CD uses 44.1 kHz, and oversampling makes the filters easier. Next lesson: the second step of the ADC, quantization, and how many bits we need.
key_points: After sampling, a tone only shows the ratio f/fs; tones that differ by multiples of fs (or mirror around them) give identical samples.
Alias frequency: fa = |f - k fs| with k chosen so fa lies between 0 and fs/2 (7 kHz at 10 kHz looks like 3 kHz).
Sampling theorem: perfect recovery needs fs > 2 fmax; 2 fmax is the Nyquist rate, fs/2 is the Nyquist (folding) frequency.
Sampling at exactly 2 fmax can lose the signal (sin(pi n) = 0 for all n), so the inequality is strict.
Sampling creates spectrum copies at multiples of fs; overlap of copies is aliasing.
The analog anti-aliasing filter before the ADC is the only cure; a guard band gives it room to roll off.
Telephone: 8 kHz sampling, voice 300 to 3,400 Hz. CD: 44.1 kHz, Nyquist 22.05 kHz, guard band above 20 kHz.
Oversampling spreads the spectrum copies apart so cheap analog filters suffice.
lessons.tip: For every alias problem draw the folding line: mark 0, fs/2, fs, 3fs/2 and so on, zig-zag the line, and drop the tone onto it. It is faster and safer than memorising the formula.
lessons.task: With your phone camera at a normal video setting, film a running ceiling fan as you slowly change the regulator speed. Watch the playback for moments when the blades seem to stop or run backwards. Then, on paper, compute the alias frequencies of 9 kHz, 11 kHz, 18 kHz and 23 kHz for fs = 10 kHz (answers: 1, 1, 2 and 3 kHz).

quiz.q: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. At what frequency does it appear?
quiz.explain: fa = |7 - 10| = 3 kHz, which is inside 0 to fs/2 = 5 kHz.

quiz.q: What is the Nyquist rate of x(t) = 3cos(2 pi 1000 t) + 2cos(2 pi 4000 t)?
quiz.explain: The highest frequency is 4 kHz, so the Nyquist rate is 2 x 4 = 8 kHz.

quiz.q: Why must the anti-aliasing filter be placed before the ADC?
options: Because once aliasing happens, the alias is indistinguishable from a real in-band signal
Because the ADC cannot work without it
Because it increases the number of bits
quiz.explain: After sampling, the alias has the same samples as a genuine in-band tone, so no digital filter can separate them.

quiz.q: CD audio uses fs = 44.1 kHz. What is its Nyquist frequency?
quiz.explain: The Nyquist frequency is fs/2 = 44.1 / 2 = 22.05 kHz.

quiz.q: A wheel turning 23 times per second is filmed at 24 frames per second. What do you see?
options: It turns forward at 23 turns per second
It turns forward at 1 turn per second
It turns slowly backwards at 1 turn per second
quiz.explain: 23/24 of a turn forward per frame looks like 1/24 of a turn backward, so it seems to roll backwards at |23 - 24| = 1 turn per second.

lessons.title: Quantization, Bits and the 6.02N + 1.76 dB Rule
lessons.content:
Imagine paying for jhalmuri with only 5 taka coins. If the price is 23 taka, you either pay 20 or 25; you can never pay exactly 23. The shopkeeper loses or gains up to 2.5 taka every time. Now imagine you had 1 taka coins: the error drops to at most half a taka. Quantization is exactly this problem. After sampling, each sample has an exact real value, but the ADC can only store one of a fixed set of levels, like coins of one size. This lesson is about that rounding error: how big it is, how it behaves like noise, and how many bits are enough.

What quantization is: Quantization maps each sample value to the nearest of a finite set of allowed levels. With N bits we can label 2^N levels. If the ADC's full input range is R volts, the spacing between neighbouring levels, called the step size or quantization step, is delta = R / 2^N. A 3-bit ADC has 8 levels; a 16-bit ADC has 65,536.

A small worked quantizer: Take a 3-bit ADC with range minus 1 V to plus 1 V, so R = 2 V and delta = 2 / 8 = 0.25 V. The levels are -1.00, -0.75, -0.50, -0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 (eight levels in two's complement style). A sample of 0.30 V is rounded to the nearest level, 0.25 V, with error 0.05 V. A sample of -0.62 V goes to -0.50 V or -0.75 V; the nearer is -0.50 (distance 0.12) versus -0.75 (distance 0.13), so it becomes -0.50 V with error 0.12 V. Every in-range sample has an error of at most delta/2 = 0.125 V.

Clipping, the other error: In that same quantizer, a sample of 0.90 V has no level above 0.75 V, so it is stuck at 0.75 V with error 0.15 V, bigger than delta/2. Any input beyond the range is clipped, and clipping creates harsh distortion, the crackle you hear when someone shouts into a cheap microphone. So there are two kinds of quantization trouble: small granular error inside the range, and overload error outside it. Engineers keep some headroom so loud peaks do not clip.

Mid-tread and mid-rise: A quantizer that has a level exactly at 0, like the one above, is called mid-tread: silence stays exactly 0. A quantizer whose levels sit at plus and minus delta/2 around zero is called mid-rise: silence flickers between two small values. Most audio ADCs behave as mid-tread. The noise analysis below works the same for both.

Quantization error as noise: For a busy signal like speech or music, the error e[n] = xq[n] - x[n] jumps around unpredictably between minus delta/2 and plus delta/2. A standard model treats it as random noise, uniformly spread over that range, with average zero and independent of the signal. The power (mean square value) of a uniform variable over a width delta is delta^2 / 12. So the quantization noise power is delta^2 / 12. This is the number that every SNR formula is built on.

Deriving the famous rule, step 1: Take a full-scale sine wave A sin(w n) that just fills the range from minus A to plus A. Its power is A^2 / 2. The range is 2A, split into 2^N steps, so delta = 2A / 2^N. Noise power = delta^2 / 12 = 4A^2 / (12 x 4^N) = A^2 / (3 x 4^N).

Deriving the famous rule, step 2: The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio is signal power over noise power: SQNR = (A^2 / 2) / (A^2 / (3 x 4^N)) = 1.5 x 4^N. In decibels, SQNR = 10 log10(1.5) + N x 10 log10(4) = 1.76 + 6.02 N dB. So SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB. The A cancelled out, which tells us the result only depends on the number of bits, as long as the sine fills the range.

The rule in words: Every extra bit halves the step size, which cuts noise power by 4, which is 6.02 dB. So each bit buys about 6 dB of signal-to-noise ratio. That is the single most useful number in this lesson. A quick reminder about decibels: dB = 10 log10 of a power ratio, so 10 dB means 10 times the power, 20 dB means 100 times, and 60 dB means a million times. An SQNR of 98 dB means the signal power is about six billion times the noise power, which is why well-recorded 16-bit audio sounds silent between songs.

Worked values: For N = 8 bits, SQNR = 6.02 x 8 + 1.76 = 48.16 + 1.76 = 49.92 dB. For N = 12, SQNR = 72.24 + 1.76 = 74.00 dB. For N = 16 (CD audio), SQNR = 96.32 + 1.76 = 98.08 dB, about 98 dB. For N = 24 (studio audio), the formula gives 146.24 dB, though in practice the analog electronics are noisier than that, so real 24-bit converters do not reach it.

Worked in reverse: A sensor system needs at least 60 dB SQNR. Solve 6.02N + 1.76 >= 60: N >= (60 - 1.76) / 6.02 = 58.24 / 6.02 = 9.67. Bits come in whole numbers, so choose N = 10. A 10-bit ADC gives 6.02 x 10 + 1.76 = 61.96 dB, which meets the target.

When the signal is quiet: The formula assumes a full-scale sine. If your signal peaks at only one tenth of full scale, its amplitude is 20 dB lower, so the SQNR drops by 20 dB. A 16-bit system playing a passage 20 dB below full scale gets about 98.08 - 20 = 78.08 dB. Quiet signals effectively use fewer bits. That is why recording engineers set levels carefully: loud enough to use the bits, but not so loud that peaks clip.

Where the noise sits in frequency: Under the noise model, quantization noise is white: its power delta^2 / 12 is spread evenly over all frequencies from 0 to fs/2. Now a neat trick appears. If you sample twice as fast as needed and then low-pass filter down to the useful band, you throw away half of the noise power, a gain of about 3 dB. Sampling 4 times faster gains about 6 dB, which is worth one bit. Plain oversampling therefore buys resolution slowly, half a bit per doubling. Sigma-delta converters do much better by also shaping the noise, pushing most of it to high frequencies before the filter removes it.

Quantization you can see: Images are quantized too. A normal grayscale photo uses 8 bits per pixel, so 256 shades from black to white. If you reduce it to 3 bits, only 8 shades remain, and smooth areas like a sky or a face break into visible bands with sharp edges between them, an effect called banding or posterization. That is quantization error you can see with your eyes. Adding a little random noise before reducing the bits, the same dither idea from audio, hides the bands and makes the picture look smoother, even though it is technically noisier. Many photo apps and printers use exactly this trick.

Bit rate and storage: An uncompressed (PCM) digital signal needs bit rate = fs x N x channels. CD audio: 44,100 x 16 x 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second, about 1.41 Mbps. One minute is 1,411,200 x 60 / 8 = 10,584,000 bytes, about 10.6 MB. Classic digital telephone (G.711 PCM): 8,000 x 8 x 1 = 64,000 bits per second, the famous 64 kbps channel. This is why compression codecs like MP3, AAC and modern speech codecs exist: they shrink those numbers many times while keeping the sound acceptable.

Non-uniform quantization: Speech has many quiet parts and a few loud ones. A uniform quantizer wastes levels on loud values that are rare and gives quiet sounds poor SNR. Telephone systems therefore compress the signal logarithmically before uniform quantization, so small amplitudes get fine steps and large amplitudes get coarse steps. The two standards are mu-law, used in North America and Japan, and A-law, used in Europe and many other regions. Both fit good-quality telephone speech into 8 bits per sample.

Dither: For very quiet signals, quantization error stops being noise-like and follows the signal, producing an ugly distortion pattern. A surprising fix is to add a tiny amount of random noise, called dither, before quantizing. The error becomes random again and sounds like gentle hiss instead of harsh distortion. Audio engineers often add dither when reducing 24-bit studio recordings to 16-bit for release.

Real life example 1, a Bangladeshi FM station going online: A radio station in Chattogram streams its show on the internet. In the studio, the mixer uses 24-bit, 48 kHz audio for headroom and editing. For the stream, the audio is encoded with a compressed codec at perhaps 128 kbps, far below the 1.5 Mbps that raw 16-bit stereo at 48 kHz would need (48,000 x 16 x 2 = 1,536,000 bps). The engineers keep peaks below full scale to avoid clipping and accept that the quietest moments use fewer effective bits.

Real life example 2, a water-level sensor on the Jamuna: A flood-warning station measures river level with a pressure sensor giving 0 to 3.3 V for 0 to 10 m of water. With a 10-bit ADC, delta = 3.3 / 1024 = 3.2 mV, which corresponds to 10 m / 1024 = about 9.8 mm of water per step. With a 12-bit ADC the step becomes 10 m / 4096 = about 2.4 mm. For flood warning, centimetre accuracy is enough, so 10 bits is fine and saves cost and power.

Common mistakes: Using 20 log instead of 10 log when the ratio is of powers (SQNR is a power ratio, so 10 log10). Forgetting the 1.76 dB term, or using the formula for signals that are not full-scale sines. Thinking quantization noise can be removed by filtering afterwards; it is spread across the whole band, so only part of it can be removed, and only by trading away bandwidth. Confusing clipping with granular quantization error.

What exams ask: Derive SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sinusoid. Compute SQNR for given N, or the bits needed for a target SQNR. Find step size and maximum error for an N-bit ADC with a given range. Compute PCM bit rate. Explain uniform vs non-uniform quantization, companding (mu-law and A-law), and dither.

Recap: Quantization rounds each sample to one of 2^N levels with step delta = R / 2^N. In-range error is at most delta/2 and behaves like noise with power delta^2 / 12. For a full-scale sine, SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB: about 6 dB per bit, 98 dB for 16 bits. Quiet signals lose SNR, loud ones clip. Bit rate = fs x N x channels (CD 1,411,200 bps, phone 64 kbps). Next lesson: working with the numbers themselves, discrete-time signals and their operations.
key_points: Quantization rounds each sample to one of 2^N levels; step size delta = range / 2^N.
In-range error is at most delta/2; out-of-range inputs clip and cause harsh distortion.
Modelled as uniform noise, quantization noise power is delta^2 / 12.
For a full-scale sine, SQNR = 1.5 x 4^N, i.e. 6.02N + 1.76 dB: about 6 dB per extra bit.
Worked: 8 bits 49.92 dB, 12 bits 74.00 dB, 16 bits 98.08 dB; 60 dB needs N = 10.
A signal 20 dB below full scale loses 20 dB of SQNR, so levels must be set with care.
PCM bit rate = fs x N x channels: CD 1,411,200 bps, telephone 64 kbps.
mu-law/A-law companding gives quiet speech finer steps; dither turns low-level distortion into gentle noise.
lessons.tip: Remember just two anchors: 6 dB per bit and 16 bits is about 98 dB. With those you can sanity-check almost any quantization answer in your head.
lessons.task: Choose three ADCs: 8-bit, 10-bit and 14-bit. For each, compute the step size over a 0 to 5 V range and the SQNR with 6.02N + 1.76. Then compute how many megabytes one hour of mono audio at 16 kHz would take with each (no compression).

quiz.q: What is the SQNR of a 16-bit quantizer for a full-scale sine?
Adding one more bit to a quantizer improves SQNR by about:
quiz.explain: One more bit halves the step, cutting noise power by 4, which is 10 log10(4) = 6.02 dB.

quiz.q: A 3-bit ADC covers minus 1 V to plus 1 V. What is its step size?
What is the uncompressed bit rate of CD audio?
quiz.explain: 44,100 samples/s x 16 bits x 2 channels = 1,411,200 bps.

quiz.q: What is the power of quantization noise when the error is uniform over a width delta?
quiz.explain: A uniform variable over width delta has mean square value delta^2 / 12.

lessons.title: Discrete-Time Signals and Their Operations
lessons.content:
Think of the scoreboard of a T20 match. After every over, the total runs are written down: 8, 15, 21, 34 and so on. Nobody records the score at 3.7 overs; the list only has values at whole overs. That list is a discrete-time signal: a sequence of numbers indexed by whole numbers. In DSP, every signal inside the computer looks like this. Before we can build filters and transforms, we need to be fluent with these sequences: the basic building blocks, how to shift and flip them, and how to measure their size.

How we write a sequence: A discrete-time signal is written x[n], where n is an integer. The value x[n] is defined only at integer n; between them, the signal is not zero, it simply does not exist. A short sequence is often written as a list with an arrow or a mark under the n = 0 entry, for example x[n] = {1, 2, 3} with 1 at n = 0. Plots use stems: a vertical line from the axis to a dot at each integer. In these lessons we will say which value sits at n = 0 in words.

The unit impulse: The simplest sequence is the unit impulse, delta[n], which is 1 at n = 0 and 0 everywhere else. It is the discrete version of a single click. Unlike the continuous delta function, which is an infinitely tall spike with area 1, the discrete impulse is perfectly ordinary: just a 1 among zeros. A shifted impulse delta[n - k] is 1 at n = k.

The unit step: The unit step u[n] is 1 for n >= 0 and 0 for n < 0. It models a switch turned on at time 0. Impulse and step are tied together: delta[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1] (the step minus the step delayed by one leaves a single 1 at n = 0), and u[n] = sum of delta[k] for k from minus infinity to n (adding up impulses gives the step). These are discrete versions of derivative and integral, called the first difference and the running sum.

The ramp: The unit ramp is r[n] = n u[n]: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on for n >= 0. It is the running sum of a delayed step: r[n] = sum of u[k - 1] for k up to n. Ramps model steadily growing quantities, like the number of SMS messages sent if you send one per minute.

Real exponentials: x[n] = a^n u[n]. If 0 < a < 1 it decays: with a = 0.5 the values are 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125. If a > 1 it grows: with a = 2 the values are 1, 2, 4, 8. If -1 < a < 0 it alternates sign while decaying: with a = -0.5 the values are 1, -0.5, 0.25, -0.125. These sequences will appear again and again, because they are exactly the impulse responses of simple recursive filters (lesson 8) and the building blocks of inverse z-transforms (lesson 11).

Sinusoids and digital frequency: A discrete sinusoid is x[n] = A cos(w0 n + phi). Here w0 is the digital frequency in radians per sample. When the sinusoid comes from sampling an analog tone of f hertz at fs samples per second, w0 = 2 pi f / fs. Worked: f = 1,000 Hz, fs = 8,000 Hz gives w0 = 2 pi x 1000 / 8000 = pi / 4. Since one full cycle is 2 pi radians, that is 2 pi / (pi/4) = 8 samples per cycle, which matches 8,000 / 1,000 = 8.

The unique range of digital frequency: Because n is an integer, cos((w0 + 2 pi) n) = cos(w0 n + 2 pi n) = cos(w0 n). So digital frequencies that differ by 2 pi are the same signal. All distinct sinusoids live in a range of width 2 pi, usually taken as minus pi to pi. The highest possible oscillation is at w0 = pi, which gives cos(pi n) = 1, -1, 1, -1: the sequence flips every sample. Low frequencies are near 0 (and near 2 pi), high frequencies are near pi. This is the same aliasing you met in lesson 3, seen from the digital side.

When a discrete sinusoid is periodic: A sequence is periodic with period N if x[n + N] = x[n] for all n, with N a positive integer. For cos(w0 n) this needs w0 N to be a whole multiple of 2 pi, i.e. w0 / (2 pi) = k / N must be a rational number. Worked: cos(pi n / 4): w0 / (2 pi) = 1/8, so N = 8. cos(3 pi n / 8): w0 / (2 pi) = 3/16, so N = 16 (the pattern repeats after 16 samples, during which 3 full cycles of the underlying wave pass). cos(0.5 n): w0 / (2 pi) = 0.5 / (2 pi) = 1 / (4 pi), which is irrational, so this sequence is not periodic at all, even though the continuous cos(0.5 t) is. That surprises many students.

Complex exponentials: The sequence e^(j w0 n) = cos(w0 n) + j sin(w0 n) is a point moving around the unit circle by w0 radians per sample. It is the most important signal in DSP because LTI systems only scale and rotate it, never change its shape. The DTFT, DFT and frequency response are all built from it.

Time shift: y[n] = x[n - k] delays x by k samples (moves the plot right) when k > 0, and advances it (moves left) when k < 0. Worked: x[n] = {1, 2, 3} with 1 at n = 0. Then x[n - 2] has 1 at n = 2, 2 at n = 3 and 3 at n = 4. In a real-time system, a delay is easy (store old samples) but an advance needs future samples, which is why advances only appear in offline processing.

Time reversal (folding): y[n] = x[-n] mirrors the sequence around n = 0. With the same x, x[-n] has 1 at n = 0, 2 at n = -1 and 3 at n = -2. Folding is a key step in convolution (lesson 7), so practise it.

Combining shift and fold: To get x[2 - n], write it as x[-(n - 2)]: first fold, then shift right by 2. Check directly: at n = 2, x[0] = 1; at n = 1, x[1] = 2; at n = 0, x[2] = 3. So x[2 - n] has values 3, 2, 1 at n = 0, 1, 2. The safest method in exams is always to substitute a few values of n and read off x, rather than guess the order of operations.

Time scaling: downsampling and upsampling: In discrete time, y[n] = x[2n] keeps every second sample (n = 0 takes x[0], n = 1 takes x[2], n = 2 takes x[4]) and throws the rest away. This is called downsampling or decimation by 2, and information can be lost. The opposite, upsampling by 2, inserts a zero between samples: {1, 2, 3} becomes {1, 0, 2, 0, 3}. These are the raw operations of multirate DSP in lesson 23.

Amplitude operations: Scaling y[n] = c x[n] multiplies every sample by c, like a volume knob. Adding two sequences adds them sample by sample, like mixing two microphones. Multiplying sample by sample, y[n] = x1[n] x2[n], is used for windowing (lesson 18) and modulation. All of these are simple loops in code.

Energy and power: The energy of a sequence is E = sum of |x[n]|^2 over all n. Worked: {1, 2, 3} has E = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. For x[n] = 0.5^n u[n], E = 1 + 0.25 + 0.0625 + ... = 1 / (1 - 0.25) = 4/3, a geometric series. A signal with finite energy is an energy signal. Signals that go on forever, like u[n] or a sinusoid, have infinite energy but finite average power P = limit of (1 / (2N + 1)) x sum of |x[n]|^2 from -N to N. For u[n], P = 1/2; for a sinusoid of amplitude A (not at w0 = 0 or pi), P = A^2 / 2. These are power signals.

Even and odd parts: Any sequence splits as x[n] = xe[n] + xo[n], where xe[n] = (x[n] + x[-n]) / 2 is even (symmetric) and xo[n] = (x[n] - x[-n]) / 2 is odd (anti-symmetric). Worked with x = {1, 2, 3} at n = 0, 1, 2: xe has values 1.5, 1, 1, 1, 1.5 at n = -2 to 2, and xo has values -1.5, -1, 0, 1, 1.5. Check at n = 2: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3, correct; at n = -2: 1.5 - 1.5 = 0, correct.

Every sequence is a sum of impulses: Any sequence can be written as x[n] = sum over k of x[k] delta[n - k]. For {1, 2, 3}: x[n] = 1 delta[n] + 2 delta[n - 1] + 3 delta[n - 2]. This looks trivial but it is the doorway to convolution: if we know what a system does to one impulse, we know what it does to everything.

Real life example 1, Dhaka air quality: An air quality monitor records PM2.5 every hour, giving a sequence x[n]. The hourly change d[n] = x[n] - x[n - 1] is a first difference that highlights sudden pollution spikes, like when brick kilns start or traffic peaks. A 24-sample running sum gives the daily total exposure. Both are operations from this lesson.

Real life example 2, reversing a voice note for fun: Apps that play your voice backwards simply compute y[n] = x[N - 1 - n] for a recording of N samples, which is fold plus shift. Speeding a song to double speed without care is x[2n], downsampling, which raises the pitch and can cause aliasing unless filtered first.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Shifting the wrong way (x[n - 2] moves right, not left). Doing fold and shift in the wrong order. Assuming every discrete sinusoid is periodic. Forgetting that digital frequency repeats every 2 pi. Exams ask you to sketch x[2 - n], x[2n] or x[n] u[1 - n], test periodicity and find N, compute energy or power, and split a sequence into even and odd parts.

Recap: Discrete signals are sequences x[n] defined at integer n. The building blocks are impulse, step, ramp, exponentials and sinusoids, with w0 = 2 pi f / fs and distinct frequencies only in a 2 pi range. A discrete sinusoid is periodic only if w0 / (2 pi) is rational. Shift, fold, downsample and upsample move samples around; energy and power measure size; even and odd parts split any signal. Next lesson: discrete-time systems and their properties.
key_points: A discrete-time signal x[n] exists only at integer n; plot it with stems.
delta[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1] and u[n] is the running sum of delta[n]; r[n] = n u[n].
a^n u[n] decays for |a| < 1, grows for |a| > 1, alternates for negative a.
Digital frequency w0 = 2 pi f / fs; frequencies 2 pi apart are identical; w0 = pi is the fastest oscillation.
cos(w0 n) is periodic only if w0 / (2 pi) = k/N is rational (cos(0.5 n) is not periodic).
x[n - k] delays (moves right); x[-n] folds; x[2 - n] = fold then shift right by 2; check by substituting n.
Energy E = sum |x[n]|^2 ({1,2,3} gives 14, 0.5^n u[n] gives 4/3); u[n] and sinusoids are power signals.
Any x[n] = sum x[k] delta[n - k], and any x[n] = even part + odd part.
lessons.tip: For any shift-and-fold question, make a small table with n in one row and the argument (like 2 - n) in the next, then read the value of x. It never lets you down, even when the expression looks scary.

quiz.q: What is the digital frequency of a 1 kHz tone sampled at 8 kHz?
quiz.explain: w0 = 2 pi f / fs = 2 pi x 1000 / 8000 = pi / 4 radians per sample.

quiz.q: Which sequence is NOT periodic?
quiz.explain: 0.5 / (2 pi) is irrational, so no integer N makes 0.5 N a multiple of 2 pi.

quiz.q: If x[n] = {1, 2, 3} with 1 at n = 0, what is x[2 - n] at n = 0?
What is the energy of x[n] = 0.5^n u[n]?
Which relation between impulse and step is correct?

lessons.title: Discrete-Time Systems and Their Properties
lessons.content:
Imagine your bKash balance. Every day some money comes in or goes out; that daily amount is the input x[n]. Your balance y[n] is yesterday's balance plus today's change: y[n] = y[n - 1] + x[n]. That is a discrete-time system: a rule that takes one sequence and produces another. Before designing filters, engineers ask a few yes/no questions about any system: does it remember the past, does it need the future, does it obey superposition, does it behave the same tomorrow as today, can it blow up? This lesson teaches you to answer each question with a quick, reliable test.

What a system is: A discrete-time system is a rule T that maps an input sequence x[n] to an output sequence y[n] = T{x[n]}. The rule can be a formula, a program or a circuit. Some examples we will test throughout: an amplifier y[n] = 2x[n]; a delay y[n] = x[n - 1]; a 3-point moving average y[n] = (x[n] + x[n - 1] + x[n - 2]) / 3; the accumulator y[n] = sum of x[k] for k up to n; a squarer y[n] = x[n]^2; an offset amplifier y[n] = 2x[n] + 3; a time-varying gain y[n] = n x[n]; an advance y[n] = x[n + 1]; and a downsampler y[n] = x[2n].

Property 1, memory: A system is memoryless (static) if y[n] depends only on x[n] at the same n. The amplifier, the squarer and the offset amplifier are memoryless. The delay, moving average and accumulator have memory: they need stored past values. In code, a memoryless system needs no variables that survive between samples; a system with memory needs a buffer.

Property 2, causality: A system is causal if y[n] depends only on the present and past inputs, never on future ones. Real-time systems must be causal because the future has not arrived yet. Test: look for any input index larger than n. y[n] = x[n + 1] is non-causal. y[n] = x[2n] is non-causal too: y[1] = x[2], which is in the future at time 1. y[n] = x[-n] is non-causal: y[-1] = x[1]. The moving average and accumulator are causal. Non-causal systems are fine offline, for example when you edit a recorded audio file and can look ahead.

Property 3, linearity: A system is linear if it obeys superposition: for any inputs x1, x2 and any constants a, b, T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2}. This combines additivity (sum in gives sum out) and homogeneity (scaled input gives scaled output). A quick first check: a linear system must give zero output for zero input. If that fails, stop: the system is not linear.

Linearity tests, worked: The offset amplifier y = 2x + 3 gives output 3 for zero input, so it is not linear (engineers call it affine or incrementally linear). The squarer: input x gives x^2, input 2x gives 4x^2, not 2x^2, so it fails homogeneity and is not linear. The time-varying gain y = n x[n]: T{a x1 + b x2} = n(a x1[n] + b x2[n]) = a n x1[n] + b n x2[n], so it is linear. The moving average and accumulator are linear because they only add and scale inputs. The downsampler x[2n] is linear too: it only picks samples.

Property 4, time invariance: A system is time-invariant if a delay in the input causes the same delay in the output and nothing else. Test in two lines. Line one: feed the delayed input x[n - k] and write the output, call it y1[n]. Line two: take the original output and delay it, y[n - k]. If y1[n] = y[n - k] for every x and k, the system is time-invariant.

Time invariance tests, worked: For y[n] = n x[n], line one gives y1[n] = n x[n - k]. Line two gives y[n - k] = (n - k) x[n - k]. These differ, so the system is time-variant: the gain depends on the clock. For y[n] = x[2n], line one: y1[n] = x[2n - k]. Line two: y[n - k] = x[2(n - k)] = x[2n - 2k]. Different, so time-variant. A concrete check: input delta[n] gives output delta[n] (only n = 0 picks x[0] = 1). Input delta[n - 1] gives y[n] = delta[2n - 1], which is zero for every integer n because 2n - 1 is never 0. The delayed input produced no output at all, not a delayed copy. For the moving average, both lines give (x[n - k] + x[n - k - 1] + x[n - k - 2]) / 3, so it is time-invariant.

Property 5, stability (BIBO): A system is bounded-input bounded-output stable if every bounded input (all |x[n]| <= some finite Mx) produces a bounded output. To prove instability, one bounded input with an unbounded output is enough. The accumulator with input u[n] gives y[n] = n + 1 for n >= 0, which grows forever: unstable. The gain y = n x[n] with input u[n] gives n, also unbounded: unstable. The moving average output is at most the largest input: stable. The squarer: if |x| <= Mx then |y| <= Mx^2: stable, even though it is non-linear.

Property 6, invertibility: A system is invertible if distinct inputs always give distinct outputs, so the input can be recovered. y = 2x is invertible: x = y / 2. The accumulator is invertible: its inverse is the first difference x[n] = y[n] - y[n - 1]. The squarer is not: inputs 3 and -3 both give 9. The downsampler is not: it throws away every odd sample, and many different inputs give the same output.

A summary table in words: Amplifier 2x: memoryless, causal, linear, time-invariant, stable, invertible. Offset 2x + 3: memoryless, causal, not linear, time-invariant, stable, invertible. Delay x[n - 1]: memory, causal, linear, time-invariant, stable, invertible. Moving average: memory, causal, linear, time-invariant, stable, not invertible in general. Accumulator: memory, causal, linear, time-invariant, unstable, invertible. n x[n]: memoryless, causal, linear, time-variant, unstable. x[n + 1]: memory, non-causal, linear, time-invariant, stable. x[2n]: memory, non-causal, linear, time-variant, stable, not invertible. Squarer: memoryless, causal, non-linear, time-invariant, stable, not invertible.

One system, all six tests: Take y[n] = x[n] x[n - 1], a product of the current and previous sample. Memory: it needs x[n - 1], so it has memory. Causality: the largest index is n, so it is causal. Linearity: doubling the input gives (2x[n])(2x[n - 1]) = 4 x[n] x[n - 1], four times the output, not twice, so it is not linear. Time invariance: the response to x[n - k] is x[n - k] x[n - k - 1], and the delayed output y[n - k] is also x[n - k] x[n - k - 1], so it is time-invariant. Stability: if |x| <= Mx then |y| <= Mx^2, so it is stable. Invertibility: the inputs x and -x give exactly the same output, so it is not invertible. Doing a full sweep like this for one system is the best practice for exams.

Why LTI is the star: Systems that are both linear and time-invariant (LTI) are special. Linearity means we can break any input into simple pieces, process each piece and add the results. Time invariance means every shifted piece is processed the same way. Together they mean one test signal, the impulse, tells us everything about the system. That is the convolution sum of lesson 7, and almost every tool in this course (z-transform, frequency response, DFT filtering) works only for LTI systems.

Interconnections: Systems can be joined in series (cascade: output of one feeds the next), in parallel (same input, outputs added), or with feedback (output fed back into the input). Two LTI systems in cascade form another LTI system, and for LTI systems the order of a cascade does not change the result. Feedback is how recursive filters are built, and it is also how instability sneaks in, as the accumulator shows: it is just a delay with its output added back.

Initial rest: A system with memory stores past values, and those stored values must start somewhere. We say a system is at initial rest when all stored values are zero before the input begins. Systems described by difference equations, like y[n] = 0.5 y[n - 1] + x[n], are LTI and causal if they start at rest. We will iterate such equations by hand in lesson 8. Keep in mind that a system can be stable but non-causal, causal but unstable, linear but time-variant: the properties are independent of each other.

Real life example 1, automatic gain control in a phone call: When you move the phone closer to your mouth, your voice gets louder, but the other person hears roughly the same level. An automatic gain control measures the recent loudness and adjusts the gain: y[n] = g[n] x[n], where g[n] changes over time based on the signal. This is time-variant (the gain depends on what happened before) and, because g depends on x, non-linear. It is still very useful, but our LTI tools cannot analyze it directly, which is why engineers treat it separately.

Real life example 2, a shop's daily sales ledger: A shop in New Market records daily sales x[n]. The running total since the first of the month is the accumulator: linear, time-invariant, causal, but unstable in the BIBO sense, because steady sales of 5,000 taka per day make the total grow without bound. The 7-day average of sales is a moving average: linear, time-invariant, causal and stable. The owner uses the first to pay taxes and the second to spot trends.

Common mistakes: Testing linearity with only one example input and declaring success; you need the general proof, or one counterexample to disprove. Forgetting the zero-in, zero-out shortcut. In time invariance, replacing n by n - k inside the coefficient for line one (n x[n] should become n x[n - k], not (n - k) x[n - k]). Thinking that a non-linear system must be unstable, or that a time-variant system must be non-causal.

What exams ask: For a list of systems such as y = x[n] + 2, y = x[n] cos(w0 n), y = x[-n], y = x[n] x[n - 1], y = sum of x[k] from n - 2 to n, decide memory, causality, linearity, time invariance and stability, with a reason for each. Also: show that two LTI systems in cascade commute, or prove that the accumulator is unstable with a step input.

Recap: A system maps x[n] to y[n]. Memoryless means only the present input matters. Causal means no future inputs. Linear means superposition holds; zero in must give zero out. Time-invariant means a delayed input gives the same delayed output; test with the two-line method. BIBO stable means bounded in gives bounded out. Invertible means the input can be recovered. LTI systems are the heart of DSP. Next lesson: why the impulse response describes an LTI system completely, and how to compute convolution by hand.
key_points: A system is a rule y[n] = T{x[n]}; test each property separately.
Memoryless: y[n] depends only on x[n]. Causal: no input index larger than n (x[n + 1], x[2n], x[-n] are non-causal).
Linear: T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2}; quick check: zero input must give zero output (2x + 3 fails).
Time-invariant: compare the response to x[n - k] with y[n - k]; n x[n] and x[2n] are time-variant.
BIBO stable: every bounded input gives a bounded output; the accumulator with u[n] gives n + 1, so it is unstable.
Invertible: input can be recovered (accumulator inverse is the first difference; x^2 and x[2n] are not invertible).
The properties are independent: a system can be non-linear but stable, linear but time-variant, and so on.
Linear + time-invariant (LTI) systems are fully described by their impulse response, the basis of convolution.
lessons.tip: Memorize the two quick filters: zero-in-zero-out for linearity and the two-line method for time invariance. They settle most exam questions in under a minute.
lessons.task: Make a table with 6 systems as rows and 6 properties as columns: y = 3x[n - 2], y = x[n]^3, y = x[n] + x[n + 2], y = cos(x[n]), y = x[n] u[n], y = 0.5 y[n - 1] + x[n] (assume initial rest). Fill each cell with yes or no and one line of reason. Check your answers with a friend.

quiz.q: Why is y[n] = 2x[n] + 3 not linear?
options: Because zero input gives output 3, not 0
quiz.explain: A linear system must give zero output for zero input; this one gives 3.

quiz.q: Which system is time-variant?
quiz.explain: Response to x[n - k] is n x[n - k], but the delayed output is (n - k) x[n - k]; they differ.

quiz.q: Which system is non-causal?
quiz.explain: y[1] = x[2] needs a future input, so x[2n] is non-causal.

quiz.q: The accumulator y[n] = sum of x[k] for k up to n, with input u[n], gives:
options: y[n] = n + 1 for n >= 0, so it is unstable
quiz.explain: Adding 1 at every step gives 1, 2, 3, ..., which grows without bound from a bounded input.

quiz.explain: x and -x give the same square, so the input cannot be recovered.

lessons.title: LTI Systems and Discrete Convolution by Hand
lessons.content:
Imagine you clap once in a big empty hall at your university. You hear the clap, then a quick echo, then a softer echo, then silence. Now imagine someone plays a song in the same hall. Every single sound in that song gets the same treatment: a copy, a quick echo, a softer echo. If you know exactly what the hall does to one clap, you can predict what it does to any song. That one idea is the heart of this lesson. The clap is called an impulse, what the hall does to it is the impulse response, and the rule for predicting the song is called convolution.

Where we are: In the last lesson we tested systems for linearity and time invariance. A system that has both properties is called LTI, linear time-invariant. You already met the convolution sum in Signals & Systems, so here we recap the why quickly and spend most of our time doing it by hand, with real numbers, until it feels as easy as long multiplication. Every number below was checked with a small script, so you can trust them and redo them yourself.

Step 1, every signal is a stack of impulses: Recall the unit impulse delta[n]: it is 1 at n = 0 and 0 everywhere else. A shifted impulse delta[n-k] is 1 at n = k and 0 elsewhere. Now take the short signal x = [1, 2, 3] starting at n = 0. You can write it as x[n] = 1 delta[n] + 2 delta[n-1] + 3 delta[n-2]. Check it: at n = 1 only the middle term is alive and gives 2. So any discrete signal is just a weighted sum of shifted impulses, x[n] = sum over k of x[k] delta[n-k]. This is not a trick of notation, it is literally how a list of samples works: sample value times its position.

Step 2, feed the stack into an LTI system: Suppose we know the system's answer to delta[n]; call it h[n], the impulse response. Time invariance says the answer to delta[n-k] is just h[n-k], the same shape moved k steps later. Linearity says the answer to x[k] delta[n-k] is x[k] h[n-k], and the answer to a sum is the sum of answers. Put the two together and the output is y[n] = sum over k of x[k] h[n-k]. That formula is the convolution sum, written y = x * h. The star here means convolution, not multiplication.

Why this is a big deal: An LTI system might be a hall, an amplifier, a phone's noise filter or a digital equalizer. Whatever it is inside, once you know h[n] you know everything about it. You do not need its circuit diagram or its source code. For a computer this is perfect, because h[n] is just a list of numbers in memory and convolution is just multiply and add, the operations a processor loves most.

Reading the formula slowly: To get one output sample y[n], you take every input sample x[k], multiply it by the impulse response value h[n-k], and add everything. The index n-k means: look at h at the distance between the output time n and the input time k. So y[n] is a weighted mix of the present and past inputs, with h telling how much each one counts. An input that arrived 2 steps ago gets weight h[2].

Method 1, flip and slide: This is the picture method. Write h[k] on a strip of paper, flip it around k = 0 to get h[-k], then slide it to the right by n to get h[n-k]. Line it up under x[k], multiply the overlapping pairs, and add. Each shift n gives one output sample. Let us do x = [1, 2, 3] and h = [1, 1, 1], both starting at n = 0. Flipped h is still [1, 1, 1] because it is symmetric, which keeps the arithmetic friendly for a first try.

The slides one by one: At n = 0 the flipped strip overlaps only x[0], so y[0] = 1 x 1 = 1. At n = 1 it overlaps x[0] and x[1], so y[1] = 1 + 2 = 3. At n = 2 it covers all three, y[2] = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. At n = 3 it has slid past x[0], so y[3] = 2 + 3 = 5. At n = 4 only x[2] remains, y[4] = 3. At n = 5 there is no overlap and the output is 0 from then on. So y = [1, 3, 6, 5, 3]. Notice how the output rises while the strip slides in, peaks when fully overlapped, and falls as it slides out.

Method 2, the table method: Flipping can be confusing when h is not symmetric, so many students prefer a table, which works exactly like multiplying two numbers by hand without carrying. Write x along the top and h down the side. Row for h[0] = 1 is 1, 2, 3 starting at column 0. Row for h[1] = 1 is 1, 2, 3 shifted one column right. Row for h[2] = 1 is 1, 2, 3 shifted two columns right. Now add each column: column 0 gives 1, column 1 gives 2 + 1 = 3, column 2 gives 3 + 2 + 1 = 6, column 3 gives 3 + 2 = 5, column 4 gives 3. Same answer, [1, 3, 6, 5, 3], and no flipping needed.

Why the table works: Each row is the system's answer to one input sample alone: x[k] times the whole h, starting at time k. Adding the rows is superposition. In other words the table is the convolution formula drawn on paper. Once you see that, you can also read it the other way around: each row could be h scaled by one value of x. The total is the same either way, which hints at a property we will meet in a moment.

Output length rule: If x has L samples and h has M samples, y has L + M - 1 samples. Our example: 3 + 3 - 1 = 5, which matches. Also, if x starts at n = a and h starts at n = b, then y starts at n = a + b. These two rules give you a free check in exams: if your answer has the wrong length or starts at the wrong time, something went wrong before you even look at the values. Another free check: the sum of y equals the sum of x times the sum of h. Here 18 = 6 x 3. Correct.

A moving average example: A 3-point moving average has h = [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]. Suppose the afternoon temperature in Rajshahi over five days is x = [30, 33, 36, 33, 30] degrees. Convolving gives y = [10, 21, 33, 34, 33, 21, 10]. The first two and last two values are small because the window was only partly filled with data, they are edge effects. The middle three values 33, 34, 33 are true 3-day averages, and they are smoother than the raw data: the jump from 30 to 36 has been softened. That is low-pass filtering in its simplest form.

Properties of convolution: Commutative: x * h = h * x. Swap them in our example and you still get [1, 3, 6, 5, 3]. So you can flip whichever sequence is shorter. Associative: (x * h1) * h2 = x * (h1 * h2), which means two LTI systems in series act like one system whose impulse response is h1 * h2. Distributive: x * (h1 + h2) = x * h1 + x * h2, which means two systems in parallel act like one system with h1 + h2. These are not just algebra facts, they let engineers rearrange a chain of filters freely.

Two special impulse responses: If h = delta[n], the output equals the input: [1, 2, 3] * [1] = [1, 2, 3]. The impulse is the identity of convolution, like 1 for multiplication. If h = delta[n-1], written as [0, 1], the output is [0, 1, 2, 3], the same signal delayed by one sample.
