lessons.tip: For any filter, first evaluate H at z = 1, z = j and z = -1. Three quick numbers tell you the filter type before you draw anything.
lessons.task: On paper, compute |H| at w = 0, pi/4, pi/2, 3pi/4 and pi for the 2-point average and for the high-pass y[n] = 0.5x[n] - 0.5x[n-1]. Plot both on the same axes with a calculator, and label the x-axis in hertz for fs = 8000 Hz.

quiz.q: The frequency response H(e^jw) of a stable system is the same as:
options: H(z) evaluated on the unit circle
quiz.explain: Putting z = e^jw, which has magnitude 1, gives the DTFT of h[n]; that is H(z) on the unit circle.

quiz.q: With fs = 8000 Hz, what real frequency does w = pi/2 correspond to?
What is the gain of the 2-point average y[n] = 0.5x[n] + 0.5x[n-1] at w = pi?
quiz.explain: |H| = |cos(w/2)| = cos(pi/2) = 0; the alternating sequence 1, -1, 1, -1 averages to zero.

quiz.q: On a pole-zero plot, a pole close to the unit circle at angle w0 makes the magnitude response:
quiz.explain: The distance to the pole is in the denominator; when it is small the magnitude rises into a peak.

quiz.q: The 2-point average has phase -w/2. What is its group delay?
quiz.explain: Group delay = -d(phase)/dw = 0.5 samples, constant, so the filter has linear phase.

lessons.title: The DTFT: The Spectrum of a Sequence of Samples
lessons.content:
Think of a jhalmuri seller mixing his snack. From the outside you see one paper cone. But if you could pour it out and sort it, you would find puffed rice, peanuts, onion, chilli, mustard oil, each in some amount. A signal is like that cone. In time it looks like one wiggly line, but inside it is a mixture of sinusoids of different frequencies, each with some amount and some timing. A transform that pours the signal out and sorts it by frequency is called a Fourier transform. For a sequence of samples x[n], the right tool is the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform, the DTFT.

What Signals & Systems already gave you: You have seen the continuous-time Fourier transform, which turns x(t) into X(jOmega), and you met the DTFT briefly, along with the fact that the frequency response of a filter is the DTFT of its impulse response. This lesson goes deeper on the discrete side: the definition, why the spectrum repeats, how to compute a few DTFTs by hand, the main properties used in DSP, and the very practical reason we cannot compute the DTFT on a computer directly. That reason leads straight to the DFT in the next lesson.

The definition: The DTFT of a sequence x[n] is X(e^jw) = sum over all n from minus infinity to plus infinity of x[n] e^(-jwn). Here w is the digital frequency in radians per sample. The inverse is x[n] = (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of X(e^jw) e^(jwn) dw over any interval of length 2 pi, usually from -pi to pi. Read the inverse as a recipe: the sequence is built by adding up complex exponentials e^(jwn), with weights X(e^jw), for every frequency between -pi and pi.

Input discrete, output continuous: Notice the shape of the transform. The input is a list of numbers indexed by integers n. The output is a smooth function of a real variable w. You can ask for X at w = 0.1 or at w = 0.10001. This mix, discrete time but continuous frequency, is the defining feature of the DTFT, and it is both its beauty and its problem.

Why the DTFT repeats every 2 pi: Replace w by w + 2 pi. Then e^(-j(w + 2pi)n) = e^(-jwn) e^(-j2 pi n), and e^(-j2 pi n) = 1 for every integer n. So X(e^(j(w + 2 pi))) = X(e^jw). The spectrum is periodic with period 2 pi. The physical meaning is aliasing: once you have samples, a sinusoid at w and a sinusoid at w + 2 pi produce exactly the same numbers, so the transform cannot tell them apart. Low frequencies sit near w = 0 (and near every multiple of 2 pi); the highest frequency is w = pi, which corresponds to fs/2.

When the DTFT exists: If x[n] is absolutely summable, meaning sum of |x[n]| is finite, the sum converges and the DTFT exists as a nice continuous function. Every finite-length sequence qualifies. Every stable impulse response qualifies, because stability means sum |h[n]| is finite. Some signals like a pure sinusoid or the unit step are not absolutely summable; their DTFTs exist only in a generalised sense with impulses, and we will not need those details here.

Worked DTFT 1, the impulse: x[n] = delta[n], which is 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere. Only one term survives: X(e^jw) = 1 times e^0 = 1. The impulse contains every frequency equally, with zero phase. Shift it: x[n] = delta[n - 3]. Now X(e^jw) = e^(-j3w). The magnitude is still 1 everywhere, but the phase is -3w, a straight line. A pure delay of 3 samples shows up as a linear phase with slope -3. Remember this, because it explains linear phase filters later.

Worked DTFT 2, the decaying exponential: x[n] = a^n u[n] with |a| < 1. Then X(e^jw) = sum from n = 0 to infinity of (a e^(-jw))^n. This is a geometric series with ratio a e^(-jw), whose size is |a| < 1, so it converges to 1/(1 - a e^(-jw)). Take a = 0.5. At w = 0: X = 1/(1 - 0.5) = 2. At w = pi: e^(-j pi) = -1, so X = 1/(1 + 0.5) = 0.667. The sequence 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 changes slowly and smoothly, so most of its content is at low frequencies: magnitude 2 at DC, only 0.667 at the highest frequency. If a were -0.5, the sequence would flip sign every sample and the picture would reverse, large at pi and small at 0.

Worked DTFT 3, the rectangular pulse: x[n] = 1 for n = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 0 otherwise, a pulse of length N = 4. Then X(e^jw) = 1 + e^(-jw) + e^(-j2w) + e^(-j3w). Using the finite geometric series, this simplifies to e^(-j1.5w) times sin(2w)/sin(w/2). At w = 0 every term is 1, so X = 4, the sum of the samples. At w = pi/2 the four terms are 1, -j, -1, j, which add to 0. At w = pi they are 1, -1, 1, -1, which also add to 0. So the magnitude has a main lobe centred at 0 with zeros at plus and minus pi/2, then smaller side lobes. In general a length-N pulse has its first zeros at plus and minus 2 pi / N: a longer pulse gives a narrower main lobe. This shape, the discrete cousin of the sinc, comes back when we study windows and spectral leakage.

The sum-at-DC trick: For any sequence, X(e^j0) = sum of x[n]. And X(e^j pi) = sum of x[n] (-1)^n, the alternating sum. These two checks take seconds and catch many algebra mistakes. For the pulse above, the sum is 4 and the alternating sum is 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 = 0, matching the formula.

Symmetry for real signals: Almost all real-world samples are real numbers. For a real x[n], X(e^(-jw)) is the complex conjugate of X(e^jw). That means |X| is an even function and the phase is an odd function. Together with the 2 pi periodicity, all the information lives in 0 to pi. That is why spectrum plots in audio software show only positive frequencies from 0 to fs/2.

Property, linearity: The DTFT of a x1[n] + b x2[n] is a X1 + b X2. Spectra of mixed signals simply add, which is why we can analyse a chord as separate notes.

Property, time shift: x[n - n0] has DTFT e^(-jwn0) X(e^jw). Delay does not change the magnitude, only adds a linear phase. Your voice reaching a friend a moment later sounds the same.

Property, frequency shift (modulation): e^(jw0 n) x[n] has DTFT X(e^(j(w - w0))). Multiplying by a complex exponential slides the whole spectrum by w0. Multiplying by cos(w0 n) creates two half-size copies at plus and minus w0. This is how digital radios move signals up and down in frequency.

Property, time reversal: x[-n] has DTFT X(e^(-jw)). Playing a recording backwards keeps the same magnitude spectrum, and for a real signal only flips the sign of the phase. So a reversed song has exactly the same frequency content but sounds strange, because the timing information carried by the phase is now wrong. This is a nice reminder that the phase is not a minor detail: it holds where things happen in time.

Property, convolution: If y[n] = x[n] * h[n], then Y(e^jw) = X(e^jw) H(e^jw). This is the most important property in DSP. A slow, messy convolution in time becomes a simple multiplication at each frequency. It is the reason filters are designed in the frequency domain: decide which frequencies to keep, shape H(e^jw), and the output spectrum is just the product.

Property, multiplication: The reverse also holds, with a twist. If y[n] = x[n] w[n], then Y(e^jw) is (1/(2 pi)) times the periodic convolution of X and W. Cutting a long signal with a window w[n] therefore smears its spectrum by the window's spectrum. That is the root of spectral leakage, which we will meet in the spectral analysis lesson.

Parseval's theorem: The energy in time equals the energy in frequency: sum of |x[n]|^2 = (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of |X(e^jw)|^2 over one period. Check with x[n] = 0.5^n u[n]. In time, the energy is 1 + 0.25 + 0.0625 + ... = 1/(1 - 0.25) = 4/3. The frequency side gives the same 4/3. Parseval lets you measure how much energy sits in a band, for example how much of an ECG's energy is mains noise.

Link to sampling: If x[n] came from sampling x(t) at rate fs, the DTFT is the analog spectrum, scaled and repeated: copies centred at every multiple of fs, with w = 2 pi f / fs. When the analog signal is band-limited below fs/2, the copies do not overlap and the part between -pi and pi is a faithful picture of the original spectrum. When it is not, the copies overlap and alias, exactly the sampling theorem from earlier lessons, seen from the DTFT side.

The practical problem: A computer cannot evaluate the DTFT exactly for two reasons. First, the sum runs over infinitely many n, and real recordings are finite. Second, X(e^jw) is defined for infinitely many values of w, and a computer can only store a finite list. The cure is to take a finite block of N samples and evaluate the DTFT only at N equally spaced frequencies. That sampled DTFT is the Discrete Fourier Transform, the DFT, and its fast algorithm, the FFT, is what every spectrum analyser actually runs.

Real life example 1, Shazam-style music matching: A song recognition app records a few seconds through your phone's microphone, computes spectra of short blocks, and looks for strong peaks in time and frequency. Those peak patterns act like a fingerprint. The theory behind every block's spectrum is the DTFT, computed in practice with the FFT.

Real life example 2, a vibrating motor in a garment factory: A sensor on a sewing machine motor in Gazipur records vibration at 1000 samples per second. A healthy motor shows a strong line at its rotation frequency. A worn bearing adds new frequency lines. Looking at the spectrum, a technician can spot trouble before the machine breaks, which is called condition monitoring.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students forget the DTFT is periodic and treat w = 3 pi as a new frequency. Some confuse the DTFT (continuous w) with the DFT (N discrete bins). Others drop the e^(-jwn0) phase factor in the time shift property. Exams ask you to find the DTFT of a^n u[n], of a short finite sequence, or of a shifted pulse; to state and use the convolution and Parseval properties; to evaluate the magnitude at w = 0 and pi; and to explain why the DTFT is periodic.

Recap: The DTFT X(e^jw) = sum x[n] e^(-jwn) turns a sequence into a continuous, 2 pi periodic spectrum. It exists for absolutely summable signals, including all stable impulse responses. Key pairs: delta gives 1, a^n u[n] gives 1/(1 - a e^-jw), a length-N pulse gives a sinc-like shape with first zeros at 2 pi/N. Convolution becomes multiplication, delay becomes linear phase, and energy is preserved. Because the DTFT is continuous and needs infinite data, computers use its sampled version, the DFT.
key_points: DTFT: X(e^jw) = sum x[n] e^(-jwn); inverse integrates over one 2 pi interval.
Time is discrete but frequency w is continuous; the spectrum repeats every 2 pi because of aliasing.
It exists for absolutely summable sequences, so for every finite sequence and every stable h[n].
Pairs: delta[n] gives 1, delta[n - n0] gives e^(-jwn0), a^n u[n] gives 1/(1 - a e^(-jw)).
For a = 0.5 the magnitude is 2 at w = 0 and 0.667 at w = pi; X at 0 is the sum, X at pi the alternating sum.
A length-4 pulse has X = 4 at DC and zeros at pi/2 and pi; a length-N pulse has first zeros at 2 pi/N.
Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency; Parseval preserves energy (4/3 for 0.5^n u[n]).
Computers cannot evaluate infinite sums at infinitely many w, so they use the DFT.
lessons.tip: Before trusting any DTFT you derived, plug in w = 0 and w = pi and compare with the plain sum and the alternating sum of the samples.
lessons.task: Take x = [1, 1, 1, 1]. Using a calculator, evaluate X(e^jw) = 1 + e^(-jw) + e^(-j2w) + e^(-j3w) at w = 0, pi/4, pi/2, 3pi/4 and pi (write each e^(-jkw) as cos - j sin). Plot the magnitudes and confirm the zeros at pi/2 and pi.

quiz.q: Why is the DTFT of any sequence periodic with period 2 pi?
options: Because e^(-j2 pi n) = 1 for every integer n
Because only real signals are allowed
quiz.explain: Adding 2 pi to w multiplies each term by e^(-j2 pi n) = 1, so nothing changes; sampled sinusoids 2 pi apart are identical.

quiz.q: What is the DTFT of x[n] = 0.5^n u[n] at w = 0?
Delaying a sequence by n0 samples changes its DTFT by:
options: Multiplying by e^(-jwn0), a linear phase
quiz.explain: x[n - n0] has DTFT e^(-jwn0) X(e^jw): the magnitude stays, the phase gets a straight-line term.

quiz.q: For the pulse x = [1, 1, 1, 1], where are the first zeros of |X(e^jw)|?
options: At w = plus and minus pi/4
At w = plus and minus pi/2
quiz.explain: A length-N pulse has first zeros at 2 pi/N = 2 pi/4 = pi/2; at pi/2 the terms 1, -j, -1, j sum to zero.

quiz.q: Which property makes filtering easy to design in the frequency domain?
options: Convolution in time equals multiplication of DTFTs
quiz.explain: y = x * h gives Y = X H, so shaping H(e^jw) directly decides which frequencies pass.

lessons.title: The DFT: A Spectrum a Computer Can Actually Compute
lessons.content:
Imagine a doctor checking a patient's temperature. In theory the temperature exists at every instant of the day, but the nurse writes it in the chart only every four hours. Six numbers a day are enough to see a fever rising. The DFT does the same trick to a spectrum. The DTFT gives a smooth curve at every frequency, which a computer cannot store. The Discrete Fourier Transform writes that curve down at just N equally spaced frequencies, and from those N numbers a computer can do almost anything: plot a spectrum, filter a signal, compress music, or decode a Wi-Fi packet.

The problem it solves: From the last lesson, the DTFT X(e^jw) = sum x[n] e^(-jwn) has two problems for a computer: infinitely many samples and infinitely many frequencies. The DFT fixes both. Take a finite block of N samples, x[0] to x[N-1]. Then evaluate the DTFT only at the N frequencies w_k = 2 pi k / N, for k = 0, 1, ..., N-1. That is all the DFT is: a finite input and a finite output.

The definition: X[k] = sum from n = 0 to N-1 of x[n] e^(-j2 pi kn/N), for k = 0 to N-1. To shorten the writing, define the twiddle factor W_N = e^(-j2 pi/N), a point on the unit circle. Then X[k] = sum x[n] W_N^(kn). For N = 4, W_4 = e^(-j pi/2) = -j, so the powers are W^0 = 1, W^1 = -j, W^2 = -1, W^3 = j, and then they repeat. Every DFT computation is just multiplying samples by these points on the circle and adding.

The inverse DFT: x[n] = (1/N) sum from k = 0 to N-1 of X[k] e^(+j2 pi kn/N). The only differences from the forward transform are the plus sign in the exponent and the 1/N in front. N numbers go in, N numbers come out, and nothing is lost: the inverse gives back the exact samples. So the DFT is a change of viewpoint, not an approximation of the data.

Worked example, 4-point DFT of x = [1, 2, 3, 4]: We need X[0] to X[3].

X[0]: k = 0, so every twiddle is 1. X[0] = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The first DFT value is always the plain sum, the DC content.

X[1]: k = 1, twiddles W^0, W^1, W^2, W^3 = 1, -j, -1, j. So X[1] = 1(1) + 2(-j) + 3(-1) + 4(j) = 1 - 2j - 3 + 4j = -2 + 2j.

X[2]: k = 2, twiddles W^0, W^2, W^4, W^6 = 1, -1, 1, -1. So X[2] = 1 - 2 + 3 - 4 = -2. This is the alternating sum, the content at the highest frequency w = pi.

X[3]: k = 3, twiddles W^0, W^3, W^6, W^9 = 1, j, -1, -j. So X[3] = 1 + 2j - 3 - 4j = -2 - 2j. The result is X = [10, -2 + 2j, -2, -2 - 2j]. You can confirm it with one line of Python: numpy.fft.fft([1, 2, 3, 4]).

Checking with the inverse: x[0] = (1/4)(X[0] + X[1] + X[2] + X[3]) = (1/4)(10 + (-2 + 2j) + (-2) + (-2 - 2j)) = (1/4)(4) = 1. Correct. Try x[1] yourself: the inverse twiddles for n = 1 are 1, j, -1, -j, giving (1/4)(10 + j(-2 + 2j) - (-2) - j(-2 - 2j)) = (1/4)(10 - 2j - 2 + 2 + 2j - 2) = (1/4)(8) = 2. Correct again.

The matrix view: The whole DFT is one matrix multiplied by a vector. For N = 4, row k of the matrix holds W^(kn): row 0 is [1, 1, 1, 1], row 1 is [1, -j, -1, j], row 2 is [1, -1, 1, -1], row 3 is [1, j, -1, -j]. Multiply this 4 by 4 matrix by the column [1, 2, 3, 4] and you get [10, -2 + 2j, -2, -2 - 2j]. Each row is a sampled complex sinusoid, and each output is a dot product that measures how much the signal looks like that sinusoid. That is the intuition behind every Fourier transform: correlation with test waves.

Magnitude and phase of a bin: X[1] = -2 + 2j has magnitude sqrt(4 + 4) = 2.828 and angle 135 degrees. The magnitude tells how strong frequency bin 1 is; the angle tells where that wave starts. A spectrum plot usually shows only the magnitude, but the phase is needed to rebuild the signal.

Conjugate symmetry: Notice X[3] = -2 - 2j is the complex conjugate of X[1] = -2 + 2j. For real input, X[N - k] is always the conjugate of X[k]. So for N real samples, only about half of the DFT values are new information: bins 0 to N/2. X[0] and X[N/2] are always real. This is why a real 1024-sample FFT gives a useful spectrum of 513 bins, from 0 to fs/2.

A pure tone example: Let x[n] = cos(2 pi n/4), which for n = 0 to 3 is [1, 0, -1, 0]. Then X[0] = 0, X[1] = 1 + 0 + (-1)(-1) + 0 = 2, X[2] = 1 + 0 + (-1)(1) + 0 = 0, and X[3] = 2. So the energy appears only in bins 1 and 3 (which is bin -1 in disguise), each with value N A/2 = 4(1)/2 = 2, where A = 1 is the amplitude. A real cosine always shows up as a pair of mirror bins. To read the amplitude from a bin, divide its magnitude by N/2.

Which real frequency is bin k: Bin k corresponds to w_k = 2 pi k/N, which in hertz is f_k = k fs / N. The spacing between bins, fs/N, is called the frequency resolution or bin width. Example: fs = 8000 Hz and N = 1024 give a bin width of 8000/1024 = 7.8125 Hz. Bin 128 is 128 x 7.8125 = 1000 Hz. Bin 512 is 4000 Hz, which is fs/2. Bins above 512 are the mirror (negative frequency) half. If you want finer resolution, you need a longer recording: bin width fs/N depends on N, so N = 8000 samples (one second at 8 kHz) gives exactly 1 Hz bins.

Two tiny examples worth memorising: The DFT of a single impulse x = [1, 0, 0, 0] is X = [1, 1, 1, 1]: only the n = 0 term survives and its twiddle is always 1, so every frequency is present equally, just like the DTFT of delta. The DFT of a constant x = [1, 1, 1, 1] is X = [4, 0, 0, 0]: all the energy sits at DC, and every other bin cancels because the twiddles of each row add up to zero. Time spike means flat spectrum; flat time means spike spectrum.

Shift in a circle: Because of the periodic view, delaying the block inside the DFT is a circular shift: samples pushed past the end reappear at the start. A circular shift by m multiplies X[k] by W_N^(km), which changes only the phases, never the magnitudes. Linearity holds as usual: the DFT of a x + b y is a X + b Y.

The hidden assumption, periodicity: The DFT treats the N samples as one period of an endlessly repeating signal. Both x[n] and X[k] behave as if they were periodic with period N. That is harmless when you just want a spectrum, but it has two consequences you must remember. First, if the block does not contain a whole number of cycles of a tone, the jump where the end meets the start spreads energy into many bins; this is spectral leakage, studied soon. Second, multiplying two DFTs gives circular convolution, not linear convolution, studied in the circular convolution lesson.

Parseval for the DFT: sum of |x[n]|^2 = (1/N) sum of |X[k]|^2. Check: 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30. On the other side: |10|^2 + |-2 + 2j|^2 + |-2|^2 + |-2 - 2j|^2 = 100 + 8 + 4 + 8 = 120, and 120/4 = 30. Energy is the same seen from either side, a useful numeric check.

How the DFT relates to the DTFT, seen with zero padding: If you append zeros to the block, say turning 4 samples into 8, the DTFT of the data does not change at all, because the extra samples are zero. But now the DFT samples that same DTFT curve at 8 points instead of 4, so you see the curve in more detail. This is why software pads to a power of two or more: the plot looks smoother. It does not reveal anything that was not already in the original 4 samples.

The cost: Each X[k] needs N complex multiplications and there are N values of k, so the direct DFT needs about N^2 complex multiplications. For N = 1024 that is 1,048,576 multiplications for one spectrum. For real-time audio at many spectra per second, that is too slow on small chips. The FFT, coming next lesson, computes exactly the same numbers far faster.

Real life example 1, a guitar tuner app: A tuner app records a short block from the microphone, takes its DFT (with the FFT), finds the bin with the largest magnitude, and converts that bin to hertz with f = k fs/N. If the string is the A string, the app expects about 110 Hz and tells you whether you are above or below. If the bin width is too coarse, the app cannot distinguish small detuning, which is why tuners use long enough blocks or refine the peak.

Real life example 2, 4G and Wi-Fi: Modern mobile and Wi-Fi systems use OFDM, where data is placed on many closely spaced subcarriers. The transmitter builds the time signal with an inverse FFT, and the receiver in your phone, whether on a Grameenphone 4G network in Chattogram or your home router, recovers the data with an FFT. Every second your phone computes a very large number of DFTs without you noticing.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the 1/N in the inverse (or putting it in the forward transform without saying so; some books split it as 1/sqrt(N) both ways, which is fine if consistent). Using e^(+j) in the forward transform. Reading bin k as k Hz instead of k fs/N Hz. Forgetting that bins above N/2 are negative frequencies. Thinking more zero-padding gives better resolution: it gives a smoother plot, not the ability to separate closer tones.

What exams ask: Compute a 4-point (sometimes 8-point) DFT by hand, often of [1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 1, 0, 0] or [1, 0, 0, 0]; verify with the inverse; write the DFT matrix for N = 4; state and use conjugate symmetry; find the bin frequency for given fs and N; explain the relationship between DFT and DTFT; and state the N^2 cost to motivate the FFT.

Recap: The DFT X[k] = sum x[n] e^(-j2 pi kn/N) samples the DTFT of an N-sample block at N frequencies 2 pi k/N. It is exactly invertible with the 1/N inverse. For [1, 2, 3, 4] it gives [10, -2 + 2j, -2, -2 - 2j]. Bin k means k fs/N hertz, and resolution is fs/N. Real inputs give conjugate-symmetric outputs. The DFT assumes periodic repetition, and its direct cost is N^2, which the FFT will slash.
key_points: The DFT samples the DTFT of an N-sample block at w_k = 2 pi k/N: finite in, finite out.
X[k] = sum x[n] W_N^(kn) with W_N = e^(-j2 pi/N); inverse has e^(+j) and a 1/N factor.
For x = [1, 2, 3, 4], X = [10, -2 + 2j, -2, -2 - 2j]; X[0] is the sum, X[N/2] the alternating sum.
For real input, X[N - k] is the conjugate of X[k], so only bins 0 to N/2 are new.
Bin k is k fs/N hertz; fs = 8000, N = 1024 gives 7.8125 Hz bins and bin 128 = 1000 Hz.
A cosine of amplitude A on an exact bin shows two mirror bins of size N A/2.
The DFT treats the block as periodic, which causes leakage and circular convolution.
Direct DFT costs about N^2 complex multiplies (1,048,576 for N = 1024), motivating the FFT.
lessons.tip: Memorise the four points 1, -j, -1, j. With them you can do any 4-point DFT in under two minutes, and X[0] and X[2] as plain and alternating sums give instant checks.
lessons.task: By hand, compute the 4-point DFT of x = [1, 1, 0, 0] using the 4 x 4 matrix. Then check Parseval (sum of x squared versus sum of |X| squared divided by 4) and run the inverse for x[0].

quiz.q: What is X[0] of the DFT of x = [1, 2, 3, 4]?
quiz.explain: At k = 0 every twiddle is 1, so X[0] is the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

quiz.q: For N = 4, what is the twiddle factor W_4 = e^(-j2 pi/4)?
quiz.explain: e^(-j pi/2) = cos(pi/2) - j sin(pi/2) = -j.

quiz.q: With fs = 8000 Hz and N = 1024, what frequency is bin 128?
For a real input, X[3] of a 4-point DFT equals:
quiz.explain: Conjugate symmetry: X[N - k] = conj(X[k]), so X[3] = conj(X[1]); for [1,2,3,4], -2 - 2j and -2 + 2j.

quiz.q: Roughly how many complex multiplications does a direct DFT of N points need?
quiz.explain: N outputs, each a sum of N products, gives about N^2 multiplications; the FFT reduces this.

lessons.title: The FFT: Computing the DFT Hundreds of Times Faster
lessons.content:
Imagine a teacher at a school in Rajshahi who must add up marks for 1,024 students across 1,024 small tests. Done one by one, that is over a million additions. A clever teacher notices that many partial sums are shared between students and reuses them, finishing in a tiny fraction of the time with exactly the same totals. The Fast Fourier Transform is that clever teacher. It is not a different transform and not an approximation. It computes exactly the same DFT numbers as the formula from the last lesson, but it reorganises the work so that almost nothing is computed twice.

The problem: The DFT X[k] = sum from n = 0 to N-1 of x[n] W_N^(kn), with W_N = e^(-j2 pi/N), needs N complex multiplications for each of the N outputs, so about N^2 in total. For N = 1024 that is 1,048,576 complex multiplications per spectrum. If a chip does one multiplication per nanosecond, that is about 1 ms per spectrum, which is too slow when you need thousands of spectra per second, and far too slow for N in the millions.

A bit of history: The idea of splitting a Fourier sum into smaller ones is old, and traces of it appear in Gauss's unpublished work. The method became famous in 1965 when James Cooley and John Tukey published an efficient algorithm for computers. It spread quickly because suddenly spectrum analysis, fast filtering and later digital communication became practical. Today the radix-2 Cooley-Tukey FFT is the version every student learns first.

The key trick, split even and odd: Assume N is a power of 2. Split the input into even-indexed samples x[0], x[2], x[4], ... and odd-indexed samples x[1], x[3], x[5], .... Each half has N/2 samples. Write the DFT as two sums: X[k] = sum over even n plus sum over odd n. In the odd sum, take out one factor W_N^k. With the identity W_N^2 = W_(N/2), each sum becomes an N/2-point DFT. So X[k] = E[k] + W_N^k O[k], where E is the N/2-point DFT of the even samples and O is the N/2-point DFT of the odd samples.

The second half for free: E[k] and O[k] are periodic with period N/2, so for k in the second half they repeat values we already have. And W_N^(k + N/2) = W_N^k times W_N^(N/2) = -W_N^k, because W_N^(N/2) = e^(-j pi) = -1. Therefore X[k + N/2] = E[k] - W_N^k O[k]. With one multiplication, W_N^k O[k], we get two outputs: add it to E[k] for X[k] and subtract it for X[k + N/2]. This pair of operations is the famous butterfly.

The butterfly picture: Draw two inputs on the left, a and b. Multiply b by the twiddle W. Then the top output is a + W b and the bottom output is a - W b. The crossing lines look like a butterfly's wings. One complex multiplication and two complex additions. Every FFT, however large, is built from nothing but these butterflies arranged in stages.

Keep splitting: The N/2-point DFTs can be split the same way into N/4-point DFTs, and so on, until we reach 2-point DFTs. A 2-point DFT of [a, b] is just [a + b, a - b], a butterfly with twiddle 1. The number of halvings from N down to 2 points, plus the final 2-point step, is log2 N stages. Because each sample is split by its index bits, this version is called decimation in time.

Worked 4-point FFT of x = [1, 2, 3, 4]: Step 1, split. Even samples: x[0], x[2] = [1, 3]. Odd samples: x[1], x[3] = [2, 4]. Step 2, 2-point DFTs. E = [1 + 3, 1 - 3] = [4, -2]. O = [2 + 4, 2 - 4] = [6, -2]. Step 3, twiddles for N = 4: W_4^0 = 1, W_4^1 = -j. Step 4, butterflies. For k = 0: W^0 O[0] = 6, so X[0] = 4 + 6 = 10 and X[2] = 4 - 6 = -2. For k = 1: W^1 O[1] = (-j)(-2) = 2j, so X[1] = -2 + 2j and X[3] = -2 - 2j. Result: X = [10, -2 + 2j, -2, -2 - 2j], exactly the same as the direct DFT in the previous lesson. Only 2 twiddle multiplications were needed here, one of them by 1, instead of the 16 multiplications of the direct 4 by 4 matrix form.

Counting the work: There are log2 N stages. Each stage has N/2 butterflies. Each butterfly needs one complex multiplication and two complex additions. So the FFT needs about (N/2) log2 N complex multiplications and N log2 N complex additions. Many twiddles are trivial (1 or -j), so real implementations do even fewer, but (N/2) log2 N is the standard textbook count.

Worked comparison: For N = 8: direct DFT needs 8^2 = 64 multiplications, FFT needs (8/2) x 3 = 12. For N = 1024: direct needs 1024^2 = 1,048,576, FFT needs 512 x 10 = 5,120. The ratio is 1,048,576 / 5,120 = 204.8, so about 205 times faster. At one multiplication per nanosecond, that is the difference between about 1 ms and about 5 microseconds. For N = 2^20 (about a million points), direct needs about 1.1 x 10^12 multiplications while the FFT needs 10,485,760, roughly 100,000 times fewer. This is why the FFT is called one of the most important algorithms ever written: N^2 grows terribly, N log N barely more than N.

The 8-point FFT stage by stage: For N = 8 there are log2 8 = 3 stages, each with 4 butterflies. Stage 1 pairs neighbouring bit-reversed inputs, (x[0], x[4]), (x[2], x[6]), (x[1], x[5]), (x[3], x[7]), using twiddle 1: these are four 2-point DFTs. Stage 2 combines pairs into two 4-point DFTs, using twiddles W_8^0 = 1 and W_8^2 = -j, with butterflies two positions apart. Stage 3 combines the two 4-point DFTs into the final 8-point result, using W_8^0, W_8^1, W_8^2, W_8^3, with butterflies four positions apart. Notice the pattern: the butterfly span doubles each stage, and the number of distinct twiddles doubles too.

Bit reversal: When you keep splitting even and odd, the input order gets shuffled. For N = 8, the order of inputs at the first stage is x[0], x[4], x[2], x[6], x[1], x[5], x[3], x[7]. Write each index in 3 bits and reverse the bits: 1 = 001 becomes 100 = 4, 3 = 011 becomes 110 = 6, and so on. That is why it is called bit-reversed order. Implementations shuffle the input once into bit-reversed order, then run the stages, and the output comes out in natural order.

In-place computation: Each butterfly reads two numbers and writes two numbers into the same two memory slots. So the whole FFT can run inside one array of N complex numbers without extra memory. On a small microcontroller with limited RAM this matters a lot.

Twiddle tables: The twiddles W_N^k = cos(2 pi k/N) - j sin(2 pi k/N) do not depend on the data, so programs compute them once and store them in a table. On small chips without fast sine functions, this table is often precomputed and stored in program memory. A 1024-point FFT needs only 512 distinct twiddles, and thanks to symmetry of sine and cosine, an even smaller table is enough.

Decimation in frequency: There is a mirror version where you split the outputs into even and odd k instead of the inputs. It uses the same number of butterflies, takes the input in natural order and produces output in bit-reversed order. Exams sometimes ask you to draw both flow graphs; the cost is the same.

When N is not a power of 2: The radix-2 FFT needs N = 2, 4, 8, 16, .... If you have 1000 samples, the usual trick is to zero-pad to 1024. Zero padding does not add information but makes the radix-2 algorithm usable and gives a slightly finer plotted grid. Other FFT algorithms handle radix 3, 5 or mixed sizes, and libraries such as FFTW or numpy pick a good algorithm for any N automatically.

Real-valued inputs: Audio and sensor samples are real, but the FFT works with complex numbers, so half the effort would be wasted on zero imaginary parts. A standard trick packs a real sequence of N samples into a complex sequence of N/2 samples (even samples as real part, odd as imaginary part), runs an N/2-point FFT, and then untangles the result with one extra pass. Libraries call this a real FFT, and it roughly halves the work again.

The inverse FFT trick: The inverse DFT differs from the forward one only by the sign in the exponent and the 1/N. So you can reuse a forward FFT routine: conjugate X[k], run the FFT, conjugate the result, and divide by N. That gives x[n]. One routine, both directions.

Why the FFT also speeds up filtering: Convolution in time equals multiplication of DFTs. So to filter a long signal with a long filter, you can FFT both, multiply bin by bin, and inverse FFT back. For long filters this is much cheaper than direct convolution. There is one catch, the DFT's periodic view turns this into circular convolution, and the next lesson shows exactly how to handle it with zero padding.

Real life example 1, your phone's music visualiser: When a music app shows dancing bars, it is running an FFT on short blocks of audio, maybe 1024 or 2048 samples, dozens of times per second, and drawing the magnitudes grouped into bands. Without the FFT, a phone's processor would struggle to do this smoothly while also playing the music.

Real life example 2, mobile data in Bangladesh: Every 4G connection, from a Banglalink user in Khulna to a Teletalk user in Rangpur, uses OFDM. The base station builds each symbol with an inverse FFT, and the phone takes an FFT to separate hundreds of subcarriers. Wi-Fi does the same. The FFT is the reason these systems can be built cheaply into small chips.

Common mistakes: Thinking the FFT gives an approximate or different answer from the DFT (it is exact, apart from tiny rounding). Forgetting the minus sign in the lower butterfly output. Using the wrong twiddle exponent (W_N^k, with N of the current stage). Feeding inputs in natural order into a decimation-in-time diagram that expects bit-reversed order. Quoting the cost as N log N multiplications instead of (N/2) log2 N.

What exams ask: Derive X[k] = E[k] + W^k O[k] and X[k + N/2] = E[k] - W^k O[k]; draw the 8-point decimation-in-time flow graph with bit-reversed inputs; compute a 4-point FFT by hand; count multiplications for given N and compare with the direct DFT (often N = 1024 or 512); explain in-place computation and bit reversal.

Recap: The FFT computes exactly the DFT by splitting it into smaller DFTs. Splitting even and odd samples gives X[k] = E[k] + W^k O[k] and X[k + N/2] = E[k] - W^k O[k], the butterfly. Repeating this gives log2 N stages of N/2 butterflies, about (N/2) log2 N multiplications instead of N^2: 5,120 instead of 1,048,576 for N = 1024, about 205 times faster. Inputs go in bit-reversed order, computation can be in place, and the same routine also does the inverse.
key_points: The FFT gives exactly the DFT values; it only reorganises the computation.
Split even and odd samples: X[k] = E[k] + W_N^k O[k] and X[k + N/2] = E[k] - W_N^k O[k].
A butterfly takes a, b and gives a + Wb and a - Wb: one multiply, two adds.
log2 N stages of N/2 butterflies give about (N/2) log2 N multiplications versus N^2.
N = 1024: 5,120 versus 1,048,576 multiplications, about 205 times fewer.
Decimation in time takes inputs in bit-reversed order (N = 8: 0, 4, 2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 7) and works in place.
Inverse FFT: conjugate, forward FFT, conjugate, divide by N; pad to a power of 2 for radix-2.
lessons.tip: Draw the 8-point butterfly diagram once on a full page, with bit-reversed inputs on the left and twiddles marked. Most FFT exam questions are just that picture plus counting.
lessons.task: Compute the 4-point FFT of x = [1, 0, -1, 0] by splitting into even [1, -1] and odd [0, 0], then doing the butterflies. Check that you get [0, 2, 0, 2]. Then count how many multiplications a direct DFT and an FFT would need for N = 256.

quiz.q: Compared with the direct DFT, the FFT result is:
options: Only the magnitude of the DFT
Exactly the same DFT values, computed faster
quiz.explain: The FFT is an algorithm for the DFT; it reorganises the sums but produces the same numbers (up to rounding).

quiz.q: In a radix-2 butterfly, if the top output is E[k] + W^k O[k], the bottom output X[k + N/2] is:
quiz.explain: Because W_N^(N/2) = -1, the twiddle flips sign for the second half, giving E[k] - W^k O[k].

quiz.q: About how many complex multiplications does a radix-2 FFT need for N = 1024?
quiz.explain: (N/2) log2 N = 512 x 10 = 5,120, versus 1024^2 = 1,048,576 for the direct DFT.

quiz.q: For an 8-point decimation-in-time FFT, which input order is used at the first stage?
quiz.explain: Bit reversal of 3-bit indices: 001 becomes 100 (4), 011 becomes 110 (6), giving 0, 4, 2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 7.

quiz.q: You have 1000 samples and a radix-2 FFT routine. The usual fix is:
quiz.explain: Appending zeros up to the next power of two (1024) makes radix-2 usable without adding new information.

lessons.title: Circular vs Linear Convolution: Filtering with the FFT Without Mistakes
lessons.content:
Picture a round dining table at a family dawat in Cumilla, with chairs numbered 0, 1, 2. If you ask everyone to move one chair to the right, the person on chair 2 does not fall off the edge; they come around to chair 0. A straight bench works differently: move everyone right and the last person needs a new seat at the end. Linear convolution is the straight bench. Circular convolution is the round table. The DFT secretly sits everyone at a round table, and if you forget that, your FFT-based filter gives wrong answers. This lesson shows exactly when the two agree and how to make them agree on purpose.

Why we care: Earlier you computed outputs of FIR filters with linear convolution, y[n] = sum over k of x[k] h[n - k]. For a long signal and a long filter, that costs a lot: every output needs as many multiplications as the filter has taps. You also learned that the DTFT turns convolution into multiplication. The tempting idea is: take DFTs (with the fast FFT), multiply them bin by bin, take the inverse FFT. Cheap. But the DFT is not the DTFT, and multiplying DFTs gives something slightly different, circular convolution.

Linear convolution recap: For x = [1, 2, 3] (n = 0, 1, 2) and h = [1, 1] (n = 0, 1), flip h, slide it along x, multiply and add. y[0] = 1 x 1 = 1. y[1] = 2 x 1 + 1 x 1 = 3. y[2] = 3 x 1 + 2 x 1 = 5. y[3] = 3 x 1 = 3. So y = [1, 3, 5, 3]. The output length is L + M - 1 = 3 + 2 - 1 = 4, where L and M are the input and filter lengths. This is what a real filter does to the signal, and it is the answer we want.

What circular convolution is: For two sequences of length N, the N-point circular convolution is y_c[n] = sum over m from 0 to N-1 of x[m] h[(n - m) mod N]. The index (n - m) mod N wraps around: -1 becomes N - 1, -2 becomes N - 2, and so on. Everything lives on a circle of N positions. The key theorem: if X[k] and H[k] are the N-point DFTs, then the inverse DFT of X[k] H[k] is exactly the N-point circular convolution of x and h. Not the linear one.

Worked circular convolution with N = 3: Take x = [1, 2, 3] and h = [1, 1, 0] (h padded to length 3). Compute each output. y_c[0] = x[0] h[0] + x[1] h[(0 - 1) mod 3] + x[2] h[(0 - 2) mod 3] = 1 x h[0] + 2 x h[2] + 3 x h[1] = 1 + 0 + 3 = 4. y_c[1] = x[0] h[1] + x[1] h[0] + x[2] h[2] = 1 + 2 + 0 = 3. y_c[2] = x[0] h[2] + x[1] h[1] + x[2] h[0] = 0 + 2 + 3 = 5. So y_c = [4, 3, 5]. Compare with the linear answer [1, 3, 5, 3]. They differ.

A quick sanity check, the sum rule: For linear convolution, the sum of the output equals the sum of x times the sum of h. Here 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 and 1 + 1 = 2, so the output must sum to 12: indeed 1 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 12. Circular convolution obeys the same rule, because wrapping only moves values, it never loses them: 4 + 3 + 5 = 12. This check takes five seconds and catches most arithmetic slips. It also reminds you that wrap-around is not random error; it is the same numbers in the wrong seats.

Why they differ, time aliasing: Look closely. The linear result has 4 values, but a 3-point circle only has 3 seats. The last linear value y[3] = 3 had nowhere to go, so it wrapped around and landed on seat 0, adding to y[0] = 1, giving 4. In general, the N-point circular convolution equals the linear convolution folded onto N positions: y_c[n] = sum over r of y[n + rN]. When the linear output is longer than N, the tail overlaps the head. This is called time-domain aliasing, the time-side twin of frequency aliasing from undersampling.

The fix, zero padding: If N is at least L + M - 1, the linear output fits on the circle and nothing wraps. So pad both sequences with zeros to length N >= L + M - 1, then take N-point DFTs, multiply, and inverse. For our example L + M - 1 = 4. With N = 4: x = [1, 2, 3, 0] and h = [1, 1, 0, 0]. The 4-point circular convolution is [1, 3, 5, 3], exactly the linear result. Going through the DFT route (numpy.fft.ifft of the product of the two FFTs) gives the same: N = 3 gives [4, 3, 5] and N = 4 gives [1, 3, 5, 3]. Any N larger than 4 also works; the extra outputs are just zeros.

The circle method for hand calculation: Exams often want circular convolution by hand. Draw two concentric circles with N marks each. Write x[0], x[1], ... counterclockwise on the outer circle. Write h[0], h[1], ... clockwise on the inner circle (that is the flip). Multiply aligned pairs and add to get y_c[0]. Then rotate the inner circle one step counterclockwise and repeat for y_c[1], and so on. It is the flip-and-slide method on a ring.

The matrix method: Another way is the circulant matrix. For N = 3 and h = [1, 1, 0], build a 3 x 3 matrix whose first column is h and each next column is h rotated down by one: columns [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1]. Rows are then [1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]. Multiply by x = [1, 2, 3]: row 1 gives 1 + 0 + 3 = 4, row 2 gives 1 + 2 + 0 = 3, row 3 gives 0 + 2 + 3 = 5. Again [4, 3, 5]. This view also explains why the DFT diagonalises circular convolution: circulant matrices are exactly the matrices the DFT turns into diagonal ones.

Which one does nature do: A real filter, a room, a cable or an RC circuit always performs linear convolution. Sound does not wrap around from the end of a song to its beginning. Circular convolution is purely an artefact of looking at signals through the DFT, which treats every block as one period of a repeating signal. So the job of the engineer is always the same: use the DFT for speed, but arrange the padding or the block method so that the result equals what nature would do.

Fast convolution, the whole recipe: To filter a block x of length L with an FIR filter h of length M: choose N as a power of 2 with N >= L + M - 1; zero-pad x and h to N; compute X = FFT(x) and H = FFT(h); multiply Y[k] = X[k] H[k]; compute y = IFFT(Y). The result is the exact linear convolution. H can be computed once and stored, since the filter does not change.

Is it really faster: Direct convolution costs about L x M multiplications. Fast convolution costs two FFTs (one forward, one inverse) of size N, plus N multiplications, which is about N log2 N plus N. For short filters, say 5 taps, direct convolution wins because it is so simple. For long filters, say hundreds or thousands of taps, as in room reverberation or long channel models, the FFT route wins clearly. Rules of thumb vary with hardware, so engineers usually measure on the target device.

Long signals, block processing: A live microphone stream never ends, so you cannot FFT the whole thing. You cut it into blocks and filter block by block. There are two classic ways to stitch the blocks together correctly.

Overlap-add: Cut the input into non-overlapping blocks of length L. Filter each block with fast convolution using N >= L + M - 1, which gives an output block of length L + M - 1, longer than L by M - 1 samples. The tail of each output block overlaps the head of the next one, so you add the overlapping parts. Example: a filter of M = 101 taps and blocks of L = 924 samples need N = 924 + 101 - 1 = 1024, a neat power of two. Each block produces 1024 outputs, of which the last 100 are added onto the start of the next block's output.

Overlap-save: Instead take input blocks of length N that overlap by M - 1 samples with the previous block. Do N-point circular convolution directly. The first M - 1 outputs of each block are corrupted by wrap-around, so you throw them away and keep the remaining N - M + 1 good samples. No adding is needed, only discarding. Both methods give exactly the same final output as one giant linear convolution.

Real life example 1, video call echo cancellation: When you talk on a video call from Dhaka to a relative in Malaysia, your laptop's speaker sound leaks back into the microphone. The software models the room's echo path with a long adaptive FIR filter, often hundreds of taps or more, and subtracts the predicted echo. Such long filters are usually run in the frequency domain with block methods like overlap-save, because direct convolution would be too expensive.

Real life example 2, reverb in music production: A music producer in a home studio wants a vocal to sound like it was sung in a big hall. They load an impulse response recorded in that hall, which can be a few seconds long; a 3-second response at 48 kHz has 144,000 taps. Convolving with that directly is very heavy; convolution reverb plugins use FFT-based block convolution to do it in real time.

Common mistakes: Multiplying DFTs of unpadded sequences and expecting the linear result. Padding to only max(L, M) instead of L + M - 1. In overlap-save, discarding the wrong end of each block (it is the first M - 1 samples that are corrupted). Forgetting that h must be padded to the same N as x before taking its DFT. Mixing up the flip direction on the circle method.

What exams ask: Compute an N-point circular convolution by circles or matrices; compare it with the linear convolution and explain the difference as wrap-around; find the minimum N for which they agree (L + M - 1); compute a circular convolution through the DFT for N = 4; describe overlap-add and overlap-save step by step with block lengths.

Recap: Multiplying N-point DFTs gives circular convolution, where indices wrap modulo N. For x = [1, 2, 3] and h = [1, 1], the 3-point circular result [4, 3, 5] differs from the linear [1, 3, 5, 3] because the last value wraps to the start. Zero-padding to N >= L + M - 1 removes the wrap and makes FFT filtering exact. For long streams, overlap-add adds overlapping tails and overlap-save discards corrupted heads, both giving the true linear output.
key_points: Linear convolution of lengths L and M has length L + M - 1; [1, 2, 3] * [1, 1] = [1, 3, 5, 3].
N-point circular convolution wraps indices modulo N; it is what the inverse DFT of X[k]H[k] gives.
3-point circular convolution of [1, 2, 3] and [1, 1] is [4, 3, 5]: the last linear value wrapped onto n = 0.
Circular equals linear folded onto N points (time aliasing); they agree when N >= L + M - 1.
Fast convolution: zero-pad to N, FFT both, multiply, inverse FFT; worth it for long filters.
Hand methods: concentric circles (flip on the inner circle) or a circulant matrix.
Overlap-add: blocks of L, outputs of L + M - 1, add the overlapping tails (e.g. L = 924, M = 101, N = 1024).
Overlap-save: overlapping input blocks, discard the first M - 1 outputs of each block.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see DFTs multiplied, ask one question: is N at least L + M - 1? If not, expect wrap-around and compute what lands where.
lessons.task: Compute the 4-point circular convolution of x = [1, 2, 3, 4] and h = [1, 1, 0, 0] with the circle method. Then compute their linear convolution (length 5) and check that folding its last value onto n = 0 gives your circular answer.

quiz.q: The inverse DFT of X[k]H[k] (both N-point DFTs) equals:
options: The linear convolution of x and h
The N-point circular convolution of x and h
The correlation of x and h
quiz.explain: The DFT convolution property gives circular convolution, with indices wrapping modulo N.

quiz.q: What is the 3-point circular convolution of x = [1, 2, 3] and h = [1, 1, 0]?
quiz.explain: The linear result [1, 3, 5, 3] has its last value 3 wrapped onto n = 0: [1 + 3, 3, 5] = [4, 3, 5].

quiz.q: To make circular convolution equal linear convolution for lengths L and M, N must be at least:
quiz.explain: The linear output has length L + M - 1; with N at least that, nothing wraps around.

quiz.q: In overlap-save, which outputs of each block are thrown away?
quiz.explain: The first M - 1 outputs of each circular block are corrupted by wrap-around, so they are discarded.

quiz.q: For an FIR filter of M = 101 taps and N = 1024, what input block length L does overlap-add use?

lessons.title: Spectral Analysis with the DFT: Resolution, Leakage, Windows and Spectrograms
lessons.content:
Imagine looking at the night sky over Bandarban through a cheap pair of binoculars. Two stars that are very close look like one blurry blob, and a very bright star throws a glare that hides the faint stars around it. Spectral analysis with the DFT has exactly these two problems. Close frequencies blur together, which is a resolution problem, and a strong frequency spreads glare into its neighbours, which is called leakage. In this lesson you learn where both problems come from, how windows reduce the glare, what zero padding can and cannot do, and how the spectrogram shows a spectrum changing over time.

The setting: You have a recording, maybe a microphone signal, a vibration sensor or an ECG, sampled at fs. You take a block of N samples, compute the FFT, and plot the magnitude of bins 0 to N/2. Bin k sits at k fs/N hertz. This seems simple, but the picture you get depends strongly on N, on how the block is cut, and on what you do before the FFT. Knowing these effects is what separates someone who just runs numpy.fft from someone who can trust the plot.

Resolution, the basic limit: Two tones can only be told apart if they are separated by roughly at least the bin spacing fs/N, which equals 1/T where T = N/fs is the length of the recording in seconds. So resolution depends on how long you listen, not on fs. Example: with fs = 8000 Hz and N = 1024, bins are 7.8125 Hz apart and the block lasts 0.128 s. Tones at 1000 Hz and 1010 Hz are 10 Hz apart, so you need fs/N of about 10 Hz or less, meaning N of at least about 800 samples at 8 kHz, or 0.1 s of signal. Want to separate tones 1 Hz apart? You need about one second of data. No trick of processing can get around this time-frequency trade-off.

Where leakage comes from: The DFT assumes the block is one period of a signal that repeats forever. If the block contains an exact whole number of cycles of a tone, the repeated version is a perfect smooth sinusoid, and all the energy lands in one bin (plus its mirror). If it does not, the end of the block does not join smoothly onto the start; there is a jump. That jump is not part of the real signal, but the DFT sees it and needs many frequencies to build it. So energy leaks out of the true bin into all the others.

The same idea from the DTFT side: Taking N samples is like multiplying the endless signal by a rectangular window of length N. Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency, so the true spectrum (a sharp line for a tone) is smeared by the window's spectrum, the sinc-like shape with a main lobe and side lobes you met in the DTFT lesson. The DFT then samples that smeared curve. If the tone sits exactly on a bin, the samples land on the main lobe peak and on all the zeros of the sinc, so you see one clean bin. If the tone sits between bins, the samples land on the side lobes, and every bin shows something.

A worked leakage test: Take a 64-point block with a rectangular (no) window. A cosine at exactly bin 10 gives one nonzero bin in the lower half, bin 10, and nothing else. Move the cosine to bin 10.5, halfway between bins, and two things happen. First, the peak drops by about 4 dB, because no bin sits on the top of the main lobe; this is called scalloping loss. Second, energy appears everywhere: in a quick test, bin 20, ten bins away, was only about 23 dB below the peak. A weak tone 30 dB quieter at that position would be completely buried in the glare.

Windows, the cure for glare: Instead of chopping the block abruptly, multiply it by a window that fades smoothly to near zero at both ends. Then the start and end of the block join with no jump, and the side lobes of the window's spectrum are much lower. The most common windows for an N-point block are: rectangular, w[n] = 1; Hann, w[n] = 0.5 - 0.5 cos(2 pi n/(N-1)); and Hamming, w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 cos(2 pi n/(N-1)), for n = 0 to N-1. Hann goes all the way to zero at the ends; Hamming stops at 0.08.

The price, a wider main lobe: Nothing is free. Fading the edges effectively shortens the useful part of the block, and a shorter block means worse resolution. The main lobe of Hann and Hamming is about twice as wide as the rectangular window's. So there is a trade-off: low side lobes (good for seeing weak tones next to strong ones) versus a narrow main lobe (good for separating close tones of similar strength).

The standard numbers: For the highest side lobe relative to the main lobe peak, the rectangular window gives about -13 dB, Hann about -31 dB and Hamming about -41 dB. Rectangular has the narrowest main lobe; Hann and Hamming are about twice as wide. In the same 64-point test with a tone at bin 10.5, a Hann window dropped the scalloping loss to about 1.4 dB and pushed the leakage at bin 20 down to about 67 dB below the peak, compared with about 23 dB for the rectangular window. That is the difference between hiding and seeing a weak tone. Hann is a good default for general spectrum plots; Hamming is popular in speech processing; rectangular is best only when tones are known to fall exactly on bins or when signals are short transients.

Other windows in one line each: The Blackman window pushes the highest side lobe down to about -57 dB, at the cost of an even wider main lobe, so it suits measurements where a very weak tone sits far from a strong one. Flat-top windows have a very wide, flat main lobe, so a tone reads almost the same amplitude wherever it falls between bins; instrument makers use them when the exact amplitude matters more than resolution.

Reading amplitudes with a window: A window reduces the total gain because its average value is less than 1. For the rectangular window, a cosine of amplitude A on a bin shows a magnitude of N A/2. With a Hann window the average value is 0.5, so the same tone shows about N A/4. To read amplitudes correctly, divide by the sum of the window values and multiply by 2. Spectrum analyser software does this correction automatically, but if you write your own code, you must do it.

Zero padding, what it does and does not do: Appending zeros to a block before the FFT samples the same DTFT curve at more points. The plot becomes smoother and peaks are located more precisely between the original bins. But zero padding does not add information. Two tones that blurred together in 100 samples still blur together after padding those 100 samples to 1000. Real resolution needs more real data. A good way to remember it: zero padding is a magnifying glass on the same blurry photo, not a better camera.

Noise and averaging: For noisy signals, the spectrum of a single block jumps around a lot from block to block. A common fix is to split a long recording into many overlapping blocks, window each one, compute each magnitude squared, and average them. This is known as Welch's method. It gives a much steadier estimate of the power spectrum, at the cost of using shorter blocks and so somewhat worse resolution.

The spectrogram, spectrum over time: Speech and music change constantly; a vowel lasts maybe a tenth of a second. One FFT of a whole sentence would mix everything together. The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) slides a window along the signal: take a short frame, window it, FFT it, move forward by a hop, repeat. Stack the magnitude spectra side by side as columns and show them as colours: time on the x-axis, frequency on the y-axis, loudness as brightness. This picture is the spectrogram.

Typical spectrogram numbers: In speech processing, frames of about 20 to 30 ms are common, with a hop of about 10 ms. At fs = 16 kHz, a 25 ms frame is 400 samples and a 10 ms hop is 160 samples. Short frames give good time detail but poor frequency detail; long frames give the opposite. Again the same trade-off: you cannot have perfect detail in both time and frequency at once.

A practical plan for one spectrum: First decide the finest frequency detail you need, say 5 Hz; that fixes the recording length T at about 1/5 = 0.2 s and N = fs T. Second, pick a window: Hann if you have no special reason. Third, round N up with zero padding to a convenient FFT size if you want a smoother plot. Fourth, compute the FFT, take magnitudes of bins 0 to N/2, correct for window gain, and convert to dB. Fifth, label the axis in hertz with k fs/N. Following these steps every time prevents most beginner errors.

Real life example 1, checking a ceiling fan's hum: Record your room with a free spectrum analyser app on your phone while the fan runs. You will likely see a peak at 50 Hz or 100 Hz, linked to the 50 Hz mains supply in Bangladesh, plus peaks from the fan's motor and blades. With a longer analysis window the peaks become sharper; switch the app's window type if it allows, and notice how weak peaks near strong ones appear or vanish.

Real life example 2, speech recognition and bird song: Voice assistants and speech-to-text systems usually start by computing spectrogram-like features from 25 ms frames. Researchers studying birds in the Sundarbans record dawn choruses and identify species from the shapes of the calls in a spectrogram, since each species draws its own pattern of rising and falling lines.

Common mistakes: Believing zero padding improves resolution. Forgetting to window and then mistaking leakage for real frequency content. Reading amplitudes from a windowed FFT without correcting for the window gain. Choosing a frame so short that two harmonics merge, or so long that a quick event is smeared. Plotting bins above N/2 as if they were new frequencies.

What exams ask: Compute the frequency resolution for given fs and N; find the minimum recording length to separate two tones; explain leakage with the periodic-extension picture or the window-convolution picture; compare rectangular, Hann and Hamming windows by side lobe level and main lobe width; explain what zero padding does; describe the STFT and the time-frequency trade-off.

Recap: Frequency resolution is about fs/N, which is 1/T, so separating close tones needs a long enough recording. Leakage happens when a tone does not fit a whole number of cycles in the block, and it spreads glare across all bins. Windows like Hann (side lobe about -31 dB) and Hamming (about -41 dB) cut the glare compared with rectangular (about -13 dB) but widen the main lobe. Zero padding smooths the picture without adding resolution. Averaging steadies noisy spectra, and the spectrogram shows how a spectrum changes over time.
key_points: Frequency resolution is about fs/N = 1/T: separating tones 10 Hz apart needs about 0.1 s of data.
Leakage comes from the jump between the end and start of a block when a tone has a non-whole number of cycles.
Cutting a block is a rectangular window; its sinc-like spectrum smears every line in the spectrum.
Side lobes: rectangular about -13 dB, Hann about -31 dB, Hamming about -41 dB; Hann and Hamming main lobes are about twice as wide.
A tone halfway between bins loses about 4 dB with rectangular and about 1.4 dB with Hann.
Window gain must be corrected when reading amplitudes (Hann shows about N A/4 instead of N A/2).
Zero padding gives a smoother plot, not more resolution; only more real data does.
The spectrogram (STFT) stacks windowed FFTs of short frames, e.g. 25 ms frames with a 10 ms hop.
lessons.tip: Before trusting a peak in any spectrum, ask: how long was the block, which window was used, and could this be leakage from a bigger peak nearby?
lessons.task: Install any free spectrum analyser or spectrogram app on your phone. Whistle a steady note, then slide it up and down, and watch the line move. Then hold the phone near a running fan or fridge and find the strongest low-frequency peak; note whether it sits near 50 Hz, 100 Hz or somewhere else.

quiz.q: With fs = 8000 Hz and N = 1024, what is the bin spacing?
quiz.explain: Bin spacing = fs/N = 8000/1024 = 7.8125 Hz.

quiz.q: What causes spectral leakage when a pure tone is analysed with the DFT?
options: Using the FFT instead of the DFT
The block not containing a whole number of cycles, creating a jump at the edges
quiz.explain: The DFT treats the block as periodic; a non-whole number of cycles makes an edge jump that spreads energy into other bins.

quiz.q: Which window has the lowest highest side lobe among these?
quiz.explain: Hamming's highest side lobe is about -41 dB, lower than Hann's -31 dB and rectangular's -13 dB.

quiz.q: What does zero padding a block before the FFT do?
options: Improves the ability to separate close tones
Samples the same spectrum more finely, giving a smoother plot
quiz.explain: Zeros add no information; the DFT just samples the same DTFT at more points.

quiz.q: In speech processing at fs = 16 kHz, how many samples is a 25 ms frame?
quiz.explain: 0.025 s x 16000 samples per second = 400 samples.

lessons.title: Digital Filter Basics: Specifications, Ideal Filters and Linear Phase
lessons.content:
Think of the sieve your mother uses in the kitchen to sift flour for pitha. Fine flour passes through, lumps stay behind. A good sieve has holes of a clear size, lets almost all the fine flour through, and blocks almost all the lumps. A digital filter is a sieve for frequencies. Before designing one, an engineer must write down, with numbers, which frequencies should pass, which should be blocked, how strictly, and how much the signal may be delayed or distorted. This lesson is about those specifications, why a perfect sieve is impossible, and why linear phase is such a prized property.

What a digital filter is: A digital filter is an LTI system, described by a difference equation or an impulse response h[n], whose frequency response H(e^jw) is shaped on purpose. You already know how to compute H(e^jw) from h[n] or from H(z). Now we turn the question around: given what we want H(e^jw) to look like, how do we describe that wish precisely? The next two lessons then show how to find coefficients that meet the wish, with FIR windowing and IIR bilinear design.

The four basic types: A low-pass filter keeps frequencies below a cutoff and removes those above, for example removing hiss from a voice. A high-pass filter does the opposite, for example removing slow baseline drift from an ECG. A band-pass filter keeps only a range, for example 300 to 3400 Hz for telephone speech. A band-stop or notch filter removes a narrow range, for example 50 Hz mains hum. Most other filters, such as equalizers, are combinations of these.

The ideal low-pass: The dream filter has |H| = 1 exactly for |w| below the cutoff wc and |H| = 0 exactly above it, with zero phase. Its impulse response, from the inverse DTFT, is h_ideal[n] = sin(wc n)/(pi n), with value wc/pi at n = 0. For wc = pi/2 the values are 0.5 at n = 0, 0.3183 at n = plus and minus 1, 0 at plus and minus 2, -0.1061 at plus and minus 3, and so on, shrinking slowly like 1/n forever in both directions.

Why the ideal is impossible: That impulse response has two fatal problems. First, it is infinitely long, so no finite computer can store it or run it as an FIR filter. Second, it is non-zero for negative n, which means the output at time n depends on future inputs: it is non-causal. A real-time filter cannot see the future. Also, its sum of absolute values grows without bound, so it is not even BIBO stable. So all practical filters are approximations: they allow a little error in the passband, a little leakage in the stopband, and a gradual region in between.

The specification, a tolerance box: A practical low-pass specification has five numbers. The passband edge wp: frequencies from 0 to wp must pass. The stopband edge ws: frequencies from ws to pi must be blocked. The transition band between wp and ws, where we do not care exactly what happens. The passband ripple delta_p: |H| must stay between 1 - delta_p and 1 + delta_p. The stopband ripple delta_s: |H| must stay below delta_s. Draw it as a box: the response curve must pass through the open windows of the box.

Worked specification in hertz: A telephone-style low-pass with fs = 8000 Hz might ask for: passband 0 to 1000 Hz, stopband from 1500 Hz to 4000 Hz, passband ripple delta_p = 0.01, stopband attenuation 40 dB. In digital frequency: wp = 2 pi (1000)/8000 = pi/4, ws = 2 pi (1500)/8000 = 3 pi/8. The transition band is 500 Hz wide, or pi/8 in radians. Narrow transition bands are expensive: the narrower you make it, the longer the filter must be.

Specs for the other types: A high-pass box is the mirror image: a stopband from 0 to ws, a transition band, then a passband from wp to pi, with ws below wp. A band-pass has two transition bands and two stopbands, one on each side of the passband, so it needs four edge frequencies. A notch for 50 Hz hum is usually specified by its centre frequency, its depth in dB at the centre, and its width, for example the band where the attenuation is more than 3 dB. Writing all edges both in hertz and in radians per sample avoids most confusion later.

Ripple and attenuation in dB: Engineers often state ripple and attenuation in decibels. A passband ripple of delta_p = 0.01 means |H| between 0.99 and 1.01, which is between about -0.087 dB and +0.086 dB. A stopband ripple of delta_s = 0.01 means an attenuation of 20 log10(0.01) = -40 dB. delta_s = 0.001 means -60 dB. Every factor of 10 smaller in delta_s adds 20 dB of attenuation, and also adds filter length or order.

Phase matters too: Magnitude says how much of each frequency survives. Phase says how much each is delayed. If different frequencies are delayed by different amounts, a sharp pulse comes out smeared, a phenomenon called phase distortion. For audio, the ear is fairly tolerant of mild phase distortion. For ECG, radar pulses, digital data and images, the shape of the waveform carries the information, so phase distortion can change the diagnosis or the decoded bits.

Group delay: The group delay tau(w) = -d(phase)/dw tells how many samples a narrow group of frequencies around w is delayed. If tau is the same constant for all w, every frequency is delayed equally, and the output is just a delayed copy of the filtered input, no smearing. A constant group delay happens exactly when the phase is a straight line through the origin: phase = -alpha w. That is called linear phase.

How FIR gets linear phase, symmetry: An FIR filter of length N whose coefficients are symmetric, h[n] = h[N-1-n], has exactly linear phase with delay alpha = (N-1)/2 samples. Worked example: h = [1, 2, 1], N = 3. Then H(e^jw) = 1 + 2 e^(-jw) + e^(-j2w). Factor e^(-jw): H = e^(-jw)(e^(jw) + 2 + e^(-jw)) = e^(-jw)(2 + 2 cos w). The bracket is real and never negative, so the phase is exactly -w, a delay of exactly 1 sample, which is (3-1)/2. The magnitude 2 + 2 cos w is 4 at w = 0, 3.08 at w = 1 rad, 1.17 at w = 2 rad, and 0 at w = pi, so it is a simple low-pass. A 7-tap symmetric filter delays by 3 samples, which at fs = 8000 Hz is 0.375 ms.

The four types of linear-phase FIR: Type I: symmetric, odd length (like [1, 2, 1]); it can make any filter type. Type II: symmetric, even length; H is forced to zero at w = pi, so it cannot be a high-pass. Type III: antisymmetric, h[n] = -h[N-1-n], odd length; forced zeros at w = 0 and w = pi, used for differentiators and Hilbert transformers. Type IV: antisymmetric, even length; forced zero at w = 0, so it cannot be a low-pass. Exams like to ask which type can or cannot realise a given filter.

Can IIR filters have linear phase: A causal, stable IIR filter cannot have exactly linear phase. IIR filters are efficient, giving sharp magnitude responses with few coefficients, but their phase bends, especially near the cutoff. When the whole signal is recorded first, an offline trick removes this: filter forward, reverse the result, filter again, and reverse back. The phase shifts cancel and the result has zero phase, though the magnitude response is squared. MATLAB and SciPy call this filtfilt. It is not possible in real time because it needs the future.

The trade-off triangle: In practice you juggle four things: how sharp the transition is, how small the ripples are, how long or complex the filter is, and how much delay you can accept. A linear-phase FIR with a narrow transition and 60 dB attenuation may need many taps and a delay of many samples. An IIR filter meets the same magnitude spec with far fewer coefficients but with non-linear phase. Choosing is engineering, not a single right answer.

Reading a response plot: When you look at a designed filter's magnitude plot in dB, check four things in order. Is the passband flat within the allowed ripple? Does the curve fall through the transition band without bumps? Is every stopband lobe below the required attenuation line, including the highest one near the transition? And finally, is the phase plot a straight line (for FIR) or at least smooth in the passband (for IIR)? A design that fails any one of these must be changed, usually by increasing the length or order.

Normalised frequency, a warning: Different tools use different units. Some express frequency in radians per sample (0 to pi), some as a fraction of fs (0 to 0.5), and MATLAB often normalises to the Nyquist frequency (0 to 1, where 1 means fs/2). A cutoff of 1000 Hz at fs = 8000 Hz is pi/4 rad per sample, 0.125 of fs, or 0.25 of Nyquist. Always check which convention a function uses; mixing them is a classic bug.

Real life example 1, ECG monitors in a hospital: An ECG machine in a Dhaka hospital filters the heart signal with a high-pass to remove breathing-related baseline wander, a low-pass to cut muscle noise, and often a notch at 50 Hz for mains hum. Because doctors read the exact shape of the waves, designers prefer linear-phase FIR filters or offline zero-phase filtering for diagnostic recordings, so that the waveform shape is not distorted.

Real life example 2, a digital crossover in a speaker: A powered speaker splits music into a low band for the woofer and a high band for the tweeter. The low-pass and high-pass must meet at the crossover frequency so that the sum sounds natural. Engineers specify the crossover frequency, the slope of each filter in dB per octave, and the phase behaviour, so that the two outputs add up correctly in the air.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students forget the transition band and draw a brick wall. Others confuse ripple delta_s with attenuation in dB or forget the minus sign. Many think every FIR filter is linear phase; only symmetric or antisymmetric ones are. Exams ask you to convert a hertz specification into digital frequencies, express ripples in dB, explain why the ideal filter is non-causal and unrealisable, show that a given symmetric h[n] has linear phase and find its delay, and state which FIR type suits a low-pass or high-pass.

Recap: A filter specification is a tolerance box: passband edge, stopband edge, transition band, passband ripple and stopband attenuation, usually converted from hertz with w = 2 pi f/fs. The ideal brick-wall filter has an infinite, non-causal sinc impulse response, so real filters approximate it. Phase matters when waveform shape matters, and constant group delay means linear phase. Symmetric FIR filters have exact linear phase with delay (N-1)/2, as in h = [1, 2, 1] with a 1-sample delay. IIR filters are efficient but not linear phase in real time.
key_points: Four basic filters: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop (notch).
The ideal low-pass has h[n] = sin(wc n)/(pi n): infinitely long and non-causal, so it cannot be built.
Specs form a tolerance box: wp, ws, transition band, passband ripple and stopband attenuation.
Convert hertz with w = 2 pi f/fs: 1000 Hz at 8 kHz is pi/4; delta_s = 0.01 means 40 dB.
Group delay = -d(phase)/dw; constant group delay means linear phase and no waveform smearing.
Symmetric FIR h[n] = h[N-1-n] has exact linear phase with delay (N-1)/2 samples.
h = [1, 2, 1] gives H = e^(-jw)(2 + 2cos w): delay 1 sample, gain 4 at DC and 0 at pi.
Type II cannot be high-pass, Type IV cannot be low-pass; causal IIR cannot be exactly linear phase.
lessons.tip: For every filter problem, first draw the tolerance box with wp, ws and the ripples marked in both hertz and radians. Half the exam marks come from getting the specification right.
lessons.task: Write a specification for a filter that keeps a guitar's sound below 5 kHz and removes hiss above 6 kHz with 50 dB attenuation, at fs = 44,100 Hz. Convert both edges to radians per sample and to fractions of Nyquist, and draw the tolerance box.

quiz.q: Why can the ideal brick-wall low-pass filter not be built?
options: Its impulse response is infinitely long and non-causal
It needs a sampling rate above 1 MHz
quiz.explain: h[n] = sin(wc n)/(pi n) extends forever in both directions, so it needs infinite length and future inputs.

quiz.q: With fs = 8000 Hz, a passband edge of 1000 Hz is what digital frequency?
A stopband ripple of delta_s = 0.01 corresponds to an attenuation of:
quiz.explain: 20 log10(0.01) = -40 dB, so the stopband is attenuated by 40 dB.

quiz.q: What is the delay of the symmetric FIR filter h = [1, 2, 1]?
quiz.explain: H = e^(-jw)(2 + 2cos w), so the phase is -w: a constant delay of (N-1)/2 = 1 sample.

quiz.q: Which symmetric linear-phase FIR type cannot be used for a high-pass filter because H is forced to zero at w = pi?
quiz.explain: Type II (symmetric, even length) always has a zero at w = pi, so it cannot pass the highest frequencies.

lessons.title: FIR Filter Design by Windowing: From the Ideal Filter to Real Coefficients
lessons.content:
Imagine you want a perfect sieve for rice: every grain below a certain size falls through, every grain above stays, and nothing in between gets confused. In DSP the perfect low-pass filter is exactly that sieve: every frequency below the cutoff passes untouched, every frequency above is removed completely. The bad news is that this perfect sieve needs an infinitely long list of coefficients that starts before time zero. The good news is that we can cut that list short in a clever way and get a filter that is very close to perfect. That clever cutting is called the window method, and it is the most common way students design their first FIR filter.

Where we are: In the last lesson you learned filter specs (passband, stopband, transition band, ripple, attenuation in dB) and why a symmetric FIR filter has linear phase. Now we answer the practical question: given a cutoff frequency and a quality target, how do we actually compute the numbers h[0], h[1], ..., h[N-1] that go into the filter equation y[n] = sum h[k] x[n-k]? The window method gives a recipe you can do with a calculator.

Step 1, the ideal low-pass impulse response: An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff wc (in radians per sample, between 0 and pi) has frequency response 1 for |w| < wc and 0 for wc < |w| <= pi. If you take the inverse DTFT of that rectangle in frequency, you get h_ideal[n] = sin(wc n) / (pi n), with the value at n = 0 equal to wc/pi. This is the famous sinc shape: a tall middle value and ripples that slowly die away on both sides, forever. It never ends in either direction, so it is non-causal and infinitely long. No real chip can store infinite coefficients or look into the future.

Step 2, shift so it can be causal: We decide to keep N coefficients, with N odd for a nice symmetric filter. We shift the sinc to the right by a = (N-1)/2 samples, so its peak sits in the middle of our list. The desired response becomes h_d[n] = sin(wc (n - a)) / (pi (n - a)) for n = 0 to N-1, with h_d[a] = wc/pi. Shifting only adds a delay of a samples, which shows up as linear phase. The magnitude is not changed. Because the sinc is symmetric around its peak, our shifted list is symmetric too: h_d[n] = h_d[N-1-n]. That symmetry is what gives the finished filter linear phase.

Step 3, truncate and see the damage: Simply keeping N values and throwing the rest away is the same as multiplying h_d by a rectangular window, a window that is 1 inside and 0 outside. Multiplying in time means convolving in frequency. The rectangle's spectrum has a main lobe and side lobes, and convolving the ideal brick-wall response with it smears the sharp edge into a transition band and adds ripples. Near the edge there is an overshoot of about 9 percent that does not shrink when you make N bigger. This is the Gibbs phenomenon, the same thing you saw with Fourier series of a square wave in Math III. More taps make the transition narrower, but the ripple height stays stuck.

Why windows help: The trouble comes from the sudden jump at the ends of the rectangle. If instead we multiply h_d[n] by a window that tapers smoothly to small values at both ends, the side lobes of the window's spectrum become much lower. Lower side lobes mean smaller ripples in the passband and stopband. The price is a wider main lobe, which means a wider transition band for the same N. Every window is a trade-off between ripple (side lobes) and sharpness (main lobe width).

The three windows you must know: The rectangular window is w[n] = 1. The Hann window is w[n] = 0.5 - 0.5 cos(2 pi n / (N-1)). The Hamming window is w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 cos(2 pi n / (N-1)), for n = 0 to N-1. Hann goes exactly to 0 at the ends. Hamming stops at 0.08 at the ends, and that small change in its numbers is chosen to push down its highest side lobe. Blackman and Kaiser windows exist too; Kaiser even has a knob to trade ripple against width, but the three above are the exam favourites.

The numbers that come with each window: These are approximate values from the standard textbook table. Rectangular: highest side lobe about -13 dB, stopband attenuation of the finished filter about 21 dB, transition width about 0.9/N (as a fraction of the sampling rate). Hann: side lobe about -31 dB, stopband about 44 dB, transition about 3.1/N. Hamming: side lobe about -41 dB, stopband about 53 dB, transition about 3.3/N. Notice the pattern. Rectangular is sharpest but leaks badly. Hann and Hamming give much better stopbands but need roughly three to four times more taps for the same transition width.

Picking a window from a spec: The stopband attenuation of the window method depends almost only on the window type, not on N. So first look at the required stopband.
