If the spec says at least 40 dB, the rectangular window (21 dB) fails, Hann (44 dB) passes, Hamming (53 dB) passes with margin. If the spec says 50 dB, only Hamming among these three passes. After choosing the window, use the transition width to choose N.

Choosing the length, worked: Say fs = 8000 Hz, the passband ends at 1000 Hz and the stopband starts at 1400 Hz, with 50 dB attenuation needed. The window must be Hamming. The transition width is 400 Hz, which as a fraction of fs is 400 / 8000 = 0.05. Using transition about 3.3/N, we need N about 3.3 / 0.05 = 66. We prefer an odd length for a symmetric type I filter, so we take N = 67. The cutoff wc is usually placed in the middle of the transition band, 1200 Hz here, which is wc = 2 pi x 1200 / 8000 = 0.3 pi radians per sample.

A tiny full design, worked by hand: Let us design a 7-tap Hamming low-pass with wc = pi/2, which is a quarter of the sampling rate. N = 7, so a = 3. Compute h_d[n] = sin(pi/2 (n-3)) / (pi (n-3)). At n = 3 the value is wc/pi = 0.5. At n = 2 and 4: sin(pi/2) / pi = 1/pi = 0.3183. At n = 1 and 5: sin(pi) / (2 pi) = 0. At n = 0 and 6: sin(3 pi/2) / (3 pi) = -1 / (3 pi) = -0.1061. So h_d = [-0.1061, 0, 0.3183, 0.5, 0.3183, 0, -0.1061]. Notice the symmetry.

Applying the Hamming window: With N = 7, w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 cos(2 pi n / 6). This gives w = [0.08, 0.31, 0.77, 1, 0.77, 0.31, 0.08]. Multiply term by term: h[0] = -0.1061 x 0.08 = -0.0085, h[1] = 0, h[2] = 0.3183 x 0.77 = 0.2451, h[3] = 0.5, then the mirror image. Final filter: h = [-0.0085, 0, 0.2451, 0.5, 0.2451, 0, -0.0085]. Checking with a script: the DC gain (sum of coefficients) is about 0.973, the gain at the cutoff pi/2 is exactly 0.5 (about -6 dB, typical for window designs at wc), and the gain at pi is about 0.027. A 7-tap filter is tiny, so the DC gain is a bit below 1; you could divide every coefficient by 0.973 to make it exactly 1. Real designs use far more taps.

Using the filter: Now the filter equation is y[n] = -0.0085 x[n] + 0.2451 x[n-2] + 0.5 x[n-3] + 0.2451 x[n-4] - 0.0085 x[n-6]. Two coefficients are zero, which saves two multiplies, and because of symmetry a smart implementation adds x[n] and x[n-6] first, then multiplies once. Symmetry nearly halves the multiplications. The delay of this filter is a = 3 samples for every frequency, which is the linear phase promise.

Other filter types from the same recipe: A high-pass filter can be made as delta minus low-pass: h_hp[n] = delta[n - a] - h_lp[n]. A band-pass filter is the difference of two low-pass filters with different cutoffs. A band-stop is delta minus a band-pass. The same window is then applied. So once you can do low-pass, you can do all four. One warning: a high-pass or band-stop with even N would have a forced zero at w = pi, so use odd N for those.

Other FIR design methods, named only: The frequency sampling method picks the desired response at N equally spaced frequencies and uses the inverse DFT to get h[n]. The Parks-McClellan (equiripple) method uses an optimisation algorithm to get the shortest filter for a given spec; it is what tools like MATLAB firpm and scipy remez compute. In practice engineers use such tools, but the window method is the one you must understand and do by hand.

Real life example 1, cleaning a voice recording: A student in Rajshahi records a lecture on a phone at 8 kHz, but there is a high-pitched hiss from a ceiling fan regulator above 2 kHz. Speech intelligibility mostly lives below about 3.4 kHz, but this hiss is annoying. She designs a Hamming low-pass with cutoff around 2.5 kHz and about 60 taps in a Python notebook, applies it, and the hiss drops while voices stay clear. Because the FIR has linear phase, consonants like t and k keep their sharp shape instead of being smeared.

Real life example 2, a digital audio crossover: A home speaker sold in Dhaka's Elephant Road market may split music into bass for the woofer and treble for the tweeter. Many digital crossovers use linear phase FIR filters so the two speakers' sounds line up in time when they recombine. A low-pass and a matching high-pass made as delta minus low-pass add back to a pure delay, so nothing is lost at the crossover point.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the n = a case, where sin(0)/0 must be replaced by wc/pi. Using wc in hertz instead of radians per sample; always convert with wc = 2 pi fc / fs. Mixing up N (number of taps) and the order N - 1. Thinking more taps reduce the Gibbs ripple of a rectangular window: they only narrow the transition. Using the window formula with N instead of N-1 in the denominator; different books differ, so state which form you use.

What exams ask: Write the ideal impulse response for a low-pass, high-pass or band-pass filter. Design an N-tap filter with a given window and list the coefficients. Choose a window and length from a spec of stopband attenuation and transition width. Explain the Gibbs phenomenon and why tapered windows reduce ripple. Compare rectangular, Hann and Hamming using side lobe level and main lobe width. Show that the result has linear phase.

Recap: The ideal filter is an infinite sinc. Shift it by (N-1)/2, keep N samples, multiply by a window, and you have a causal, linear phase FIR filter. The window type sets the ripple and stopband (rectangular about 21 dB, Hann about 44 dB, Hamming about 53 dB); the length N sets the transition width (roughly 0.9/N, 3.1/N, 3.3/N of fs). Next lesson we design IIR filters, which reach a sharp cutoff with far fewer coefficients but give up linear phase.
key_points: The ideal low-pass has h[n] = sin(wc n)/(pi n), infinitely long and non-causal, with value wc/pi at n = 0.
Window method: shift the sinc by a = (N-1)/2, keep N samples, multiply by a window w[n].
Plain truncation (rectangular window) causes Gibbs ripple of about 9 percent that does not shrink with more taps.
Tapered windows lower side lobes (rect -13 dB, Hann -31 dB, Hamming -41 dB) but widen the transition band.
Stopband attenuation depends on the window type (about 21, 44, 53 dB); the length N sets the transition width (about 0.9/N, 3.1/N, 3.3/N of fs).
Worked 7-tap Hamming low-pass at wc = pi/2: h = [-0.0085, 0, 0.2451, 0.5, 0.2451, 0, -0.0085], gain 0.5 at the cutoff.
Symmetric coefficients give linear phase with a delay of (N-1)/2 samples and let you halve the multiplies.
High-pass = delta minus low-pass; band-pass = difference of two low-pass filters; Parks-McClellan and frequency sampling are the other methods.
lessons.tip: Keep a one-line table in your notebook: window, side lobe, stopband, transition. Rect -13/21/0.9, Hann -31/44/3.1, Hamming -41/53/3.3. With that table, most window-design exam questions become plug-in arithmetic.
lessons.task: With a calculator or a short Python script, design a 9-tap Hamming low-pass with wc = pi/4. Compute h_d[n], the window values and the final coefficients, check the symmetry, and add the coefficients to see how close the DC gain is to 1.

quiz.q: What is the value of the ideal low-pass impulse response sin(wc n)/(pi n) at n = 0?
quiz.explain: The limit of sin(wc n)/(pi n) as n goes to 0 is wc/pi, so the middle tap equals wc/pi (0.5 for wc = pi/2).

quiz.q: Why does plain truncation (rectangular window) give an overshoot that does not go away with more taps?
options: Because the coefficients are not symmetric
Because of the Gibbs phenomenon from the sharp edges of the rectangle
Because the sampling rate is too low
quiz.explain: The rectangle's sudden ends produce high side lobes; more taps narrow the transition but the Gibbs overshoot stays about 9 percent.

quiz.q: A spec needs at least 50 dB of stopband attenuation. Which of these windows meets it?
quiz.explain: Typical stopband attenuation: rectangular about 21 dB, Hann about 44 dB, Hamming about 53 dB, so only Hamming passes.

quiz.q: With fs = 8000 Hz and a Hamming window, what length is needed for a 400 Hz transition band?
options: About 66 taps, so 67 for odd length
quiz.explain: The transition is 400/8000 = 0.05 of fs; N is about 3.3/0.05 = 66, rounded to 67 to keep N odd.

quiz.q: What does symmetric coefficients h[n] = h[N-1-n] give an FIR filter?
options: A gain of exactly 1 at all frequencies
Linear phase with a constant delay of (N-1)/2 samples
quiz.explain: Symmetric FIR filters delay every frequency by the same (N-1)/2 samples, which is linear phase; they also let you share multiplies.

lessons.title: IIR Filter Design with the Bilinear Transform
lessons.content:
Think about how a tailor in Islampur copies a good shirt. He does not invent a new design from scratch. He takes a shirt that already fits well, lays it on the cloth, and traces it, adjusting a little where the new cloth stretches differently. IIR filter design works the same way. Analog engineers spent decades perfecting filters like Butterworth and Chebyshev with resistors, capacitors and inductors. Instead of inventing digital filters from zero, we take those proven analog designs and translate them into the z-domain. The most popular translation tool is the bilinear transform, and the small adjustment for the stretch is called pre-warping.

Why IIR at all: In the last lesson a decent FIR low-pass needed around 67 taps. An IIR filter feeds the output back, y[n] depends on old y values, so its impulse response goes on forever with only a few coefficients. A fourth-order IIR filter has about nine or ten coefficients and can give a sharper cutoff than an FIR with dozens of taps. Less computation per sample means less battery and cheaper chips. The price: IIR filters usually do not have linear phase, and because of feedback they can become unstable if designed or implemented carelessly.

The overall recipe: First, write the digital spec (passband edge, stopband edge, ripple, attenuation). Second, convert the digital edge frequencies to analog ones using the pre-warp formula. Third, design an analog prototype filter H(s) that meets the analog spec. Fourth, replace s by the bilinear expression to get H(z). Fifth, check the response and write the difference equation. We will walk through each step and finish with a complete worked first-order design.

Analog prototypes in one paragraph: A Butterworth low-pass of order N has squared magnitude |H(jOmega)|^2 = 1 / (1 + (Omega/Omega_c)^(2N)). It is maximally flat in the passband, has no ripple at all, and is exactly -3 dB at the cutoff Omega_c. Far above the cutoff it falls by 20N dB per decade. For example, a fourth-order Butterworth is about -24 dB at twice the cutoff. Chebyshev type I filters allow ripple in the passband to get a steeper fall; Chebyshev type II put the ripple in the stopband; elliptic filters ripple in both and are the steepest for a given order. For this course, Butterworth is the one to know well.

The bilinear transform: The bilinear transform replaces s with s = (2/T) (1 - z^-1) / (1 + z^-1), where T = 1/fs is the sampling period. It comes from approximating an integrator using the trapezoidal rule, the same trapezoid you met in Numerical Methods. Wherever s appears in H(s), you substitute this fraction and simplify. The result is a ratio of polynomials in z^-1, which is exactly the H(z) of a difference equation.

Why it is a good mapping: The bilinear transform maps the whole left half of the s-plane into the inside of the unit circle in the z-plane, and the jOmega axis onto the unit circle itself. Because a stable analog filter has all poles in the left half-plane, the digital filter will have all poles inside the unit circle, so stability is preserved automatically. And because the entire infinite analog frequency axis is squeezed onto one trip around the unit circle, there is no aliasing at all. This is the big advantage over other methods.

The catch, frequency warping: Squeezing an infinite axis into a finite circle cannot be uniform. The relation between analog frequency Omega (rad/s) and digital frequency w (rad/sample) is Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2). For small w, tan(w/2) is about w/2 and the mapping is nearly linear, Omega is about w/T, which is what you would expect. But as w approaches pi, tan(w/2) shoots to infinity, so high frequencies are compressed more and more. If you ignore this, your digital cutoff lands at the wrong place.

Pre-warping, the fix: Before designing the analog filter, we take each important digital edge frequency w and compute the analog frequency that will land exactly there after the transform: Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2). We design the analog filter with these warped frequencies. After the bilinear transform, the warping and pre-warping cancel at those edges, and the digital filter hits the spec exactly where it matters. Other frequencies are still squeezed, which is why bilinear filters keep their flat or ripply shape but not their exact frequency spacing.

Worked example, step 1, the spec: We want a first-order Butterworth low-pass digital filter with cutoff fc = 1000 Hz at fs = 8000 Hz. In digital frequency, w_c = 2 pi fc / fs = 2 pi x 1000 / 8000 = pi/4 radians per sample. T = 1/8000 s, so 2/T = 16000.

Worked example, step 2, pre-warp: Omega_c = (2/T) tan(w_c / 2) = 16000 x tan(pi/8) = 16000 x 0.41421 = 6627.4 rad/s. Compare this with the naive value 2 pi x 1000 = 6283.2 rad/s. The pre-warped value is about 5 percent higher. If we had used 6283.2 rad/s without pre-warping, the digital cutoff would have landed near 953 Hz instead of 1000 Hz.

Worked example, step 3, the analog prototype: A first-order Butterworth low-pass is H(s) = Omega_c / (s + Omega_c). Its gain is 1 at DC and 1/sqrt(2), which is -3 dB, at Omega_c.

Worked example, step 4, substitute: Put s = (2/T)(1 - z^-1)/(1 + z^-1) into H(s). Multiply top and bottom by (1 + z^-1) and divide everything by 2/T. Let K = Omega_c T / 2 = tan(pi/8) = 0.41421. We get H(z) = K (1 + z^-1) / ((1 + K) + (K - 1) z^-1). Dividing by (1 + K) to make the leading denominator coefficient 1: H(z) = [K/(1+K)] (1 + z^-1) / (1 + [(K-1)/(K+1)] z^-1). Numerically K/(1+K) = 0.29289 and (K-1)/(K+1) = -0.41421. So H(z) = 0.2929 (1 + z^-1) / (1 - 0.4142 z^-1).

Worked example, step 5, check and implement: The difference equation is y[n] = 0.4142 y[n-1] + 0.2929 x[n] + 0.2929 x[n-1]. Check the gains with a script: at DC (w = 0) the gain is 1; at w = pi/4, which is 1000 Hz, the gain is 0.7071, exactly -3 dB as designed; at w = pi, which is 4000 Hz, the gain is 0 because the zero at z = -1 kills it. The pole is at z = 0.4142, inside the unit circle, so the filter is stable. Its impulse response starts 0.2929, 0.4142, 0.1716, 0.0711, 0.0294 and keeps shrinking by a factor of 0.4142 forever: truly infinite.

Choosing the order, worked: Suppose the spec at fs = 8000 Hz is -3 dB at 1000 Hz and at least 20 dB of attenuation at 2000 Hz. Pre-warp both edges: Omega_p = 16000 x tan(pi/8) = 6627.4 rad/s and Omega_s = 16000 x tan(pi/4) = 16000 rad/s, a ratio of 2.414. For Butterworth, 20 dB attenuation means 1 + (Omega_s/Omega_p)^(2N) must reach 10^(20/10) = 100, so N >= log10(99) / (2 log10(2.414)) = 1.996 / 0.766 = 2.61. Orders must be whole numbers, so N = 3. If you forgot to pre-warp and used the plain ratio 2000/1000 = 2, you would get N >= 3.31 and pick N = 4, a bigger filter than needed. Warping actually helps a low-pass here, because it squeezes the stopband closer to pi.

Where the poles and zeros go: An analog Butterworth low-pass has no finite zeros; all its zeros sit at s = infinity. The bilinear transform sends s = infinity to z = -1, which is w = pi, the highest digital frequency. So a digital Butterworth low-pass of order N made this way has N zeros piled up at z = -1, which is why its response drops to exactly zero at fs/2. The poles land inside the unit circle near the passband. In our first-order example you can see both: one zero at z = -1 and one pole at z = 0.4142.

Higher orders: For a higher-order Butterworth you find the order N from the pre-warped passband and stopband edges, write the analog H(s) from tables, apply the bilinear transform, and usually split the result into second-order sections for implementation. Doing this by hand above order two is tedious; scipy.signal.butter and MATLAB butter do exactly these steps, including the pre-warp, when you pass a digital cutoff.

Impulse invariance, named only: Another method samples the analog impulse response: h[n] = T h_a(nT). It keeps the time-domain shape and maps frequency linearly, but because sampling causes aliasing, it is only suitable for low-pass and band-pass filters whose analog response has already died down by fs/2. It is not used for high-pass filters. The bilinear transform has no aliasing, which is why it is the default.

FIR versus IIR, the honest comparison: IIR wins on efficiency, a sharp cutoff with few coefficients and low delay. FIR wins on exact linear phase, guaranteed stability, and good behaviour with fixed-point arithmetic. Audio equalizers, hearing aids and simple sensor smoothing often use IIR. Data communications, image processing and anything where waveform shape matters often use FIR.

Real life example 1, a guitar tuner app: A tuner app on a phone in Mymensingh records at 48 kHz, but a guitar's low E string is about 82 Hz and the useful pitch energy sits in the lower range. A low-order Butterworth IIR low-pass, designed with the bilinear transform, removes fan noise and hiss before pitch detection at a tiny cost per sample, leaving the phone's battery happy.

Real life example 2, a weighing scale: A digital scale at a Kawran Bazar shop reads a load cell through an ADC. The raw reading jitters because of vibration. A first-order IIR low-pass, exactly like our worked example but with a much lower cutoff, smooths the number so the display settles quickly. Phase does not matter here, only a calm, steady reading, so IIR is the natural choice.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to pre-warp, then wondering why the cutoff is off. Pre-warping with degrees instead of radians in tan. Using fc in hertz where w in radians per sample is needed. Forgetting to normalise so the a0 coefficient is 1. Writing the feedback term with the wrong sign: if H(z) has 1 - 0.4142 z^-1 in the denominator, the difference equation has +0.4142 y[n-1].

What exams ask: State the bilinear transform and derive Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2). Explain why it preserves stability and has no aliasing. Design a first or second order Butterworth digital filter with pre-warping and give H(z) and the difference equation. Compare bilinear and impulse invariance. Compare FIR and IIR filters.

Recap: IIR design borrows analog prototypes such as Butterworth. The bilinear transform s = (2/T)(1 - z^-1)/(1 + z^-1) maps stable analog filters to stable digital ones without aliasing, but warps frequency as Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2). Pre-warp the edge frequencies first. Our worked filter for 1 kHz at 8 kHz is H(z) = 0.2929(1 + z^-1)/(1 - 0.4142 z^-1). If you remember only three things, remember the substitution, the tan warping formula, and that pre-warping comes before the analog design, never after. With those, any first or second order design is a page of careful algebra. Next, we look at how to arrange these equations inside a chip: filter structures.
key_points: IIR filters use feedback, so a few coefficients give a sharp cutoff, but phase is not linear and stability must be checked.
Recipe: digital spec, pre-warp edges, analog prototype H(s), bilinear substitution, check H(z).
Butterworth: |H|^2 = 1/(1 + (Omega/Omega_c)^(2N)), maximally flat, -3 dB at cutoff, 20N dB per decade fall.
Bilinear transform: s = (2/T)(1 - z^-1)/(1 + z^-1); left half-plane maps inside the unit circle, so stability is kept and there is no aliasing.
Frequency warping: Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2); pre-warp each critical edge so it lands exactly right.
Worked: fs = 8 kHz, fc = 1 kHz gives Omega_c = 6627.4 rad/s (not 6283.2) and H(z) = 0.2929(1 + z^-1)/(1 - 0.4142 z^-1).
Impulse invariance samples h_a(t) and suffers aliasing, so it is not used for high-pass filters.
Choose IIR for efficiency and low delay, FIR for linear phase and robustness.
lessons.tip: Always write the pre-warp line first in an exam answer, even when the question forgets to ask. Examiners look for Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2), and it saves you from a cutoff that lands a few percent off.
lessons.task: Repeat the worked design for fc = 2000 Hz at fs = 8000 Hz. Compute w_c, K = tan(w_c/2), then b0 = K/(1+K) and a1 = (K-1)/(K+1). Write the difference equation and check by hand that the DC gain is 1.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to choose an IIR filter over an FIR filter?
options: IIR filters always have linear phase
It needs far fewer coefficients for a sharp cutoff
IIR filters can never be unstable
quiz.explain: Feedback lets an IIR filter reach a sharp cutoff with few coefficients; it gives up linear phase and needs a stability check.

quiz.q: Which formula describes the frequency warping of the bilinear transform?
quiz.explain: The bilinear transform maps the digital frequency w to Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2), which is nearly linear only for small w.

quiz.q: For fs = 8000 Hz and fc = 1000 Hz, what is the pre-warped analog cutoff?
quiz.explain: Omega_c = 16000 x tan(pi/8) = 16000 x 0.41421 = 6627.4 rad/s, about 5 percent above 2 pi x 1000.

quiz.q: Why does the bilinear transform keep a stable analog filter stable?
options: It maps the left half s-plane to the inside of the unit circle
quiz.explain: Stable analog poles lie in the left half-plane, which the bilinear transform maps inside the unit circle, so the digital poles are stable.

quiz.q: For H(z) = 0.2929(1 + z^-1)/(1 - 0.4142 z^-1), what is the difference equation?
quiz.explain: A denominator 1 - 0.4142 z^-1 means y[n] - 0.4142 y[n-1] equals the numerator terms, so the feedback term is +0.4142 y[n-1].

lessons.title: Filter Structures: Direct Form, Transposed, Cascade and Parallel
lessons.content:
Two cooks can follow the same biryani recipe and still arrange their kitchens very differently. One keeps all spices in one big rack, another keeps small trays next to each pot. The biryani tastes the same on a good day, but when something goes wrong, like a slightly wrong measure, one kitchen survives it better than the other. Filter structures are the kitchen arrangement of DSP. The same H(z) can be built from delays, multipliers and adders in several ways. With perfect arithmetic they all give identical output. With real chips, which store numbers in a limited number of bits, some arrangements are far more robust, cheaper or faster than others.

The three building blocks: Every digital filter structure is drawn with only three blocks. A unit delay, drawn as a box with z^-1, stores a sample and hands it out one sample later. A multiplier scales a signal by a constant coefficient. An adder sums two or more signals. A structure is just a wiring diagram of these blocks. Counting them tells you the cost: delays are memory, multipliers are the expensive operations, adders are cheap.

The general filter we want to build: A filter with M zeros and N poles has H(z) = B(z)/A(z) = (b0 + b1 z^-1 + ... + bM z^-M) / (1 + a1 z^-1 + ... + aN z^-N). Its difference equation is y[n] = b0 x[n] + b1 x[n-1] + ... + bM x[n-M] - a1 y[n-1] - ... - aN y[n-N]. Notice the minus signs on the a terms when the denominator is written with plus signs. Every structure below computes this same equation, just in a different order.

FIR transversal form: For an FIR filter there is no denominator. The input goes into a chain of delays, called a tapped delay line. At each tap the delayed sample is multiplied by h[k], and all the products are added. An N-tap FIR needs N multipliers, N - 1 adders and N - 1 delays. It is so common that DSP chips have special instructions for it. When the coefficients are symmetric, as in a linear phase filter, we first add the pair of samples that share a coefficient and then multiply once. For an odd N this needs only (N+1)/2 multipliers: our 7-tap filter from lesson 20 needs 4 instead of 7.

Direct form I: This is the difference equation drawn literally. One delay line holds past inputs x[n-1] ... x[n-M] for the numerator. A second delay line holds past outputs y[n-1] ... y[n-N] for the feedback. The output is the sum of all weighted taps. It needs M + N delays and M + N + 1 multipliers. Its big advantage for fixed-point chips is that everything is summed in one place, so a DSP can keep a single wide accumulator and round only once at the end.

Direct form II, the canonic form: Since B(z) and 1/A(z) are both LTI, their order can be swapped: first apply the feedback part, then the feedforward part. After swapping, both parts need delayed copies of the same internal signal, so the two delay lines can be merged into one. Define an internal signal w[n] = x[n] - a1 w[n-1] - a2 w[n-2] - ..., and then y[n] = b0 w[n] + b1 w[n-1] + b2 w[n-2] + .... Now only max(M, N) delays are needed, the minimum possible, which is why it is called canonic. The weakness: the internal signal w[n] can be much larger than x or y, so in fixed point it may overflow even when the output is fine.

Direct form II, stepped through by hand: Take H(z) = (1 + z^-1)/(1 - 0.5 z^-1). In direct form II the internal signal is w[n] = x[n] + 0.5 w[n-1], and the output is y[n] = w[n] + w[n-1]. Feed an impulse x = 1, 0, 0, .... Then w[0] = 1, w[1] = 0.5, w[2] = 0.25, and y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0.5 + 1 = 1.5, y[2] = 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75. Now do it with direct form I, y[n] = x[n] + x[n-1] + 0.5 y[n-1]: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0 + 1 + 0.5 = 1.5, y[2] = 0 + 0 + 0.75 = 0.75. Same output, but direct form II used one delay instead of two. That is the whole idea of the canonic form in three lines of arithmetic.

The biquad, worked count: A second-order section has H(z) = (b0 + b1 z^-1 + b2 z^-2)/(1 + a1 z^-1 + a2 z^-2). In direct form I it needs 4 delays (x[n-1], x[n-2], y[n-1], y[n-2]) and 5 multipliers. In direct form II it needs only 2 delays (w[n-1], w[n-2]) and still 5 multipliers. Both need 4 additions. This little five-coefficient block is called a biquad, and it is the Lego brick of IIR filtering.

Transposed forms: There is a neat rule: if you reverse the direction of every arrow in a signal flow graph, turn branch points into adders and adders into branch points, and swap input and output, the transfer function stays the same. This gives the transposed direct form II. In it, each delay holds a partial sum rather than a past sample. It has the same count as direct form II, and it behaves well in floating point. For example, the scipy function lfilter is documented as using the transposed direct form II structure.

Why high-order direct forms are dangerous: Suppose you design an eighth-order IIR filter and implement it as one big direct form with coefficients a1 ... a8. The poles are roots of an eighth-degree polynomial. When poles are clustered close together, as in sharp low-pass filters, tiny changes in the coefficients move the roots a lot. Rounding coefficients to 16 bits can shift a pole across the unit circle and make the filter unstable, or it can wreck the response. The higher the order, the worse the sensitivity.

Cascade form, the cure: Factor H(z) into a product of first and second order sections: H(z) = G x H1(z) x H2(z) x ... x HK(z). Each section is a small biquad with its own pole pair, so rounding a coefficient only disturbs that one pair. Complex conjugate poles are kept together in one section so all coefficients stay real. An eighth-order filter becomes four biquads in a row. As direct form it would need 9 + 8 = 17 multipliers; as four direct form II biquads it needs 4 x 5 = 20 multipliers and 8 delays. At a 48 kHz audio rate, those 20 multipliers mean 20 x 48,000 = 960,000 multiplications per second, easily handled by any modern phone chip. Three extra multiplies is a cheap price for a filter that will not blow up. This is why tools offer second-order sections output, such as scipy's sos format and sosfilt.

Cascade, worked: Take H(z) = 1 / (1 - 0.9 z^-1 + 0.2 z^-2). The denominator's roots are z = 0.5 and z = 0.4, so H(z) = [1/(1 - 0.5 z^-1)] x [1/(1 - 0.4 z^-1)]. Section 1: v[n] = x[n] + 0.5 v[n-1]. Section 2: y[n] = v[n] + 0.4 y[n-1]. Feed an impulse: the direct equation y[n] = x[n] + 0.9 y[n-1] - 0.2 y[n-2] gives 1, 0.9, 0.61, 0.369, 0.2101, and the cascade gives exactly the same numbers. Checked with a script.

Parallel form: Use partial fractions instead of factoring: H(z) = C + sum of first and second order sections, all fed the same input, with outputs added. For our example, H(z) = 5/(1 - 0.5 z^-1) - 4/(1 - 0.4 z^-1). Check at n = 0: 5 - 4 = 1. At n = 1: 5 x 0.5 - 4 x 0.4 = 2.5 - 1.6 = 0.9. Same as before. Parallel form is also robust to coefficient rounding, and because the branches are independent they can run on separate processor cores or hardware blocks at the same time.

Ordering and pairing in a cascade: In a real cascade you also decide which zeros go with which poles and in what order the sections run. A common rule is to pair each pole pair with the zeros closest to it, so each section has a modest gain, and to order sections so that the signal level never gets too large in the middle. Good scaling between sections avoids overflow in fixed point. You do not need the full theory now; just know that design tools do this pairing for you.

Other structures, named only: The lattice structure uses reflection coefficients and is popular in speech coding, where linear prediction naturally produces those coefficients; a lattice filter is stable exactly when every reflection coefficient has magnitude below 1, which is easy to check. Frequency sampling structures and polyphase structures also exist; polyphase comes up in the multirate lesson.

Real life example 1, a phone music equalizer: The five-band equalizer in a music app on a phone used in Chattogram is usually five peaking or shelving biquads in cascade. Moving a slider changes the five coefficients of one biquad only. Because each band is its own section, adjusting the bass never disturbs the treble section's poles, and the whole chain stays stable while you drag the slider.

Real life example 2, a low-cost medical monitor: A patient monitor built around a small microcontroller filters ECG data in fixed point. The designer converts a sixth-order IIR band-pass into three biquads, uses direct form I in each so the accumulator can be wide, and scales between sections. Written as one sixth-order direct form, the same filter could drift or even become unstable once its coefficients are rounded to 16 bits; the cascade version keeps each pole pair under control. This is a typical choice in embedded DSP.

Common mistakes: Getting the sign of the feedback taps wrong when drawing a structure from H(z). Counting delays wrongly: direct form I has M + N, direct form II has max(M, N). Thinking all structures are the same in practice; they are only the same with infinite precision. Splitting complex conjugate poles into different sections, which forces complex coefficients. Forgetting the overall gain G in a cascade.

What exams ask: Draw direct form I, direct form II and transposed form for a given H(z) or difference equation. Count delays, multipliers and adders. Realise a filter in cascade and parallel form using factoring and partial fractions. Draw an FIR transversal structure and the folded linear phase version. Explain why cascade or parallel forms are preferred for high order IIR filters.

A quick checklist before you draw: Normalise so the first denominator coefficient is 1. Write y[n] alone on the left. Count M and N. Decide whether memory (pick direct form II), fixed-point safety (pick direct form I per section) or robustness at high order (pick cascade or parallel) matters most. Then draw, and label every multiplier with its exact value and sign.

Recap: Structures are different wiring of delays, multipliers and adders for the same H(z). FIR uses a tapped delay line, and symmetry halves the multipliers. Direct form I is literal and fixed-point friendly; direct form II is canonic with max(M, N) delays; transposed forms flip the graph. High order IIR filters should be built as cascades or parallels of biquads to keep rounding from moving poles. Next we change the sampling rate itself: multirate DSP.
key_points: Structures are built from unit delays (z^-1), multipliers and adders; different wirings give the same H(z) with perfect arithmetic.
FIR transversal form: N taps need N multipliers and N - 1 delays; symmetric coefficients cut multipliers to (N+1)/2 for odd N.
Direct form I uses M + N delays and one place to sum, which suits fixed-point accumulators.
Direct form II (canonic) merges the delay lines to max(M, N) delays but its internal signal can overflow.
A biquad has 5 coefficients: 4 delays in direct form I, 2 in direct form II.
Transposed forms reverse the signal flow graph; scipy lfilter uses transposed direct form II.
High order direct forms are sensitive to coefficient rounding; cascade or parallel biquads keep poles where they belong.
lessons.tip: When drawing any structure, first rewrite the difference equation with y[n] alone on the left. The signs you see there are the signs on the multipliers, which kills the most common mistake.
lessons.task: Take H(z) = (1 + z^-1) / (1 - 0.9 z^-1 + 0.2 z^-2). Draw it in direct form I and direct form II, count delays and multipliers for each, then write it as a cascade of two first-order sections and check the first three impulse response values by hand.

quiz.q: How many delays does direct form II need for a filter with M = 2 zeros and N = 2 poles?
quiz.explain: Direct form II needs max(M, N) delays, here max(2, 2) = 2; direct form I would need M + N = 4.

quiz.q: Why are high-order IIR filters usually built as cascades of second-order sections?
options: Rounding a coefficient then disturbs only one pole pair, so the filter stays stable and accurate
Cascade removes the need for delays
quiz.explain: Roots of a high-degree polynomial are very sensitive to coefficient rounding; small biquads limit that sensitivity to one pair of poles each.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of direct form II in fixed-point arithmetic?
options: The internal signal w[n] can become large and overflow
It needs more delays than direct form I
It only works for FIR filters
quiz.explain: Direct form II applies the feedback first, so the internal node w[n] can grow much larger than x or y and overflow.

quiz.q: A symmetric 7-tap linear phase FIR filter can be implemented with how few multipliers?
quiz.explain: Pairs of samples sharing a coefficient are added first, so an odd-length N needs (N + 1)/2 = 4 multipliers.

quiz.q: Which is the parallel form of 1/(1 - 0.9z^-1 + 0.2z^-2)?
quiz.explain: Partial fractions give A = 5 and B = -4; check n = 0: 5 - 4 = 1, n = 1: 2.5 - 1.6 = 0.9, matching the direct form.

lessons.title: Multirate DSP: Decimation, Interpolation and Sample Rate Conversion
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket highlights video. The full match was filmed at a high frame rate, but the highlights team keeps only some frames for a quick summary, and for a slow-motion replay they invent extra frames in between the real ones. Throwing frames away and inventing frames in between are exactly the two basic operations of multirate DSP: decimation and interpolation. Many real systems run different parts at different sampling rates, and moving a signal between rates cleanly, without aliasing or ugly images, is a core skill.

Why change the sampling rate at all: Music is commonly stored at 44.1 kHz, while video and many phone audio systems run at 48 kHz, so a phone must convert between them all the time. A voice call may be processed at 8 kHz or 16 kHz, while the microphone chip runs much faster. Processing at a lower rate saves computation and memory: if the useful signal is only below 4 kHz, there is no reason to process 48,000 samples a second. And oversampling converters deliberately sample very fast and then reduce the rate digitally. All of these need multirate tools.

Downsampling, the raw operation: Downsampling by an integer M keeps every Mth sample: y[n] = x[Mn]. If x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and M = 2, then y = [1, 3, 5]. The new sampling rate is fs/M. The operation is so simple that it is easy to forget its danger. It is linear but not time invariant: shift the input by one sample and the output does not simply shift, it picks entirely different samples.

The danger, aliasing: After downsampling, the new Nyquist frequency is fs/(2M). Any content above that folds down and pretends to be a lower frequency, exactly as in the sampling lesson. Worked example: take fs = 48 kHz and M = 3, so the new rate is 16 kHz and the new Nyquist is 8 kHz. A 10 kHz tone is fine at 48 kHz. After keeping every third sample without filtering, it appears at |10 - 16| = 6 kHz. A script confirms that the samples of the 10 kHz tone taken every third sample are identical to samples of a 6 kHz tone at 16 kHz. The 6 kHz tone is fake, and no later processing can tell it apart from a real one.

Decimation, done right: Decimation means low-pass filter first, then downsample. The anti-aliasing filter has cutoff pi/M in the original digital frequency, which is fs/(2M) in hertz. For our example, cut at about 8 kHz (in practice a bit lower to leave a transition band), then keep every third sample. The filter removes the 10 kHz tone before it can alias. In the frequency domain, downsampling stretches the spectrum by a factor of M, and the filter makes sure nothing is left above pi/M to overlap after stretching.

Upsampling, the raw operation: Upsampling by an integer L inserts L - 1 zeros between samples. For x = [1, 2, 3] and L = 2, the upsampled signal is [1, 0, 2, 0, 3, 0]. The new rate is L fs. No information is lost, but the zeros are obviously not a smooth signal. In the frequency domain, the spectrum is squeezed by L, and copies of the original spectrum, called images, appear inside the new band.

Interpolation, done right: Interpolation means upsample, then low-pass filter. The anti-imaging filter has cutoff pi/L and a gain of L, because inserting zeros divided the average signal level by L. The filter smooths away the images and fills the zeros with sensible in-between values.

Interpolation, worked: Take the upsampled [1, 0, 2, 0, 3, 0] and filter it with h = [0.5, 1, 0.5]. This tiny filter has a gain of 2 at DC, matching L = 2. Convolution gives [0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 1.5, 0]. Ignore the one-sample delay of the filter and look at the middle: 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3. The original samples 1, 2, 3 are still there, and the new samples 1.5 and 2.5 are exactly halfway between their neighbours. This filter is plain linear interpolation. A real interpolator uses a longer low-pass filter, which gives smoother and more accurate in-between values.

Seeing both in digital frequency, worked: A 4 kHz tone at fs = 48 kHz has digital frequency w = 2 pi x 4/48 = pi/6. After proper decimation by 3 the rate is 16 kHz and the same tone sits at w = 2 pi x 4/16 = pi/2, which is 3 times pi/6: downsampling multiplies every digital frequency by M, which is the stretching we talked about. Now go the other way. A 1 kHz tone at 8 kHz has w = pi/4. Upsample by 2 to 16 kHz: the real tone now sits at w = pi/8, half the old value, and an image appears at 8 - 1 = 7 kHz, which is w = 7 pi/8. The interpolation low-pass at pi/2 (4 kHz) keeps the 1 kHz tone and kills the 7 kHz image. If you skip the filter, you will literally hear a 7 kHz whistle that was never in the recording.

Rational rate change: To change the rate by a fraction L/M, first interpolate by L, then decimate by M. The two low-pass filters sit next to each other, so they merge into one filter with cutoff equal to the smaller of pi/L and pi/M. The famous example is 44.1 kHz to 48 kHz. The ratio 48000/44100 reduces to 160/147. So upsample by 160, filter, then downsample by 147. Check: 44,100 x 160 / 147 = 48,000 exactly.

The cost problem: In that 44.1 to 48 kHz example, the middle stage runs at 44,100 x 160 = 7,056,000 samples per second. Running a long filter at 7 MHz just to throw most of its outputs away, on an input that is mostly zeros, is wasteful. Most of the multiplications are by inserted zeros, and most outputs are discarded by the downsampler. Clever structures avoid computing those.

Polyphase, the clever trick: Split the filter coefficients into M interleaved sub-filters: coefficients 0, M, 2M, ... form the first, 1, M+1, 2M+1, ... the second, and so on. For a decimator, each sub-filter runs at the low output rate on its own share of the input, and their outputs are added. The result is mathematically identical to filtering then downsampling, but no discarded output is ever computed. Worked cost: a 60-tap decimation filter for 48 kHz to 16 kHz needs 60 x 48,000 = 2,880,000 multiplications per second if done naively. With polyphase it computes only the outputs it keeps: 60 x 16,000 = 960,000, three times fewer. For interpolators the same idea avoids multiplying by the inserted zeros.

Noble identities, named only: There are two rules that let you move a filter across a downsampler or upsampler if you change z to z^M or z^L. They are the formal reason the polyphase trick works. Exams sometimes ask you to state them; just remember that filtering with H(z^M) then downsampling by M is the same as downsampling first and then filtering with H(z).

Multi-stage conversion: A big ratio like decimating by 48 is often done in stages, for example by 8 then by 6, or by 2 several times. Each stage needs a much less demanding filter, because the transition band can be wide relative to the rate at that stage. The total computation is usually far lower than one giant filter. Half-band filters, where nearly every other coefficient is zero, are popular for decimate-by-2 stages.

Oversampling converters: A sigma-delta ADC, the type inside almost every phone and audio interface, samples at a rate many times higher than needed with very few bits, and shapes the quantization noise towards high frequencies. A digital decimation filter then removes that high-frequency noise and reduces the rate to 44.1 or 48 kHz, leaving many effective bits of resolution. Even without noise shaping, plain oversampling spreads the quantization noise over a wider band, so each doubling of the sampling rate followed by filtering improves the in-band SQNR by about 3 dB, half a bit. The anti-aliasing analog filter in front can also be very simple, because the first digital stage does the sharp filtering.

Filter banks: A bank of filters can split a signal into several frequency bands, each of which is then decimated because it holds only a slice of the spectrum. Each band can be processed or coded separately and later interpolated and recombined. MP3 audio coding starts with a 32-band filter bank of this kind, and multiband hearing aids and equalizers use similar ideas.

Real life example 1, a phone call and music on the same phone: Your phone in Khulna plays a song stored at 44.1 kHz through an audio chip running at 48 kHz, while a WhatsApp call needs the microphone at 16 kHz. Behind the scenes, sample rate converters with polyphase filters move audio between all these rates many times a second, and you never hear a glitch if they are designed well. A badly designed converter produces audible aliasing as a faint metallic whistle.

Real life example 2, software-defined radio: A hobby SDR dongle connected to a laptop in a Dhaka university lab may sample a wide chunk of radio spectrum at a few million samples per second. To listen to one FM station, the software shifts the station down to zero frequency, then decimates in stages to a few hundred kilohertz and finally to 48 kHz audio. Without multirate DSP the laptop would have to process millions of samples per second through the whole chain.

Common mistakes: Downsampling without the anti-aliasing filter. Forgetting the gain of L in the interpolation filter, which leaves the output too quiet. Applying the decimation and interpolation filters in the wrong order for an L/M converter (interpolate first, or you lose bandwidth). Thinking that inserting zeros adds information; it does not. Mixing up the original and new sampling rates when converting cutoffs between radians and hertz.

What exams ask: Define downsampling and upsampling and sketch their spectra. Explain why a filter is needed before decimation and after upsampling, and give the cutoff. Design a converter for a rational ratio such as 44.1 to 48 kHz. Show a polyphase decomposition and count the saving. Compute outputs of a small upsample-and-filter example by hand.

A design checklist for any rate converter: Write the input rate and output rate. Reduce the ratio to L/M in lowest terms. Find the cutoff as the smaller of pi/L and pi/M at the intermediate rate, and remember the gain of L. Pick a transition band and stopband attenuation, then a filter length. Finally choose a polyphase or multi-stage implementation so the chip never computes samples that are thrown away.

Recap: Decimation is low-pass at pi/M, then keep every Mth sample; without the filter, energy above the new Nyquist aliases, like 10 kHz becoming 6 kHz at 16 kHz. Interpolation is insert L - 1 zeros, then low-pass at pi/L with gain L. Rational conversion L/M combines both, with 44.1 to 48 kHz being 160/147. Polyphase structures avoid wasted work, cutting cost by the rate factor. Next lesson we look inside the hardware that runs all of this, and at what fixed-point numbers do to our neat equations.
key_points: Downsampling by M keeps every Mth sample; [1,2,3,4,5,6] by 2 gives [1,3,5]; it is linear but not time invariant.
Without an anti-aliasing filter, content above fs/(2M) folds down: 10 kHz at 48 kHz decimated by 3 appears at 6 kHz.
Decimation = low-pass at pi/M, then downsample.
Upsampling by L inserts L - 1 zeros and creates images; interpolation = upsample, then low-pass at pi/L with gain L.
Worked: [1,0,2,0,3,0] filtered by [0.5, 1, 0.5] gives 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, linear interpolation.
Rational conversion: interpolate by L, then decimate by M; 44.1 kHz to 48 kHz is 160/147.
Polyphase structures skip discarded outputs and zero inputs; a 60-tap 48 to 16 kHz decimator drops from 2.88 M to 0.96 M multiplies per second.
Oversampling ADCs, multi-stage conversion and filter banks (MP3) all rely on multirate DSP.
lessons.tip: For every multirate block, write two sampling rates on your diagram, before and after. Most mistakes come from computing a cutoff using the wrong one.
lessons.task: Take x = [2, 4, 6, 8]. Upsample by 2, filter with [0.5, 1, 0.5] by hand, and check that the middle values are halfway points. Then downsample [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] by 3 and write the new sampling rate if the original was 48 kHz.

quiz.q: What must happen before downsampling a signal by M?
quiz.explain: A low-pass anti-aliasing filter at pi/M removes content above the new Nyquist frequency so it cannot alias.

quiz.q: A 10 kHz tone at fs = 48 kHz is downsampled by 3 without filtering. Where does it appear?
quiz.explain: The new rate is 16 kHz with Nyquist 8 kHz, so 10 kHz folds to |10 - 16| = 6 kHz.

quiz.q: Upsampling [1, 2, 3] by L = 2 gives which sequence?
quiz.explain: Upsampling inserts L - 1 = 1 zero after each sample; the smooth values only appear after the interpolation filter.

quiz.q: Which ratio converts 44.1 kHz audio to 48 kHz?
Why is the interpolation filter given a gain of L?
options: Inserting zeros lowered the average level by a factor of L
quiz.explain: Inserting L - 1 zeros divides the average signal level by L, so the anti-imaging low-pass needs gain L to restore it.

lessons.title: DSP Hardware and Fixed-Point Arithmetic
lessons.content:
On paper, our filters use numbers like 0.2451 and 0.4142 with as many decimals as we like. Inside a cheap chip in a hearing aid or a mobile charger, numbers are stored in maybe 16 bits, and the chip has a budget of a few microseconds per sample. Think of a shopkeeper in a village bazar who keeps accounts with only whole taka, no paisa. Most days it works, but if he adds up many small sales and keeps dropping the paisa, the totals drift, and if one number gets too big for his ledger column, the account is ruined. This lesson is about the hardware that runs DSP in real time and the bookkeeping rules of fixed-point numbers.

What real time means: A DSP system is real time when it finishes processing each sample (or each block) before the next one arrives. At 48 kHz a new sample arrives every 1/48,000 s, about 20.8 microseconds. If the filter takes longer, samples pile up and are lost, which you hear as clicks. So the question is never just whether the maths is right, but whether it is fast enough every single time.

The heart of DSP, multiply-accumulate: Almost every DSP algorithm is a long sum of products: FIR filters, IIR sections, correlation, DFT. The basic step is acc = acc + a x b, called a MAC. A 100-tap FIR at 48 kHz needs 100 x 48,000 = 4,800,000 MACs per second. On a processor that does one MAC per clock cycle at 100 MHz, that is 4.8 percent of its time. On a general processor that needs separate load, multiply, add and loop instructions, the same work could take several times longer.

What makes a DSP processor special: Dedicated digital signal processors, such as the Texas Instruments TMS320 families and Analog Devices SHARC and Blackfin, are built around that MAC. Typical features: a hardware multiplier and accumulator that finish a MAC in one cycle; a Harvard architecture with separate buses for program and data, often with two data memories, so the coefficient and the sample can be fetched in the same cycle as the instruction; circular buffer addressing in hardware, so the delay line wraps around without any if statements; zero-overhead loops, where the hardware repeats a block without spending instructions on the loop counter; and bit-reversed addressing to help the FFT.

The circular buffer, explained: An N-tap FIR needs the last N input samples. Shifting all N samples by one place on every new sample would waste N moves. Instead, keep the samples in a fixed array and move a pointer: write the new sample where the oldest one was, and let the pointer wrap from the end back to the start, index = (index + 1) mod N. DSP chips do the mod automatically in the address unit, so the delay line costs no extra instructions.

Other hardware that runs DSP: Microcontrollers such as ARM Cortex-M4 and M7 add DSP instructions (single-cycle MAC, saturating arithmetic, small SIMD operations), and many include a floating-point unit, so a cheap board can run audio filters. Phone systems-on-chip contain dedicated DSP cores for audio, modems and camera processing. FPGAs contain hundreds or thousands of hardware multiplier blocks that can all work in parallel, so they suit very high sample rates in radar, base stations and software-defined radio. GPUs are good when the same operation runs on huge batches, such as processing many channels or images at once.

Block processing and latency: Many systems do not process one sample at a time but collect a block, for example 64 or 256 samples, using DMA to move data from the ADC into memory without the CPU. Processing a block at once reduces overhead and suits the FFT. The cost is latency: a block of 256 samples at 48 kHz takes 256 / 48,000 s, about 5.3 ms, just to fill. For music playback that is fine; for live monitoring or a hearing aid, designers keep blocks small.

Fixed point versus floating point: A floating-point number stores a mantissa and an exponent, so it handles very large and very small values automatically; IEEE single precision gives about 24 bits of mantissa. A fixed-point number is just an integer with an agreed position for the binary point. Fixed-point hardware is smaller, cheaper and uses less power, which matters in billions of earbuds, chargers and sensors. The cost is that the programmer must manage range and precision by hand.

The Q15 format: The most common fixed-point format in DSP is Q15: a 16-bit two's complement integer read as a fraction, value = integer / 2^15 = integer / 32768. It has 1 sign bit and 15 fraction bits. The range is -1 to 1 - 2^-15, which is about 0.99997. The step, one least significant bit, is 2^-15, about 0.0000305. So 0.5 is stored as 16384 and 0.75 as 24576. In general, Qm.n means m integer bits and n fraction bits; Q31 is the 32-bit version.

Multiplication in Q15, worked: Multiply 0.75 by 0.5. The integers are 24576 and 16384. Their product is 402,653,184, a 32-bit number in Q30 format, because the fractions multiply: 2^15 x 2^15 = 2^30. To get back to Q15, shift right by 15 bits: 402,653,184 >> 15 = 12288. And 12288 / 32768 = 0.375, which is exactly 0.75 x 0.5. Multiplying two numbers below 1 always gives a number below 1, which is one reason fractional formats are popular: multiplication itself never overflows (except the one corner case -1 x -1).

Addition and overflow, worked: Add 0.75 and 0.5 in Q15: 24576 + 16384 = 40960. But the largest Q15 integer is 32767. In plain two's complement the result wraps around: 40960 - 65536 = -24576, which reads as -0.75. A positive sum has turned into a large negative number. In audio this is a loud crack; in a control system it can be dangerous. This is overflow, and it is the most serious fixed-point bug.

Saturation, the safety net: Saturating arithmetic clamps the result to the largest or smallest representable value instead of wrapping. Our sum becomes 32767, which is 0.99997. Still wrong, but only slightly, and in the right direction. DSP processors and DSP extensions provide saturating add instructions for exactly this reason. Many DSPs also give the accumulator extra guard bits, for example 40-bit accumulators for 16-bit data, so intermediate sums inside a long FIR can grow beyond 1 safely and are only saturated or rounded once at the end.

Rounding versus truncation: Converting a real number or a long product to fewer bits drops information. Example: 0.1 in Q15 is 0.1 x 32768 = 3276.8. Rounding gives 3277, which is 0.100006. Truncation, simply chopping the extra bits, gives 3276, which is 0.099976. Truncation is cheaper but always errs in the same direction, so errors pile up as a bias. Rounding errors are at most half a step and average out to about zero. Either way, each rounding adds a little noise; we met the size of that noise in the quantization lesson, where 16 bits gave about 98 dB of SQNR.

Coefficient quantization: Filter coefficients must be stored in the same limited format. Our 7-tap Hamming filter from lesson 20 becomes, in Q15, [-278, 0, 8031, 16384, 8031, 0, -278]. For an FIR filter this only slightly changes the response, and symmetry is kept, so linear phase survives. For a high-order IIR filter, rounding coefficients can move poles a lot, even outside the unit circle. That is the main reason, from lesson 22, why IIR filters are built as cascades of biquads in fixed point.

Scaling to prevent overflow: For an FIR filter, the worst-case output is the input peak times the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients. For our 7-tap filter, sum of |h| is about 1.0072, slightly above 1. So a full-scale input with an unlucky pattern could overflow by about 0.7 percent. The fixes are to scale the input or the coefficients down by that factor, or to rely on guard bits and saturate only at the end. In IIR cascades, scaling factors are placed between sections for the same reason.

Limit cycles, worked: Rounding inside a feedback loop can trap an IIR filter in a small never-ending output even when the input is zero. Take y[n] = 0.9 y[n-1] with integer rounding (round half away from zero) and start at y = 10 with no input. Ideally the output decays towards zero. With rounding: 10, 9, 8.1 becomes 8, 7.2 becomes 7, 6.3 becomes 6, 5.4 becomes 5, then 4.5 rounds back to 5, and the output sticks at 5 forever. This stuck region is called a deadband, and such stuck or oscillating outputs are called limit cycles. In audio they can appear as a faint tone in silence. Fixes include more bits in the feedback path, different rounding, or adding tiny dither.

A practical workflow: Engineers usually design and test a filter in floating point first, in Python or MATLAB. Then they simulate the fixed-point version with the exact word lengths of the target chip, compare the outputs, check for overflow on worst-case inputs, and only then write the embedded code. Libraries such as ARM's CMSIS-DSP provide ready-made Q15, Q31 and floating-point filter and FFT functions, so you rarely write a MAC loop from scratch.

Real life example 1, a hearing aid: A hearing aid must run for days on a tiny battery. It uses fixed-point DSP to split sound into bands, amplify each band according to the user's hearing test, and suppress feedback whistle. Every multiply costs energy, so designers pick short word lengths and efficient structures, and use saturation so a sudden loud sound, like a pressure cooker whistle in the kitchen, does not turn into a painful crack.

Real life example 2, a solar inverter or charger: Solar home systems are common in rural Bangladesh, and the inverters and charge controllers in such equipment often use microcontrollers with DSP features to sample voltage and current, filter the measurements, and run control loops many thousands of times a second. Fixed-point arithmetic keeps them cheap; careful scaling and saturation keep them safe when a cloud passes and the panel current suddenly changes.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to shift right by 15 after a Q15 multiply. Using wrap-around addition where saturation is needed. Assuming an IIR design that works in floating point will work in 16-bit fixed point. Ignoring the sum of |h| when checking for overflow. Truncating everywhere and then wondering why the output has a DC offset.

What exams ask: List features of a DSP processor and explain why each helps (MAC, Harvard, circular buffer, zero-overhead loop). Compare fixed and floating point. Represent numbers in Q15 and multiply or add them, showing overflow and saturation. Explain coefficient quantization and why cascade forms help. Explain limit cycles with a small example.

Recap: Real-time DSP must finish each sample in time; the MAC is its core operation, and DSP chips add Harvard buses, circular buffers and zero-overhead loops to do one MAC per cycle. Fixed point is cheap but needs care: in Q15, 0.75 x 0.5 = 12288 = 0.375 after a 15-bit shift, while 0.75 + 0.5 wraps to -0.75 unless you saturate to 0.99997. Rounding, coefficient quantization, scaling and limit cycles are the price of finite bits. Next we see where all this is used: real DSP applications.
key_points: Real time means each sample is processed before the next arrives, about 20.8 microseconds at 48 kHz.
The MAC (acc = acc + a x b) is the core DSP operation; a 100-tap FIR at 48 kHz needs 4.8 million MACs per second.
DSP processors add single-cycle MAC, Harvard buses, hardware circular buffers, zero-overhead loops and bit-reversed addressing.
Overflow wraps 0.75 + 0.5 to -0.75; saturation clamps it to 0.99997; guard bits in wide accumulators help.
Rounding errs by at most half a step with zero mean; truncation is cheaper but biased (0.1 becomes 3277 vs 3276).
Coefficient quantization moves IIR poles, so fixed-point IIR filters use biquad cascades and scaling.
Limit cycles: y[n] = 0.9 y[n-1] with rounding sticks at 5 instead of decaying to 0.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a fixed-point number, translate it both ways in your head: integer to fraction (divide by 32768) and fraction to integer (multiply by 32768). Doing a few by hand makes overflow and shifting feel obvious.
lessons.task: Write 0.3, -0.6 and 0.9 in Q15. Multiply 0.3 by -0.6 using the integers and shift right by 15, then check the result. Finally add 0.9 and 0.3 and write both the wrap-around and the saturated answer.

quiz.q: What is the main reason DSP processors have a single-cycle MAC unit?
options: Most DSP algorithms are long sums of products
To run the operating system faster
quiz.explain: FIR, IIR, correlation and DFT all reduce to repeated acc = acc + a x b, so a one-cycle MAC speeds up almost everything.

quiz.q: In Q15, what integer represents 0.5?
Adding 0.75 and 0.5 in Q15 with wrap-around arithmetic gives what?
What does saturating arithmetic do on overflow?
options: Wraps to the most negative value
Clamps the result to the largest or smallest representable value
quiz.explain: Saturation clamps to the limit, so 0.75 + 0.5 becomes 32767, about 0.99997, a small error instead of a sign flip.

quiz.q: With integer rounding, y[n] = 0.9 y[n-1] starting at 10 with zero input gets stuck at 5. What is this called?
quiz.explain: Rounding in the feedback loop traps the output at a non-zero value; such stuck or oscillating outputs are limit cycles.

lessons.title: DSP Applications: Audio, Speech, Images, Communications and Biomedical
lessons.content:
Count the DSP in one ordinary morning. Your phone alarm plays a compressed music file. You take a voice call while the pressure cooker hisses, and the other person barely hears the kitchen. You scroll photos that were sharpened and compressed the moment you took them. Your Wi-Fi delivers a video that travelled as hundreds of parallel tones. An uncle at a hospital in Dhaka has an ECG strip printed that was cleaned of mains hum before anyone saw it. Every one of these is the toolkit of this course, sampling, filtering, FFTs, multirate, fixed point, applied to a real problem. This lesson walks through the major application areas and shows which tools each one uses.

Audio, the equalizer: A graphic or parametric equalizer boosts or cuts bands of frequencies, for example more bass, less harshness around a few kilohertz. Each band is usually a biquad IIR filter in a cascade, as in lesson 22. Moving a slider changes the coefficients of one section. Because IIR biquads are cheap, a phone can run ten bands on stereo audio at 48 kHz with ease.

Audio, compression: A CD-quality stereo stream is 1,411.2 kbps, which we computed in the quantization lesson. An MP3 at 128 kbps is about 11 times smaller. The trick is perceptual coding: the signal is split into frequency bands using a filter bank and transforms, a psychoacoustic model estimates which sounds are masked by louder nearby sounds, and those bands are quantized coarsely or dropped. The bits go where your ears notice. AAC, used by many streaming services, works on the same principle with improvements.

Audio, adaptive noise and echo cancellation: Some problems need a filter whose coefficients change as the situation changes. An adaptive filter adjusts its coefficients continuously to make an error signal as small as possible. The simplest algorithm, LMS (least mean squares), updates each coefficient as w = w + mu * e * x, where e is the current error, x is the input sample at that tap and mu is a small step size. In a voice call, the far-end voice comes out of your speaker and leaks back into your microphone. An echo canceller uses an adaptive FIR to model that path, predicts the echo, and subtracts it. Active noise-cancelling headphones use a microphone to measure outside noise and play an inverted version to cancel it, mostly at low frequencies.

Speech, framing: Speech changes constantly, but over a short stretch of about 20 to 30 ms its properties are nearly steady. So speech systems cut the signal into overlapping frames, multiply each frame by a window such as Hamming, and analyse frames one by one. At 8 kHz, a 20 ms frame is 0.02 x 8000 = 160 samples. This is the short-time Fourier transform idea from the spectral analysis lesson.

Speech, the source-filter model and LPC: Voiced sounds like a and o are made by the vocal cords vibrating at a pitch, roughly around 100 Hz for many men and around 200 Hz for many women, which then passes through the vocal tract, a tube whose shape sets resonances called formants. Unvoiced sounds like s and f are noise-like. Linear predictive coding models the vocal tract as an all-pole IIR filter: each sample is predicted as a weighted sum of about ten previous samples. Instead of sending the waveform, a codec sends the filter coefficients, the pitch and the loudness for each frame. The receiver rebuilds the speech by driving the filter. The original GSM full-rate codec used this kind of approach to carry speech at about 13 kbps, compared with 64 kbps for plain telephone PCM.

Speech recognition: Voice assistants and speech-to-text systems start with DSP. Each frame goes through an FFT, the spectrum is grouped into bands spaced like human hearing (the mel scale), and the result, often converted into MFCC features or a log-mel spectrogram, is fed to a machine learning model. Clean features make the model's job easier, which is why noise suppression usually runs first.

Images, 2D convolution: An image is a 2D signal, x[m, n], with pixel values typically 0 to 255. Filtering means sliding a small 2D kernel over the image, exactly like 1D convolution but in two directions. A 3 x 3 averaging kernel, all entries 1/9, blurs the image and reduces noise. Worked example: if a pixel and its eight neighbours have values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90, the averaged output is 450 / 9 = 50. A sharpening kernel with 5 in the centre and -1 above, below, left and right boosts differences: a pixel of 100 surrounded by four pixels of 50 becomes 5 x 100 - 4 x 50 = 300, which is then clipped to 255, making the bright spot stand out. Edge detectors such as Sobel use kernels that approximate derivatives.

Images, JPEG compression: JPEG splits an image into 8 x 8 blocks, 64 pixels each. Each block goes through the discrete cosine transform (DCT), a close cousin of the DFT that uses only real cosines. For natural photos most of the energy ends up in a few low-frequency coefficients. JPEG quantizes the high-frequency coefficients coarsely, many become zero, and the zeros compress very well. Compression around 10 to 1 often looks almost the same to the eye; push harder and you see the familiar blocky artefacts at block edges.

Communications, OFDM: Modern Wi-Fi and 4G LTE send data on many narrow subcarriers at once, a method called OFDM. The transmitter puts data symbols on frequency bins and uses an inverse FFT to create the time signal; the receiver uses an FFT to separate the subcarriers again. For example, classic 20 MHz Wi-Fi (802.11a/g) uses a 64-point FFT, and LTE uses subcarriers spaced 15 kHz apart. Because each subcarrier is narrow, a multipath channel that would smear a single wideband signal only multiplies each subcarrier by a complex number, which is easy to undo. Without the FFT from lesson 16, OFDM would be far too expensive to run in a phone.

Communications, filtering and correlation: Pulse-shaping filters limit the bandwidth each symbol uses. Matched filters, which are correlations with the expected pulse, maximise the signal-to-noise ratio at the decision moment. Equalizers, often adaptive, undo the distortion of the channel. Decimation and interpolation move the signal between the high rate near the antenna and the lower rate of the data. A 4G base station on a rooftop in Gulshan and the phone in your pocket are both, at heart, large DSP machines.

Biomedical, the ECG: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity, about a millivolt in size, from electrodes on the skin. The recording is noisy. Baseline wander from breathing and movement is very low frequency, below about 0.5 Hz. Power-line interference is at 50 Hz in Bangladesh (60 Hz in some other countries) plus its harmonics. Muscle noise (EMG) is broadband and higher in frequency. A typical cleaning chain is a high-pass filter for baseline wander, a notch at 50 Hz for mains, and a low-pass for muscle noise. The next lesson builds that notch in full.

Biomedical, heart rate: Once the ECG is clean, the tall spikes called R peaks can be detected. A classic method, the Pan-Tompkins algorithm, band-pass filters the ECG, differentiates it, squares it, and integrates it with a moving window before thresholding. The time between consecutive R peaks is the R-R interval, and heart rate in beats per minute is 60 divided by the R-R interval in seconds. An R-R of 0.8 s gives 60 / 0.8 = 75 bpm; 0.75 s gives 80 bpm; 1.0 s gives 60 bpm. Smartwatches estimating heart rate from light reflected through the skin (PPG) use similar filtering and peak finding.

Biomedical, other signals: EEG measures brain activity with even smaller voltages and is analysed in frequency bands, for example alpha waves around 8 to 12 Hz during relaxed rest. Ultrasound imaging, CT and MRI reconstruction all depend heavily on filtering and Fourier transforms. Hearing aids, as in the last lesson, are wearable real-time DSP.

Radar and sonar, briefly: A radar sends a known pulse and correlates the echo with it; the delay of the correlation peak gives distance. The Doppler shift of the echo, measured with an FFT across many pulses, gives speed. Weather radars, including those used by meteorological departments to track cyclones over the Bay of Bengal, use these ideas to estimate rainfall and wind.

Control and sensors, briefly: DSP is also inside things that do not look like signal processing at all. A drone reads its gyroscope and accelerometer hundreds of times a second, filters the noisy readings and fuses them to estimate its tilt. A motor drive in a factory filters current measurements before the control loop uses them. A phone's step counter low-pass filters the accelerometer and counts peaks, just like counting R peaks in an ECG. The same few ideas, filtering, sampling and peak detection, keep reappearing.

Real life example 1, an online class from Dhaka: A teacher runs a video class from a small flat in Mirpur with traffic outside and a ceiling fan running. The app applies echo cancellation so students do not hear themselves, noise suppression so the traffic fades, automatic gain control so a soft voice stays audible, and a speech codec that squeezes the audio into a small bit rate for slow connections. The video side applies its own filtering and compression. Dozens of DSP blocks run in real time on an ordinary phone.

Real life example 2, a rural health camp: A health camp in a char area of Gaibandha uses a portable ECG device. The device samples the ECG, removes baseline wander and 50 Hz hum from nearby generators or wiring, detects R peaks and prints the heart rate. A doctor far away can receive the cleaned recording over a mobile network. Every step, from the ADC to the filters to the compression for sending, is DSP from this course.

Common mistakes: Thinking DSP is only audio; it is also images, radio, medicine and control. Mixing up compression types: MP3 and JPEG throw away information you are unlikely to notice (lossy), while ZIP-style compression is lossless. Forgetting that the mains frequency is 50 Hz in Bangladesh, not 60 Hz. Applying a filter that distorts the waveform shape in applications like ECG, where doctors read shapes; that is why linear phase or zero-phase (forward-backward) filtering is preferred for offline ECG analysis.

What exams ask: Describe DSP applications in audio, speech, image, communication and biomedical engineering and name the techniques used. Explain the source-filter model or LPC. Apply a 3 x 3 kernel to a small image patch. Explain why OFDM uses the FFT. List ECG noise sources and suitable filters. Compute heart rate from an R-R interval.

Recap: Equalizers are biquad cascades; compression uses filter banks and masking; echo and noise cancellation use adaptive filters like LMS. Speech is processed in 20 to 30 ms frames, modelled by LPC. Images are 2D signals filtered by small kernels and compressed with the 8 x 8 DCT. Wi-Fi and 4G run on FFT-based OFDM. ECGs are cleaned of baseline wander, 50 Hz hum and muscle noise, then R-R intervals give heart rate. In the final lesson we build one of these from start to finish: removing 50 Hz hum.
key_points: Equalizers are cascades of biquad IIR filters; each slider changes one section.
MP3/AAC use filter banks plus a psychoacoustic masking model; 128 kbps MP3 is about 11 times smaller than 1,411.2 kbps CD audio.
Adaptive filters (LMS: w = w + mu * e * x) power echo cancellation and noise cancellation.
Speech is analysed in overlapping 20 to 30 ms windowed frames (160 samples at 8 kHz); LPC models the vocal tract as an all-pole filter.
Images are 2D signals; 3 x 3 kernels blur, sharpen or find edges; JPEG uses the 8 x 8 DCT and coarse quantization.
Wi-Fi and 4G use OFDM: inverse FFT at the transmitter, FFT at the receiver (64-point for 20 MHz 802.11a/g).
ECG noise: baseline wander (below about 0.5 Hz), 50 Hz mains in Bangladesh, muscle noise; heart rate = 60 / R-R seconds.
Radar uses correlation for range and FFT-measured Doppler for speed.
lessons.tip: For each application, practise answering three questions in one line each: what is the signal, what is the problem, which DSP tool fixes it. That habit turns long essay questions into quick structured answers.
lessons.task: Record 5 seconds of your voice with a phone, then open it in a free spectrogram app or Audacity's spectrogram view. Find the pitch harmonics as horizontal stripes and note roughly where your voice energy lies. If you can feel your pulse, time 10 beats, compute the average R-R interval and your heart rate.

quiz.q: Which DSP technique lets Wi-Fi and 4G split data across many narrow subcarriers efficiently?
options: OFDM using the FFT and inverse FFT
quiz.explain: OFDM places data on frequency bins and uses an inverse FFT to transmit and an FFT to receive.

quiz.q: If the R-R interval of an ECG is 0.8 s, what is the heart rate?
quiz.explain: Heart rate = 60 / R-R = 60 / 0.8 = 75 beats per minute.

quiz.q: Why is speech analysed in short frames of about 20 to 30 ms?
options: Because phones can only store 30 ms
Speech properties are nearly steady over such short stretches
Because the FFT only works on 160 samples
quiz.explain: Speech changes constantly but is roughly stationary over 20 to 30 ms, so frame-by-frame analysis is meaningful.

quiz.q: What transform does JPEG apply to each 8 x 8 block?
