lessons.title: Capstone: Removing 50 Hz Mains Hum from an ECG, and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
Plug a cheap microphone or an ECG amplifier into a laptop in almost any building in Bangladesh and you will often see the same uninvited guest: a smooth wave repeating 50 times a second. It is the electricity grid. Wires in the walls carry 220 V alternating at 50 Hz, and their electric and magnetic fields leak into any sensitive circuit nearby. On an ECG it looks like a fuzzy thick line hiding the small P and T waves that doctors need to read. In this final lesson we solve this real problem from start to finish using almost everything in the course: sampling, the z-plane, poles and zeros, frequency response, difference equations, verification, and implementation choices.

The problem statement: An ECG is sampled at fs = 500 Hz, a common rate for diagnostic recordings. The useful ECG content lies mostly between a fraction of a hertz and about 40 Hz for monitoring (diagnostic analysis may use more bandwidth). Mixed into it is a strong 50 Hz hum. We want a filter that removes 50 Hz almost completely, leaves the rest of the spectrum almost untouched, is stable, cheap enough for a small microcontroller, and does not distort the ECG shape badly.

Step 1, check the sampling: The Nyquist frequency is fs/2 = 250 Hz, so 50 Hz and its harmonics at 100, 150 and 200 Hz are all below Nyquist and appear at their true frequencies. Good: the hum does not alias. In digital frequency, 50 Hz becomes w0 = 2 pi x 50 / 500 = 0.2 pi radians per sample.

Why a plain low-pass is not enough: You might think: the ECG is below 40 Hz, so just low-pass at 40 Hz. But the transition from 40 to 50 Hz is narrow, so a strong low-pass would need many taps or a high order, and many diagnostic recordings deliberately keep content above 50 Hz. We want something surgical: kill one frequency, keep everything else. That is a notch filter, also called a band-stop filter with a very narrow stopband.

Step 2, place the zeros: From the frequency response lesson, a zero on the unit circle at angle w0 makes the response exactly zero at w0. For a real filter, zeros come in conjugate pairs, so put zeros at z = e^(j0.2pi) and z = e^(-j0.2pi). Multiplying out (1 - e^(jw0) z^-1)(1 - e^(-jw0) z^-1) gives 1 - 2 cos(w0) z^-1 + z^-2. With cos(0.2 pi) = 0.80902, the numerator is 1 - 1.61803 z^-1 + z^-2. This FIR on its own already kills 50 Hz, but its dip is very wide: it also attenuates a large band around 50 Hz and changes the gain at DC.

Step 3, place the poles: The trick is to put a pole just inside each zero, at the same angle but radius r slightly less than 1. Near 50 Hz the zero wins and pulls the response to zero. Further away, the pole and zero are almost the same distance from the point on the unit circle, so their effects cancel and the gain returns to about 1. The closer r is to 1, the narrower the notch. With r = 0.95, the denominator is 1 - 2 r cos(w0) z^-1 + r^2 z^-2 = 1 - 1.53713 z^-1 + 0.9025 z^-2. Both poles have radius 0.95, inside the unit circle, so the filter is stable.

The pole-zero picture: Draw the unit circle. Mark two small circles (zeros) exactly on it at plus and minus 36 degrees, because 0.2 pi radians is 36 degrees. Mark two crosses (poles) at the same angles but a little inside, at radius 0.95. Now walk around the unit circle from angle 0 to pi, which is 0 to 250 Hz. Far from 36 degrees, each cross sits almost on top of its circle, so their distances to you are nearly equal and cancel. As you reach 36 degrees you step right onto the zero, its distance becomes zero, and the gain collapses. This picture is worth drawing in any exam answer.

Step 4, normalise the gain: At DC, z = 1, the numerator is 1 - 1.61803 + 1 = 0.38197 and the denominator is 1 - 1.53713 + 0.9025 = 0.36537, so the DC gain is 0.38197 / 0.36537 = 1.0454. We want exactly 1, so divide the numerator by 1.0454. The final filter is H(z) = (0.95655 - 1.54772 z^-1 + 0.95655 z^-2) / (1 - 1.53713 z^-1 + 0.9025 z^-2). It is a single biquad, the Lego brick of lesson 22.

Step 5, the difference equation: Reading H(z) directly, y[n] = 0.95655 x[n] - 1.54772 x[n-1] + 0.95655 x[n-2] + 1.53713 y[n-1] - 0.9025 y[n-2]. Note the signs on the feedback terms flip when moved to the right-hand side. That is five multiplies and four additions per sample. At 500 samples per second this is 2,500 multiplications per second, trivial for any microcontroller.

Step 6, verify the frequency response: Evaluating |H(e^jw)| with a script at several frequencies gives: 0 Hz gain 1.0, 10 Hz gain 0.999, 40 Hz gain 0.931, 45 Hz gain 0.779, 50 Hz gain 0 (numerically about 10^-15), 55 Hz gain 0.779, 60 Hz gain 0.931, 100 Hz gain 1.003, 250 Hz gain 1.006. The -3 dB points are at about 46.0 Hz and 54.0 Hz, so the notch is about 8 Hz wide. A handy approximation for the -3 dB width is (1 - r) fs / pi = 0.05 x 500 / pi = 7.96 Hz, which matches well.

Step 7, verify in time: Feed a pure 50 Hz sine of amplitude 1 into the difference equation. In the first 0.2 s the output still shows the hum, peaking around 0.86, because the filter needs time to settle. After 200 samples (0.4 s) the output is below 0.00003, essentially zero. Feed a 10 Hz sine instead and the steady output amplitude is about 0.999. The filter does exactly what the frequency response promised.

The trade-off in r: A narrower notch removes less of the ECG near 50 Hz, so why not use r = 0.99? Because a pole close to the unit circle makes the filter ring for a long time. The transient decays roughly like r^n. To fall to 1 percent takes about ln(0.01)/ln(r) samples: about 90 samples (0.18 s) for r = 0.95, but about 458 samples (0.92 s) for r = 0.99. A long ring means every sudden change, like a movement artefact, leaves a 50 Hz tail. Narrow notch and fast settling pull in opposite directions; r = 0.95 is a reasonable middle at 500 Hz. Also, the real mains frequency drifts a little around 50 Hz, so a very narrow notch can miss it.

Step 8, harmonics: Real hum is not a perfect sine; it often has harmonics at 100 Hz and 150 Hz. Repeat the design for w = 0.4 pi (100 Hz), where cos(0.4 pi) = 0.30902, and cascade the two biquads. Each section is designed and checked separately, which is exactly why cascades are convenient.

An FIR alternative, worked: A 10-point moving average at 500 Hz has zeros at every multiple of fs/10 = 50 Hz, so it kills 50, 100, 150 and 200 Hz all at once with no multiplications except a final divide by 10. But it is also a low-pass filter: its gain is 0.936 at 10 Hz and 0.759 at 20 Hz, which smooths the sharp QRS complex of the ECG. It is a good trick for slow sensor readings like temperature, but poor for diagnostic ECG. Comparing both designs is a nice exam answer.

Phase and the ECG shape: The notch is IIR, so its phase is not linear, and near 50 Hz it shifts phase noticeably. For live monitoring this is usually acceptable. For offline analysis you can run the filter forward and then backward over the recording (zero-phase filtering, filtfilt in Python or MATLAB), which cancels the phase shift and squares the magnitude response, so the notch gets deeper and slightly wider.

The Python pipeline in words: Load the ECG samples into an array. Build b and a as above, or call scipy.signal.iirnotch(50, Q, fs=500), where Q = f0 / bandwidth, about 50 / 8 = 6.2 for our design. Plot the magnitude response with freqz to check it. Filter with lfilter for real-time style or filtfilt for zero-phase. Plot the spectrum before and after with an FFT: the tall spike at 50 Hz should disappear. Finally, convert coefficients to Q15 if the target is a fixed-point chip and re-check the response, as in lesson 24.

Real life example 1, a portable ECG in a district hospital: A small ECG device used in a district hospital in Bangladesh typically includes a hardware notch or a digital notch at 50 Hz, often selectable as 50 or 60 Hz because the same product is sold in many countries. The engineers who set that switch default to 50 Hz for Bangladesh are using exactly this design.

Real life example 2, a home studio: A young musician in Sylhet records guitar through a cheap audio interface and hears a low buzz. Recording software offers a hum removal plug-in that applies notches at 50 Hz and several harmonics. Same idea, different signal: audio at 48 kHz instead of ECG at 500 Hz, so w0 = 2 pi x 50 / 48000 is much smaller, and the poles must sit much closer to the unit circle to keep the notch only a few hertz wide.

Course recap, part 1: We began with why digital: sampling above twice the highest frequency avoids aliasing, and each bit of quantization buys about 6 dB of SQNR. We described discrete signals and systems, built LTI systems from impulse responses, and computed convolution by hand. Difference equations gave us FIR and IIR filters, and the z-transform turned them into algebra, with poles inside the unit circle meaning stability.

Course recap, part 2: The frequency response, DTFT, DFT and FFT showed what filters do to each frequency and how to compute spectra quickly: N log N instead of N squared. We designed FIR filters with windows and IIR filters with the bilinear transform, arranged them in robust structures, changed sampling rates with multirate tools, met the realities of fixed-point hardware, and toured applications. Today one biquad tied it together.

What to learn next: Adaptive filtering (LMS and RLS) for echo and noise cancellation; statistical signal processing and Kalman filters for estimation; digital image processing; digital communications, where OFDM and equalizers live; speech and audio processing; and machine learning on signals, where DSP features feed neural networks. Python with numpy and scipy is a perfect free lab for all of them.

Common mistakes and exam focus: Forgetting to convert 50 Hz to radians per sample before placing zeros. Putting poles outside or on the unit circle. Forgetting to normalise the gain. Flipping feedback signs in the difference equation. Typical questions: design a notch filter for a given fs and f0, find its coefficients and difference equation, sketch the pole-zero plot and magnitude response, and discuss the effect of r.

Recap: To remove 50 Hz hum at fs = 500 Hz, put zeros at e^(+-j0.2pi) and poles at 0.95 e^(+-j0.2pi), normalise, and you get H(z) = (0.95655 - 1.54772 z^-1 + 0.95655 z^-2)/(1 - 1.53713 z^-1 + 0.9025 z^-2): zero gain at 50 Hz, about 8 Hz wide, near 1 elsewhere, stable and cheap. That single biquad uses the whole course. Well done for getting here.
key_points: At fs = 500 Hz, 50 Hz mains hum is w0 = 0.2 pi radians per sample, well below Nyquist, so it does not alias.
Zeros at e^(+-j w0) on the unit circle give exactly zero gain at 50 Hz: numerator 1 - 1.61803 z^-1 + z^-2.
Poles at radius r = 0.95 at the same angle make the notch narrow: denominator 1 - 1.53713 z^-1 + 0.9025 z^-2.
Checked: gain 0 at 50 Hz, 0.779 at 45 and 55 Hz, about 1 at 10 and 100 Hz; -3 dB width about 8 Hz, close to (1 - r) fs / pi.
Larger r gives a narrower notch but longer ringing: about 0.18 s to settle at r = 0.95, 0.92 s at r = 0.99.
Harmonics are handled by cascading another notch, e.g. at 100 Hz; a 10-point moving average kills all multiples of 50 Hz but blurs the ECG.
The course chain: sampling, quantization, LTI and convolution, z-transform, DFT/FFT, FIR/IIR design, structures, multirate, fixed point, applications.
lessons.tip: Before an exam, design one notch filter completely by hand, from w0 to the difference equation, and check a few gains with a calculator. That single exercise revises poles, zeros, frequency response and structures in one go.
lessons.task: Design a 50 Hz notch for audio sampled at 8000 Hz with r = 0.98. Compute w0, cos(w0), the numerator and denominator coefficients and the DC gain normalisation. If you have Python, evaluate the gain at 40, 50 and 60 Hz and estimate the notch width with (1 - r) fs / pi.

quiz.q: Where should the zeros of a 50 Hz notch filter be placed at fs = 500 Hz?
options: On the unit circle at angles +-0.2 pi
Outside the unit circle at angle 0
quiz.explain: w0 = 2 pi x 50 / 500 = 0.2 pi, and zeros on the unit circle at that angle make the response exactly zero at 50 Hz.

quiz.q: What happens if the pole radius r is moved from 0.95 to 0.99?
options: The notch becomes narrower but the filter rings longer
The notch becomes wider and settles faster
quiz.explain: Poles closer to the unit circle narrow the notch but the transient decays like r^n, taking about 0.92 s instead of 0.18 s to settle.

quiz.q: Why is the numerator divided by 1.0454 in the final design?
options: To move the zeros onto the unit circle
To make the gain exactly 1 at DC
quiz.explain: Without normalisation the DC gain is 0.38197 / 0.36537 = 1.0454, so dividing the numerator by it gives a DC gain of 1.

quiz.q: A 10-point moving average at fs = 500 Hz removes 50 Hz hum. What is its main drawback for ECG?
options: It also low-pass filters the ECG, e.g. gain 0.759 at 20 Hz
quiz.explain: Its zeros at multiples of 50 Hz kill the hum and harmonics, but it also attenuates useful content (0.936 at 10 Hz, 0.759 at 20 Hz), blurring the QRS.

quiz.q: Which approximate formula estimates the -3 dB width of the notch?
quiz.explain: For poles close to the unit circle, the width is about (1 - r) fs / pi = 0.05 x 500 / pi = 7.96 Hz, matching the measured 8 Hz.
